data.title: A Boat's Purpose

images.altText: A bronze outline of a raft sits in concrete with bathrooms and other concrete features.
images.title: A Boat's Purpose
images.caption: What boat are you taking down the river?

data.bodyText:
For hundreds of years, humans have been boating down rivers. Your goal or objective on the river determines the watercraft.

If you’re an angler looking to safely get to where the fish are, you will want a drift boat. Drift boats are a common sight to see floating down the Snake River—there is usually a fishing pole nearby.

Native Americans built and used bull boats to transport meat from a successful hunt, fish they caught, and harvested plants. It could successfully move these items downstream or across the river. This sort of innovation and engineering has allowed tribes to thrive in areas like the Great Plains and Rocky Mountain regions.

A river raft is one of the most popular boats used to transport excited visitors down the river. Two large oars maneuver the rafts through the dynamic waters of the Snake. If you are one of the thousands of visitors who get to experience the park on a guided float trip, you’re likely to be in a river raft.

Here, bronze, in-ground sculptures give you a sense of the size and shape of these different water vessels. Could you navigate the riverways in a bull boat? Will you catch a fish from a drift boat? Or will you see the Teton range from the seat of a river raft?
data.audioDescription: The southern portion of the Moose Landing plaza offers a unique opportunity to learn about the different types of watercraft used to navigate the river. Spaced throughout this area are 3 bronze, life-size, 2-dimensional boat sculptures of a drift boat, bull boat, and river raft. The bronze sits flush with the concrete sidewalk so you can move on top of these different boats. At each in-ground boat are 3 4-sided wooden posts of varying heights, spaced out by 4 to 5 feet, describing the function and purpose of each type of watercraft. At each boat, the shortest post (about 4 feet high) has the name of the boat in large text laser cut into the wood running vertically along the side. The lettering is dark brown from being burnt during the laser process. One side contains a small, simple graphic, laser cut into the wood, of a boat over water and text. The text reads: Every type of boat is a solution to a complex problem. The other two posts are about 5 feet and 6 feet high. A 1 ½ foot-tall graphic wraps around the top of the two posts, providing further insight into each type of boat and how it solves a unique problem on the water. The graphics are made up of photographs of people on the river and a series of simple line-drawn graphics and text. Purple, orange, and white are the common colors used. The southernmost bronze boat and posts feature the drift boat. Starting with the southernmost post, the first graphic is a drift boat in water as seen from above. The text “Drift Boat” borders the top of the circle that the graphic is in. Text below reads: Solving Problems How do they do it? Moving right around the post, a graphic shows a person in a drift boat from the side rowing in water. Below, text reads: Steering With skillful use of the oars, the boat’s pilot maneuvers the boat across swift currents and into slow eddies. The smooth surface of the boat’s bottom allows it to spin on top of the water, moving easily. Continuing right, the graphic is of a drift boat floating through water with fish swimming as seen from above. Below, text reads: Finding Fish Drift boats sit high in the water so anglers can see the fish more easily. The bow and stern both offer high perches for people to stand. The final side of the graphic is of a person fishing in a drift boat with fish and the river bottom below. Below the graphic, text reads: Stopping Anchors help to control speed: lowering the anchor is a little bit slows you down while dropping it all the way lets you stay in one spot to fish longer. The high front and back help to keep water out of the boat. The northernmost post has a graphic of an aerial view of a drift boat in water with oars to the side and fish swimming. Large text beneath the graphic reads, “Drift Boat”. The other three sides of the panel are of one large photograph of 3 people fly fishing from a drift boat in the Snake River with trees and the Teton Range in the background. There are text boxes and a small outset photograph of a trout swimming near the bottom of the river. The three text boxes on the photograph read: Fish thrive in the Snake River’s clean, clear, and turbulent waters. They feed on insects and other food among the bottom’s rolling rocks, in the current, and at the water’s surface. The number one job for a drift boat is to bring people to the fish safely. Reading the River Watch for “seams” in the current, where you can see the rough texture of swift water as it meets smoother, slow water. Seams are often where the fish are found. It’s also where smaller boats, like kayaks, can flip. Moving north, the next bronze boat and set of posts highlight the bull boat. It is next to a small inner island of river rocks and native plants. A 7-foot-wide, 3-foot-deep flat rock sits along the island’s edge as a bench. Starting with the southernmost post the first side shows a bull boat with a paddle from above, floating on water framed in a circle. Text about the circle reads, “Bull Boat”. Beneath the graphic text reads: Solving Problems Bull boats solve the specific problem of keeping heavy and bulky materials dry while crossing a river. How do they do it? To the right, the next side shows a simple outline of aspen leaves in a circle. Below the graphic, text reads: Building locally Using plants that grow along the Snake River and its tributaries—willow, alder, or aspen—bull boats can be made when and where they’re needed. The next side of the panel shows a simple outline of a bull moose in a circle. Below, text reads: Hunting After hunting elk, bison, or moose, traditional bull boats help transport the meat. After skinning the animal and harvesting the meat, people build the boat from branches and use the animal’s skin as the boat covering. Then they float their freshly harvested food downstream, leaving the boat at the water’s edge. The final panel shows a simple line drawing of a bull boat partially in water framed in a circle. Below, text reads: Crossing currents With their bowl-shaped bottoms, bull boats can move across the current and downstream. They are used mostly during times of low water. On the northernmost post, the first side of the graphic wrap is of an aerial view of a bull boat with paddles in water. Large text beneath the graphic reads, “Bull Boat”. The other 3 sides of the panel are of one large black and white photograph of a woman floating down a river in a bull boat using one paddle. There are text boxes on each side of the photograph and a small circular-shaped photograph of a river with fallen trees in the water. The 3 text boxes on the photograph read: Native Americans in the Great Plains and Rocky Mountains have traditionally made bull boats from materials found along the water’s edge. Different tribes have moved through this valley as part of traditional seasonal rounds to fish, hunt, and collect plants. Bull boats usually transported food that’s been harvested—meat, fish, and plants—across the river or to points downstream. Reading the River The Snake River’s swift, cold water and shifting channels create a substantial barrier for people and animals. Bull boat design is an example of traditional ecological knowledge. Native innovation and engineering have produced this design that’s specific to the task and place. Moving north, beneath your feet is a life-size bronze river raft, flush with the concrete as if you were seeing it from above. The southernmost post shows a simple raft graphic with oars in water from an aerial view. It has a circle border with text that reads, “River Raft”. Below the graphic, text reads: Solving Problems River rafts solve the problem of how to move lots of visitors safely and quickly down the river for pleasure. How do they do it? The next side of the post is a simple graphic of a person rowing a river raft in water as seen from the side. It is bordered by a circle. Below, text reads: Flexible Materials The raft’s inflated rubber tubes create a strong and rigid structure. Yet they are also resilient and lightweight. The next side is a simple graphic of two raft oars lying vertically next to each other with a circle border. Below, text reads: Oars and Frame The rafts are stable and fast, big and bulky. The aluminum metal frame and oars—and the highly trained guide—do the heavy work of moving the craft across the current. The final side of the graphic has a simple scene of a river flowing towards mountains encased in a circle border. Below, text reads: Reading the Signs Rubber rafts are stable, even when bumping into most obstacles. You may notice V shapes in the water. Knowing what they mean helps experienced paddlers and guides avoid dangers. There are two smaller graphics with descriptive text to the right of them. The top graphic shows water flowing through a narrow channel towards mountains. The river current, represented by simple lines, form the shape of a “V” pointing downstream. The accompanying text reads: V’s pointing downstream usually show the safest way to go. Water flowing between two obstructions makes the V shape. Below, the second graphic shows same graphic but with a “V” shape in the water pointing upstream. The accompanying text reads: V’s pointing upstream often indicate a rock or log in the water. When the rock or log is deeper, there may be a V behind the obstacle indicating a “hole” to be avoided. The northmost post has a graphic of river raft with oars floating in water as seen from above with the text, “River Raft” below. The other 3 sides of the wrapped graphic is a photograph of a river raft, full of people, floating down the Snake River. The guide is standing, pointing towards something. There are 3 text boxes, one on each side. Two of the text boxes have accompanying photos in a circle border. The first smaller photo shows a large log jam in a river. The text box reads: Reading the River The Snake River in Grand Teton National Park is dangerous due to unique river dynamics—shifting channels, downed trees, and fluctuating water. Look along the banks where the river is cutting away the land for obstacles that the raft avoids. The next text box reads: River rafts move a lot of people down the river safely, especially when the river’s course is ever-changing. The boat’s guide uses the oars to move the raft side-to-side to stay in the current. The second small photograph featured is a historic black and white photo of a river raft with guides and guests floating on the Snake River. The accompanying text reads: In the 1950’s—during the post-war WWII park-visiting-boom—the first scenic float trips launched on the Snake River in Grand Teton. Modified war-surplus rubber rafts that were 27 feet long could carry over 50 visitors at a time. Fewer than 500 people floated in the first few years. With multiple raft companies forming in the 1960’s and 1970’s, floating the Snake became a new way of experiencing the park. Today, more than 70,000 people are on the river each year.

data.title: A Patchwork of Habitats
data.listingDescription: Stop 4 (Jackson Lake Overlook): What effects do repeated fires have on a landscape, and why is that important for forests and wildlife? Explore our Fire History page to see a map of fires in the park over the last several decades, including the ones Diane and Ron discuss.

images.altText: A map shows different fires over the years in Grand Teton National Park, which overlap and burn into one another.
images.caption: Many fires over the last 100 years have burned in Grand Teton, overlapping and burning into one another. Visit the Fire History webpage to learn more (www.nps.gov/grte/learn/nature/firehistory.htm).

data.bodyText: Stop 4 (Jackson Lake Overlook): What effects do repeated fires have on a landscape, and why is that important for forests and wildlife? Explore our Fire History page to see a map of fires in the park over the last several decades, including the ones Diane and Ron discuss.
data.audioDescription:
Host: As you look across to the west shore of Jackson Lake, you can see evidence of several fires that have burned over there-if you look carefully. Far to the south, you can see where the Waterfalls Canyon Fire burned almost 50 years ago, in 1974. Much of that area is now dense lodgepole pine forest or shrubs. The dark forested area that you see across the lake and extending south, which is left if you're facing the lake, is all regrowth from that fire. If you look directly across, you'll see that forest grow patchy and disappear, where a fire burned in 2000. Farther to the north, which is to the right, you can see burned trees on the ridgeline from the 2016 Berry Fire. Explore the fire history page on Grand Teton's website to see a map of how these fires overlap one another. Here's Diane Abendroth, the park's fire ecologist, and Ron Steffens, a fire analyst in the park, to discuss what we're seeing on the other side of the lake. Diane mentions the Moran fire in 2000, which burned even farther south than the Waterfalls Canyon Fire-you can see it from Colter Bay.

Diane: You can see across the lake now that there are a lot of little trees out there, and some areas where shrubs still dominate, and some areas where the trees are actually getting bigger. And then if you look to the north of that fire and to the south, you'll see some fires that burned in the year 2000. That's the Moran Fire, the Wilcox Fire, and the Glade Fire. Those were lightning caused fires, but those weren't fires that the Park Service was attempting to allow to just burn. But they suppressed them in a way that included letting them go up into the rocks of the Tetons, while protecting some cabins and some values in the lower elevations. But Jackson Lake is a pretty good fuel break. And if you look at the whole area on the backside of the lake, people really haven't played a very big role in fire there. And it looks like maybe it looked before settlers came and started to interfere with the landscape.

Ron: The other thing we learned with the waterfalls canyon fire and the fires afterwards is the value of. Diversity of a fire landscape. So the fire in 1974. 26 years later in 2000 there are fires burning from the south and from the north. And as those fires burned into the Waterfalls Canyon area, there was a younger forest. It is much more shaded because of the density of the regeneration of the forest, and both of those fires slowed and went out. So we're able to demonstrate and learn from the value of a diverse landscape with a diverse pattern of burns.

Host: This type of area, where several different fires overlap like a patches on a quilt, creates excellent wildlife habitat. Many species appreciate recently-burned areas for the lush plant regrowth and the high populations of wood-boring insects and small mammals. Perhaps even more important is the juxtaposition of different habitats, where old growth forest opens out to a grassy clearing, or dense young lodgepoles border a shrubby meadow. Wildlife love these so-called "edge habitats", from elk and deer that want to graze in meadows but shelter in the forest, or raptors that want to nest in the trees and hunt rodents in the open. The series of fires we've seen on the west shore of the lake is ideal for creating this mix of habitats where wildlife can thrive. Here are Ron and Diane to explain more about what we can learn from this type of landscape:

Ron: The landscape where you get a diversity of forest ages and a diversity of regeneration that supports the wildlife that people have come to cherish here. All landscapes have a cycle. Fire is such a dramatic way of resetting that cycle that I think it lets us humbly look around and learn that we need to learn from this place.

Diane: When you have towns or people's homes or other kinds of developments in the mix, with the public lands and forests, it makes it kind of dangerous to have fire on the landscape too. But here in the Greater Yellowstone we have just enormous vast areas with nobody's house in the way. And so that makes it possible to see what nature can do on its own. And we don't have to try to interfere.

data.title: A River Changed

images.altText: View point of Jackson Lake Dam with mountains in background.
images.title: View of Jackson Lake Dam
images.caption: View of Jackson Lake Dam

data.bodyText:
Did you know that Jackson Lake Dam was built years before the lake became part of Grand Teton National Park? And that it is managed by the Bureau of Land Reclamation? Jackson Lake has existed at the base of the Tetons for thousands of years, but it was in 1906 that the lake was forever changed. A log crib dam was built, but shortly after failed. In 1916, an earthen dam—built by the Bureau of Land Reclamation—raised the lake by 39 feet. Eventually, the lake, dam, and the Snake River that feeds it became part of the park. The management remains a collaborative effort with water release flows affecting various agencies beyond park borders.

Planning on exploring the river downstream? Travel the route of the Snake River by foot over the in-ground river sculpture beneath your feet. It provides an aerial view of the meandering and braided route of the river.

Jackson Lake and the Snake River have been forever changed by the dam, but the connection people have with these iconic waterways remains.

As you walk along the sidewalk, a two-lane road runs to the north of you, and a simple wooden log fence runs to the south. As you near the sidewalk intersection and the wooden fencing ends, the rocky, dark concrete narrows and turns into an in-ground concrete river sculpture of the Snake River. The surrounding concrete is light brown and smooth. Bronze markers along the concrete river mark significant points. At the beginning, a bronze rectangle marks Jackson Lake Dam. There is also a one foot in diameter raised bronze medallion with text that reads: “Jackson Lake Dam” and a star symbol with text that reads: "You Are Here”. Raised aspen leaves line the top and bottom of the medallion. Moving east on top of the concrete river, large boulders border the sidewalk to the south. 15 feet east of the start of the concrete river, a 24-inch by 48-inch panel, encased in a bronze frame, sits three feet from the ground on top of the boulders, tilted slightly towards the viewer. From this panel you are facing the dam and the mountains. The left third of the panel is dark blue with a light blue graphic of a river channel and text. The text reads: Complicated Compromise It’s a beautiful view—but why is there a dam here? It’s a complex story. The first dam was built in 1906, before any of this land was a national park. As established in 1929, Grand Teton National Park protected just the mountains. Most of this valley—including the Snake River and Jackson Lake—only became part of the national park in 1950. The center two quarters of the image is a historic black and white aerial photograph of the dam, Jackson Lake, the former location of the town Moran, and the Teton Range. Mount Moran is the most prominent peak visible and is labeled with its name and height (12,610 feet/3,844 meters). A small text box labeled “You Are Here” indicated where you are in the photo. Two small text boxes read: There’s been a natural lake in this location for thousands of years. The human-built dam has made the original lake deeper and larger. The town of Moran used to be here. Hundreds of workers lived in the town during dam construction in the early and mid-1900s. The right quarter of the page is solid blue with four circular photographs and text stacked on top of each other. Starting at the top is a historic black and white photograph of the 1916 dam being built. Text to the right of the photograph reads: Controlling Flooding Ranchers downstream lobbied for a dam to control flooding in the early 1900s. A log-crib dam built in 1906 failed within four years. The US Bureau of Reclamation built and opened a new dam in 1916. Below, a photograph shows a water irrigation system watering a crop field. Text to the right reads: Storing Water to Grow Food The new dam stores 847,000 acre-feet of water. It’s released over the summer and fall when Idaho growers downstream need it. One acre-foot of water is about the volume of water that would cover a football field one foot deep. Below is a close-up shot of a trout swimming in shallow water over pebbles. Text to the right reads: Disrupting Fish Movement The dam blocks fish from moving up the Snake River into the lake. Before the dam, fish moved freely between the river and the lake to spawn and feed. Fish still travel downstream—out of the lake and through the dam—but there’s no going back. Below, the final photograph shows a bull moose standing knee deep in water from afar, surrounded by green foliage. Text to the right reads: Changing Life Downstream People, plants, and animals have long relied on spring flooding. The dam changed that natural cycle. Now the park works with the Bureau of Reclamation so that water releases can mimic natural patterns as much as possible. data.title: A River's Story

images.altText: A man looks at multiple exhibit panels overlooking the river at a plaza with trees and rocks.
images.title: A River's Story
images.caption: The Snake River has its own unique story to tell.

data.bodyText:
The Snake River is a dynamic force of nature that has sustained life for thousands of years. The Shoshone, Bannock, and other tribes have long lived along its shores. And the shores are ever-changing—the Snake River carves new routes every year, riverbanks erode, and flow rates fluctuate. The various flows of the river at Pacific Creek also make it a prime spawning area for the native Snake River fine spotted cutthroat trout. The section south of here is one of the most free-flowing sections of the entire river. Legislation like the Wild and Scenic River Act continues to protect this vital part of Grand Teton National Park and the greater ecosystem.

Look out at the flow of the river. Can you see eddies—circular currents—forming along the shore? Can you see insects flying above the water?

Walk along the in-ground, concrete river beneath your feet to travel the journey of the Snake. Bronze medallions point out other Snake River access points. Which braided route will you take? What river obstacles might you encounter?
data.audioDescription: To the left of the bronze panel, the sidewalk leads into a plaza featuring benches, interpretive panels, and physical exhibits that provide information about river ecology. The sidewalk expands and contracts in width as it arcs around a central island of native trees, shrubs, and river rock. Starting to the left of the bronze panel, an in-ground concrete sculpture of the Snake River runs through the plaza. It depicts the river from Pacific Creek Landing to Deadman’s bar. Rockier, darker concrete differentiates the river sculpture from the paved, smooth sidewalk surrounding it. One-foot diameter bronze medallions mark Deadman’s bar and Pacific Creek. Each has raised lettering and willow leaves. The eastern medallion reads: “Deadmans Bar 12 miles (19km) downriver from Pacific Creek” and the western medallion reads: “Pacific Creek You are here” with a raised star shape in the center. Sitting south of the inner island, facing south towards the river, are two large wooden benches about eight feet in length, three feet in depth, with dark brown metal features. The two benches sit about four feet apart. The curved wall bordering the southern edge of the plaza is bordered by approximately 30 feet of wooden log fencing, followed by alternating sections of stacked rock walls (about three feet high) and three feet by three feet boulders. The large boulders hold three interpretive panels, each 24 inch by 48 inch and encased in bronze. They tilt slightly towards the viewer. Starting at the furthest east panel, the left third of the panel reads: Noomi’akwainde Moving from Place to Place The Shoshone Bannock and other tribes have long lived along the length of the Snake River. People have thrived here through a profound knowledge of the seasonal changes passed down by memory from the depths of time. Most of the bands, families, and individuals traditionally came in early summer and stayed until the snows returned. Then they moved to lower valleys for the winter. Some preferred to stay longer. People moved from places to place with moveable houses—all these places were equally called home. Below is a small circle logo for the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes of the Fort Hall Reservation. The logo has a braided border and a graphic of an indigenous man in the center. Along the border are the words, “Shoshone-Bannock Tribes of the Fort Hall Reservation Idaho”. Next to the logo, text reads: This panel developed in cooperation with the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes of the Fort Hall Reservation. The text is on a solid green background with a darker green graphic of braided river channels in the background. The right two-thirds of the panel are divided into four rectangular photographs with text boxes on the bottom half of the image. The top left photo is of a bull moose with velvet antlers standing knee deep in a body of water surrounded by grasses and willows. The slightly transparent text box reads: Daaza (Shoshone) Taza (Bannock Summer When the herd animals migrated freely across the open valley, the people monitored them with care and hunted for what they needed. There is archaeological evidence for over 12,000 years of hunting. Other tribes traveled through here during this time for hunting and trade with the Shoshone and Bannock. The bottom left image shows five female common mergansers in glassy water swimming to the left. They have thin, long orange beaks, light brown heads with spiky feathers, and grey body feathers. The slightly transparent text box reads: Dawani (Shoshone) Tawano (Bannock) Spring Ice thaws and migrating ducks return. The people collect the tender roots of bitterroot plants. In spring, fresh watercress and clover greens are tender and sweet. To catch trout and other fish, family groups set up fishing weirs at the mouths of small creeks and streams, like Pacific Creek. Camas Bulbs are gathered when in bloom. These traditions continue today. The top right photo is a close-up image of a huckleberry plant. It shows small branches with leaves and six small, round, smooth berries. The slightly transparent text box reads: Yevani (Shoshone) Yevano (Bannock) Fall Berries—pogopisha in Bannock, and bogombe in Shoshone—ripen in nearby mountain valleys. Families pass down knowledge about the exact timing and places to collect huckleberries, elderberry, currants, serviceberries, and other berries. The bottom right photo is a winter scene with a river flowing across the photo. Pine trees and downed trees line the river banks. The slightly transparent text box reads: Dommo (Shoshone) Tomm (Bannock) Winter Winter camps were chosen for their nearness to water and protection from the elements. Here the Shoshone and Bannock people could relax, finding enjoyment in traditional winter activities. This is the time especially for storytelling, teaching, and making things. Moving right, is the second panel. The left quarter of the panel is solid green, featuring text and a darker green graphic of braided river channels. The text reads: River of Movement Side to side, up and down. This section of the Snake River is on the move. The river erodes its banks and changes course year, and sometimes every week. It caves downward into cobbled and gravelly soils. The center two quarters of the panel is an aerial photograph of a braided section of the Snake River. Green trees and fields are on either side. Sand bars with some foliage appear as islands in between the braided channels. Four text boxes about the river overlay the image. Moving clockwise from the top, the four text boxes read: Outer Bends The river has more power as it swings wide. It carves away at the outer bends of the river. Look for trees that have fallen here. Inner Bends The river slows on the inside curves. Rocks, sand, and wood—carried in the river—drop out here as the water loses energy. Changing Channels Sandbars in the river change position. Channels can open and close from year to year. Water levels vary from day to day, even hour to hour as rain falls or snow melts upstream Freestone River The bed of this river rolls. Small, rounded cobbles on the river bottom create a kinetic chorus. Listen for the sound of the rocks moving when you’re in a boat. The right quarter of the panel is solid green, with text and a 3D bronze feature about eddies. You can touch and feel the carving of water flowing, swirling, and the different-sized rocks along the riverbanks. The sculpted flow of the river is labeled as “Fast Water” with an arrow pointing down. The point where the flowing water meets the eddy is labeled as “Seam”. A long arrow pointing down then looping back up shows the flow of the eddy (indicated by the texture of the water) and is labeled as “Eddy”. Below the bronze feature is text that reads: These circular currents form behind any obstacle—a boulder, an island, or a bend in the river. The seam is where fast water meets the slow water. Spot an eddy by looking for water moving in the opposite direction from the main channel. Moving right about 15 feet is the third panel. The left quarter of the panel is solid green, with a dark green graphic of braided river channels and text. The text reads: Think like a fish Pacific Creek is a spawning area for Snake River fine-spotted cutthroat trout—a true native of this river. They flourish here with all of the different water speeds and insects hatching. The center two quarters of the panel are a large close-up photograph of a Snake River fine-spotted cutthroat trout swimming in shallow water. The photograph is taken in such a way that you can see underwater and slightly above water. The water is clear with green-blue hues and multi-colored pebbles of various sizes on the river bottom. The fish takes up two-thirds of the bottom half of the photograph. It is a pale orange-yellow with small black spots over the top of its back. On top of the image are four text boxes. Moving clockwise from the top, the four text boxes read: Fast The current is like a fast-moving conveyor belt of food. Cutthroat trout dash into the swift current to eat. Shallow Trout come to feed where the water cruises quickly through the shallows. They can’t stay in these riffles for long, but when the insects are hatching, it’s the place to be. Slow Near islands and banks, the water slows. It’s easier for trout to rest here while they wait for insects to hatch. Deep Oxygen in the cold deep pools benefits fish. Here they can rest and breathe easily, safe from eagles and osprey. The right quarter of the panel is solid green with text at the bottom and a bronze 3D feature about insects. Feel the flowing water with a grasshopper at the water’s edge. It is labeled in raised bronze, “Grasshopper”. Below the flowing water are smooth river rocks of various shapes, with three insects and their names. The insects are labeled as “mayfly”, “stonefly”, and “caddisfly”. The text below the bronze feature reads: What’s to eat? Trout gulp down whatever they can fit in their mouths. Mayflies, caddisflies, and stoneflies hatch then rise to the surface. Fish have to move fast before the insects fly away. Trout also eat land insects and small mammals like voles, that enter the river. Here, the plaza area changes into an exhibit about elk, wolves, and river ecology.

Excerpt from "Diary of a Dude Wrangler": "Some of the happiest hours I have ever spent and some of the most profitable, philosophically speaking, have been spent on the top rail of a corral fence, the favorite sitting-place of all Westerners if they have nothing else to do-and, sometimes, even when they have something else to do. I don't know which makes you the more homesick for the West when you are away from it: the thought of shadowy forests and cool water, or the recollection of warm dust and the top rail of a corral fence and, on Sunday afternoons, the shady side of a cabin or saddle-shed, where you sit with some chosen companions and converse at intervals."

data.title: A World of Fish

images.altText: Two visitors look towards the dam (out of picture) standing by interpretive panels and a bench.
images.title: A World of Fish
images.caption: Casting a fly? Learn how to properly catch and release a fish.

data.bodyText: The Snake River’s headwaters begin just north of here near the south entrance of Yellowstone. Although the dam might have changed the lake and flow of the Snake River, it continues to provide life. Plants thrive along the river's shores, creating habitat for a wide variety of animals. Fish, like the native cutthroat trout, benefit from the oxygen-rich water. The river provides countless recreational opportunities to visitors from around the world. Frequently on display from this overlook, anglers can be seen casting just below the dam. New and longtime anglers can review best fishing practices shared on educational panels at this overlook.
data.audioDescription: The sidewalk continues south toward the plaza and river for about 100 feet before turning sharply east, revealing the dam, river, and the plaza. The Jackson Lake Dam, with water roaring out at its base, is fully visible. Mount Moran and several other peaks rise behind the dam. The Snake River, which calms after passing the dam, flows in front of you heading east. There are some bushes, large boulders, and a maintenance gate before reaching a large rocky beach area that extends approximately 250 feet west toward the dam and 70 feet south to the river. As you enter the plaza from the north, to the left is a center island and a two-foot-wide by three-and-a-half-foot-tall bronze panel, vertically positioned a few feet off the ground against a five-foot-tall granite boulder speckled with shades of white, black, and grey. The bronze panel displays a map of Grand Teton National Park’s waterways, text, and other symbols, all engraved into bronze that you can touch and feel. The engraving depicts the location of the Snake River and the various lakes within the park. The map is oriented running north to south. Small diamond-shaped engravings near the waterways indicate the locations of other boat launches, such as Pacific Creek, Deadmans Bar, and Moose Landing. A small star shape indicates your current location with text that reads, “You Are Here”. At the top of the panel, a small arrow points north above text that reads, “To headwaters in Yellowstone (39 miles, 44km)”. At the bottom of the panel, located next to the Snake River engraving, a small arrow points in the southwest direction below text that reads, “To Pacific Ocean (1201 miles, 1933 km)”. The words, “Jackson Lake Dam” run vertically along the left side of the panel in extra-large text. The panel bends 90 degrees around the left side of the rock and is approximately one-third the width of the front side. At the top, engraved into the bronze, text reads: This river landing revitalization was made possible by a public-private partnership between Grand Teton National Park and Grand Teton National Park Foundation. Below is a smaller panel with information about indigenous words related to the river with silhouettes of aspen leaves and branches in the background. The text reads: Baa gadede (Shoshone) “Paa katede (Bannock)” “sitting water” Jackson Lake This lake and river and all the surrounding land, plants, and animals hold special cultural significance to many of today’s American Indian tribes. Jackson Lake—in smaller form—has been at the base of the mountains for thousands of years. The dam, first built in 1906, profoundly affects the river and all the life in and around it. In the bottom right corner, an eight-inch-tall branch of an aspen tree with a partial line border is engraved into the bronze. Entering the plaza from the north, to your right are multiple boulders, some large enough to sit on like a bench, that create a border wall for about 15 feet. A 48-inch by 24-inch interpretive panel about fish sits on top of two large boulders spaced two and a half feet apart. It is slightly tilted towards the plaza and has a metal frame. The left quarter of the panel is solid blue with a light blue graphic representing a braided river channel. The text reads: A World of Fish The flow of spring snowmelt reshapes the river’s islands and banks. With water moving at different speeds, the river can support a variety of fish—which are all connected in a food web with plants and insects. The right three-quarters of the panel is an illustration of the numerous fish species found in the river. The top third of the illustration is of the dam and some of the northern peaks of the Teton range. Mount Moran is prominent in the skyline. In the clear blue sky of the illustration is text that reads: Snowmelt It all starts with the snow melting in the mountains during spring and early summer. A rush of high water pulses down the river. Water from snowmelt can carry extra oxygen due to its cold temperature. The oxygen-rich water helps this specially adapted fish—and the plants and insects they eat. The bottom two-thirds of the illustration is a cross-sectional view beneath the surface of the Snake River. Twenty-one different species of fish, some insects, and a small pelican are illustrated below and on the water. The river bottom is full of small, smooth river rocks of muted earth tones. The fish are swimming in all directions. The different types of fish shown are the brown trout, Utah chub, Utah sucker, Paiute sculpin, speckled dace, mountain whitefish, Snake River fine-spotted cutthroat trout, redside shiner, and lake trout. To the left of the panel, three steps made of large flat rocks lead down to a gravel beach along the river to the base of the dam. After the steps, an approximately three-foot-high stacked rock wall borders the plaza. It curves slightly as it borders the outer edge of the sidewalk for about twenty feet. The sidewalk is about seven to eight feet wide at this point in the plaza. A large wooden bench with metal features, approximately eight feet long and two and a half feet deep, sits about six feet back from the rock wall. Behind the bench is the small inner island. Continuing left of the stacked rock wall are more large boulders about three feet by three feet in size. A 48-inch by 24-inch interpretive panel about the history of fishing sits on top of two large boulders spaced two and a half feet apart. It is slightly tilted towards the plaza and has a metal frame. The left quarter of the panel is solid blue with a light blue graphic representing a braided river channel. The text reads: Our People Are Fishing People The Shoshone-Bannock people have been fishing these waters for generation upon generation. We use traditional methods of fishing, but sometimes we use modern materials, too. We create pools in the river—from rocks, willows, steel, concrete—to trap fish. Then we use willow baskets or birch, willow, and pine spears to catch fish from the pool. We pass down this knowledge so that there will be fish here for our children’s children. —Shoshone-Bannock Tribe, 2022 Below is a small circle logo for the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes of the Fort Hall Reservation. It has a braided border with a graphic of an indigenous man in the center. Along the border are the words, “Shoshone-Bannock Tribes of the Fort Hall Reservation Idaho”. Next to the logo, text reads: This panel and others were developed in cooperation with the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes of the Fort Hall Reservation. The center two quarters of the panel is a photograph of young Shoshone-Bannock Tribal members practicing traditional spearfishing along a river. Two young boys wear casual athletic wear, each holding a twenty-foot wooden spear. One of the boys is standing in the river near the shore with a fish, barely visible in the water, at the end of its spear. The second boy is running with the spear towards the river. A small text box in the bottom right corner reads: You use what sustains you and what can be sustained. So you can come back next year. —Bobette Haskett, Shoshone-Bannock Tribal Member Young Shoshone-Bannock Tribal members are learning to spear fish on the South Fork of the Salmon River in Idaho. Downstream from Grand Teton National Park, the Snake and Salmon rivers merge into one. The right quarter of the panel is solid blue with a map and text. The map shows the waterways of western Wyoming, Eastern Idaho, and Northern Utah. Yellowstone and Grand Teton National Parks are shown in dark green. The Fort Hall (Shoshone and Bannock Tribes) and Wind River (Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho Tribes) Reservations are shown in white. The Snake River, Bear River, Green River, and Bighorn River are labeled as well as Yellowstone Lake and Great Salt Lake. The text below the map reads: The Shoshone-Bannock’s original territories extend bar beyond this map. Today, the tribes are based in Idaho’s eastern Snake River Plain on the Fort Hall Reservation. Close relatives, the eastern Shoshone, are here in Wyoming on the Wind River Reservation. The Shoshone-Bannock are committed to preserving the fish that are guaranteed to the tribes in treaties. Tribal biologists and ecology program staff make great efforts to maintain and enhance fisheries. A large boulder separates this panel from the next. A 48-inch by 24-inch interpretive panel about how to hold a fish sits on top of two large boulders spaced two and a half feet apart. It is slightly tilted towards the plaza and has a metal frame. The left quarter of the panel is solid blue with a light blue graphic representing a braided river channel. The text reads: How to Hold a Fish Catch-and-release fishing is a delicate operation for the person fishing and the fish. Special techniques and equipment are useful for anglers who want to catch fish and then return them to the river. Your careful handling helps give these beautiful creatures a safe and quick return to their watery world. The rest of the panel is made up of photographs, text, and a bronze feature. The main photograph takes up about three-quarters of the panel. It’s a shot looking over the surface of the river with trees and the riverbank visible on the other side. On the left side of the photograph, three text boxes with smaller circular photographs explain the catch-and-release process. The top circular photograph shows an angler standing shin deep in a river in waders, casting a fishing rod. The text accompanying the photo reads: Catch Hook only the fish’s lip using barbless hooks with artificial lures and flies—so that its mouth stays undamaged and functional. Keep the fish in the water as long as possible—to allow its gills to get oxygen from the water. The plaza reconnects to the main sidewalk and runs east about 150 feet. A simple wooden log fence runs along the south side of the sidewalk. A two-way, paved road runs along the north side of the sidewalk.

data.bodyText:
The AMK Ranch represents the initial phase of vacation homes in Jackson Hole. Homesteaded by John Sargent in 1890, little remains of his lodge and store that served travelers on the road to Yellowstone. All current buildings date to the W. Lewis Johnson era (1926-1936) and the Alfred Berol era (1936-1976). Both Johnson and Berol built large log vacation homes representing two distinct periods of rustic architecture as well as various other cabins and outbuildings.

Berol, president of the Eagle Pencil Company, decorated his lodge with "pencil themed" fixtures including the wrought iron and log chandeliers. The Berols-Alfred, Madeleine, and son, Kenneth (AMK)-sold the property to the National Park Service in 1976 for more than $3 million and a life estate. Today, the ranch houses the University of Wyoming-National Park Service Research Station, hosting researchers studying the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. Attend the Summer Speaker Series on Thursday evenings during summer.
Visit the UW-NPS Research Station website for more information

images.title: Albright Turnout
images.caption: Horace Albright was an intregal figure in the early days of the National Park Service.

data.bodyText:
Albright turnout is one of many scenic viewpoints along the highway through the park. Use turnouts like this one to take photos and enjoy wildlife safely. Do not stop along the road on the main highway to keep you and other visitors safe. Although the Teton Range dominates the landscape, make sure to take in the views from all angles. Blacktail Butte and the Gros Ventre Mountains also tower over the valley.

This turnout and a prominent peak in the Teton Range (visible from this location) are named after Horace M. Albright. Albright would eventually become the second director of the National Park Service. However, his connection to Grand Teton National Park happened when he was the superintendent of Yellowstone. It was in 1923 when Horace and many other prominent figures in the valley gathered in Moose, WY to discuss the future of Jackson Hole. Horace sought to protect this area as a national park and sought out the help of John D. Rockefeller which set in motion a plan that would eventually lead to the creation of our park.    

Biography of Horace Albright

Horace Albright was born in 1890 in California. In 1913, Albright graduated from the University of California, Berkeley and moved to Washington DC to begin working as a clerk for the Secretary of the Interior. Although he worked on park issues right away, his focus became nearly exclusively their issues in 1915. That year he became the assistant of newly hired Stephen Mather. In fact, Mather would not join the department unless Albright agreed to be his assistant in order to “’keep me [Mather] out of jail.’” Together they worked to create a parks bureau that resulted in the creation of the National Park Service (NPS) on August 25, 1916.

In 1917 Stephen Mather became seriously ill from what was likely bipolar depression. This made it so Mather was unable to do the duties as director of the newly formed NPS. During a span between 1917 and 1919, Albright served as acting director.

After Mather could return, Albright took up the jobs of superintendent of Yellowstone and NPS field director. As superintendent, Albright wanted to make Yellowstone a flagship of the agency and demonstrate how a park would be managed under the new National Park Service. Many of the current agency and park-wide policies and functions have roots with Albright. Two of the functions he helped found were visitor services and park museums. He was also instrumental in achieving the enlarged Grand Teton National Park of today.

After Mather suffered a stroke in 1929, Albright became the second director of the NPS. One of his most lasting contributions to the National Park Service was to get all the war department sites placed under NPS control. This solidified the agency’s place as the keeper of both the natural and cultural heritage of the United States of America.

In 1933, Albright left the NPS to work for the United States Potash Company. He retired from the company in 1956. Although he went into the private sector, Albright was always interested and involved in the affairs of national parks. He was even awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1980 for his involvement with the creation of the NPS. Albright died in 1987.
data.audioDescription:
This paved turnout overlooks a sage-dotted plain with the Teton range beyond. The view of the mountains matches the photograph at the bottom of the wayside, which labels the various peaks. Text on the panel reads, "What's in a Name? Many natural features in this region went without names until the 1800s. The Shoshone called the mountain range "Teewinot," meaning "many pinnacles." French Canadian trappers referred to the Grand, Middle, and South Teton as "Les Trois Tetons," or "The Three Breasts." Early explorers called them "Pilot Knobs." Jackson Hole and Jackson Lake honor trapper David Jackson. The 1872 Hayden Expedition named Leigh and Jenny lakes after its guide, Richard Leigh, and his Shoshone wife. The expedition even named the Grand Teton "Mount Hayden" briefly." To the right of the text is a historic photograph of a group of six men in front of a white canvas tent. The men stand or sit on packing cases. Other cases and bedrolls are scattered around. The caption reads, "Hayden Expedition, 1872." Across the middle of the panel are five historic photographic portraits of men. The first one on the left shows a man in park service uniform with a broad brimmed hat and knee-length top boots. The caption reads, "Horace M. Albright served as the National Park Service director, 1929-33." The next shows a man in suit and waistcoat, his dark hair parted in the middle. He wears a dark mustache. The caption reads, "Novelist Owen Wister was an early Jackson Hole visitor." The middle portrait shows an older American Indian man wearing a full-feathered headdress and many strings of beads. The caption reads, "Chief Joseph. The Nez Perce Indians hunted in the surrounding area."

The next photo shows a man with sleeked-down fair hair and wearing wire-rimmed glasses. The caption reads, "William O. Owen led the first documented ascent of the Grand Teton in 1898." The last photo shows a man with full beard wearing an overcoat and black hat. The caption reads, "Thomas Moran sketched and painted scenes for the Hayden Expedition." Along the photo of the mountain range at the bottom labels identify major peaks. From left to right they are Albright Peak, 10,552 ft.; Static Peak 11,303 ft.; Buck Mountain 11,938 ft. (George A. Buck was a geological recorder in a 1898 mapping expedition.) Next in line are Mount Wister 11,490 ft.; South Teton 12,514 ft.; and Middle Teton 12,804 ft. Then are Nez Perce 11,901 ft.; Grand Teton 13,770 ft.; Mount Owen 12,928 ft. and Teewinot Mountain 12,325 ft. The final peaks at the right are St. John 11,430 ft., named for Orestes St. John who served as a geologist with the Hayden Expedition and Mount Moran 12,605 ft.

data.bodyText: The Bar BC was one of the first dude ranches in Jackson Hole, and perhaps the most iconic. Today, it's the oldest one still standing. It was founded in 1912 by Struthers Burt and Harold Carncross, Easterners who emigrated to Wyoming. Burt and his wife, Katharine Newlin Burt, were prolific writers, so their ranch attracted a more artistic and literary set. The clientele tended to be wealthy Easterners who wanted a rustic vacation experience, away from the constraints of high society. Many former guests bought ranches in the area, and some of their families are still in the valley today. During the heyday of dude ranching in the 1910s and 20s, many other ranches operated in Jackson Hole and throughout the West. At its height in the 1920s, the Bar BC was actually one of the valley's largest employers, hiring over fifty people to help run the ranch each summer. The industry declined as tourism dropped during the Great Depression and World War II, though there are still some dude ranches in Jackson Hole today.
data.audioDescription:
Host: The Bar BC was one of the first dude ranches in Jackson Hole, and perhaps the most iconic. Today, it's the oldest one still standing. It was founded in 1912 by Struthers Burt and Horace Carncross, Easterners who emigrated to Wyoming. Burt and his wife, Katharine Newlin Burt, were prolific writers, so their ranch attracted a more artistic and literary set. The clientele tended to be wealthy Easterners who wanted a rustic vacation experience, away from the constraints of high society. Many former guests bought ranches in the area, and some of their families are still in the valley today. During the heyday of dude ranching in the 1910s and 20s, many other ranches operated in Jackson Hole and throughout the West. At its height in the 1920s, the Bar BC was actually one of the valley's largest employers, hiring over fifty people to help run the ranch each summer. The industry declined as tourism dropped during the Great Depression and World War II, though there are still some dude ranches in Jackson Hole today.

Excerpt from "Jackson Hole Journal": "You couldn't see the ranch as you started toward the Gros Ventres, with the Tetons and evening at your back. It looked as though you would have to travel straight across the valley for hot miles of sagebrush to those further mountains. Then suddenly came the second bench, a prehistoric riverbank, running neat as a dam north and south, then the steep road down a gully in the jolting wagon between larkspur and mules-ears, with perhaps a last decadent little snowbank still lingering in the draw-the whole panorama of river valley opening out below. Then finally you come down the first bench right into the ranch itself-the sod of tarpaper-roofed cabins, the corrals and saddle shed and barns and ditches and willows and big pines and aspen groves and the shining square of the swimming pool dug out of the flat between cabins and river. It was coming home with a vengeance."

data.title: Arizona Meadows Turnout
data.listingDescription: This wet meadow turns blue violet in the early summer when blue camas blooms. Shoshone Indians harvested the bulbs once the flowers bloomed so that they did not confuse the plant with death camas that could be a very deadly mistake! The roasted bulbs formed an important part of their diet. Today, the meadow is an oasis surrounded by lodgepole pine forest.

images.caption: Blue Camas in Bloom

data.bodyText: This wet meadow turns blue violet in the early summer when blue camas blooms. Shoshone Indians harvested the bulbs once the flowers bloomed so that they did not confuse the plant with death camas that could be a very deadly mistake! data.audioDescription: This wayside in a turnout on the east side of the road looks out over a large, flat meadow, surrounded by conifer forest. Low mountains are in the distance. The sign shows a photo of the meadow filled with bright blue flowers on tall stalks surrounded by grass-like vegetation. The text reads, "From Bulbs to Flour. Blooms of blue camas blanket this moist meadow during summer. Shoshone Indians and other tribes gathered the "quamash" plant's bulbs and dried or roasted them. They waited for the plants to bloom, because the bulbs of a similar plant, death camas, are fatally poisonous. Indians ate the bulbs or ground them into flour to make cakes or biscuits-important additions to their diet of elk, trout, and berries."This meadow may once have been a pond. You may not see water today, but the ground is too wet for trees to grow. In the future, this meadow may become drier and a forest may flourish." In the lower left corner is an historic photo of an American Indian woman sitting beside a large pile of bulbs. She wears a kerchief on her head and has a stone pestle in her right hand. The caption reads, "Annie Yellow Bear grinds camas bulbs into meal about 1890."

images.title: Amphitheater Lake

data.bodyText:
Planning Your Trip

A trip into the backcountry requires advance planning. 

 

When planning a backcountry camping trip in Grand Teton National Park, backpackers should expect to travel no more than 2 miles per hour. Add an additional hour for every 1,000 feet of elevation gain. Trip planning that requires going over more than one pass in a day is not recommended.

All backcountry camping requires a permit. Backcountry camping permits are issued on a first-come, first-served basis no more than one day before the start of your trip. Apply for a permit at the Colter Bay Visitor Center, the Craig Thomas Discovery and Visitor Center, or the Jenny Lake Ranger Station. Climbing permits are NOT required, but backcountry camping permits are required for all climbing that involves overnight camping. Backcountry camping permits while climbing or mountaineering must be obtained at the Jenny Lake Ranger Station during the summer.

Park-approved bear canisters must be used in the backcountry. The park provides canisters free of charge for use in the park. Visit the backcountry reservations page to learn more about the reservation process and submit a reservation. To learn more about current conditions visit the Jenny Lake Ranger Station or call 307-739-3399 to talk to a ranger.

Backcountry Video

Watch the park's video to help plan your adventure to the high country in Grand Teton National Park. Learn about safe travel, camping in bear country, clean camping practices and summer weather.

Fees

A fee is charged for all backcountry permit if ordered online or in person. Check the backcountry page for the latest information.

Bears in the Backcountry

Bear-proof canisters are required for overnight stays

Backpackers are required to carry approved bear-resistant canisters except where food storage boxes are provided.
On some specific alpine routes where a climber is bivouacing on a high rocky ledge where bears cannot go, park-approved bear canisters may not be required. Bear-resistant canisters are provided by the park or visitors may use any of the following approved canisters during the overnight stays in the park backcountry.

Watch our video podcast about food storage.

To find out which food storage canisters are currently approved by the Interagency Grizzly Bear Committee, go to the safety in bear country page.

Reservations

Requests for advance reservations are only accepted beginning in January of each year, for the specific date this opens visit the backcountry page. All reservations are processed through Recreation.gov in real-time. To facilitate your reservation experience, please establish an account on Recreation.gov prior to the advance reservation season.

Some camping zones fill quickly. Individual party reservations can consist of up to six people. Groups of 7-12 people must camp in designated group sites indicated on the brochure map. View maps of the backcountry camping zones.

Backcountry Regulations

  • Pets, bicycles, and vehicles are not allowed on trails or in the backcountry.
  • All overnight camping requires a permit.
  • Carry out all of your garbage.
  • Prevent erosion by hiking on established trails. Cutting switchbacks causes soil erosion.
  • Horses have the right-of-way. Step off the trail and remain quiet while horses pass.
  • Observe and photograph wildlife from a safe distance. Do not approach or feed animals.
  • Prevent contamination of waterways by burying feces in a hole 6-8 inches deep at least 200 feet from streams and lakes. Pack out used toilet paper, tampons, sanitary napkins and diapers in sealed plastic bags. Do not bury or burn them.
  • All backpackers must carry and use an approved bear-proof canister. For more information see the bear safety page.

For Your Safety

  • This is bear country. Make bears aware of your presence and avoid surprising them by making loud noises like shouting or singing. Please watch our "Which Bear Did I See?" and "Protect Wildlife, Keep Your Food Safe" videos.
  • Carry drinking water. Bring tablets or water filtration devices to purify water in the backcountry.
  • Be prepared for rapid weather changes; bring rain gear and extra clothing. Thunderstorms occur frequently during the summer. 
  • High elevation may cause breathing difficulties; pace yourself. The best cure for altitude sickness is retreating to a lower elevation.
  • Snow melts gradually, leaving valley trails by mid-June, canyon trails by late July. Be careful crossing snowfields and streams. Do not attempt crossing steep snow without previous experience and the proper equipment.
  • Tell someone where you are going and when you expect to return.
  • Solo hiking and off-trail hiking are not recommended. Check with a ranger for current information on trail conditions.

Avoid Crowds


During July and August trailhead parking areas fill early, especially at South Jenny Lake, String Lake, Lupine Meadows, Death Canyon and Granite Canyon. Parking on natural vegetation results in permanent damage to plants; violators will be ticketed. In paved parking lots, parking illegally will also result in a ticket. An early start will help you avoid parking problems.

images.altText: A historic building, under rehabilitation, sits among sagebrush and trees in front of mountains.
images.caption: Bar BC Dude Ranch

data.bodyText:
The Bar BC Ranch was the second dude ranch in the valley. Started by Struthers Burt and Horace Carncross in 1912, their ranch attracted Eastern Dudes who wanted to experience life in the Old West. Situated on the west bank of the Snake River, the ranch had a swimming hole from water diverted from the river. Today, the park has stabilized many of the cabins. Visitors may wander through the ranch and enjoy a glimpse of early tourist life, but for your safety please do not enter the cabins. Access to the Bar BC Overlook requires a four-wheel drive vehicle.

Ranch Origins

The Bar BC Dude Ranch was the second in the valley. In 1912, Struthers Burt and Horace Carncross each filed for homesteads on 160 acres along the west bank of the Snake River, near the mouth of Cottonwood Creek. Burt, as a noted author, attracted writers and poets to visit his dude ranch.
