data.bodyText:
Fire is part of natural western landscapes. Fire helps regenerate the ecosystem by clearing dense underbrush and opening up the forest to sunlight. The Huck Fire was one of many fires during the summer of 1988 that burned across Yellowstone and the John D. Rockefeller, Jr. Memorial Parkway. Today, notice younger, smaller lodgepole pines and subalpine fir interspersed with older, taller trees. Standing and fallen dead trees remind us that in these semi-arid environments vegetation decays slowly. The patchwork or mosaic here highlights the changes brought about by fire.

Name Origin

One of the many fires sparked during the summer of 1988 - the year of the large wildland fires in Yellowstone National Park. Gale-force winds blew a tree into power lines sparking the fire on Black Saturday, August 20, 1988. The fire was named for nearby Huckleberry Mountain.
data.audioDescription:
Fire: A new Beginning. 247 words

This Wayside faces a low ridge with a meadow at its base. Directly in front of you, the ridge has small conifers growing with some dead trees on the ground and some still standing. To your right is a clear line where an older conifer forest begins.

The background photograph on the panel shows a blackened, burned section of forest with an elk grazing on patches of brown vegetation in the foreground. The caption reads, "Animals, like this elk, frequent recently burned areas." Other text reads, "Fire may seem like the death of a forest, but insects, birds and mammals return soon-just as they did after a wildfire swept through this area in 1988. Free from competition for nutrients and sunshine, new plants transform the mineral-rich soil into a lush carpet. Animals thrive in dense new meadows of native grasses and shrubs. They find shelter in burned tree snags and surrounding forested areas. Fires create new homes, such as snags and downed trees, for wildlife."

In the upper right of the panel are two round, inset photos. The upper one shows an aerial view of a forest with both black and green areas. The caption reads, "Fires burn with varying intensity, leaving a mosaic of burned and unburned vegetation. This combination provides forage and cover for a variety of animals."

The other photo shows a great grey owl perched on a fallen log. It stares directly at us, its feathers fluffed out.

data.title: Inspiration Point
data.listingDescription: The view from Inspiration Point draws thousands of visitors each year. Jenny Lake lies below to the east and the Teton Range towers to the west. On a clear day, you can see the Yellowstone Plateau to the north, the Absaroka and Gros Ventre ranges to the east, and the Snake River Range to the south. You feel as though you are high in the mountains, yet you are only 420 feet above the lake below. You are standing at the mouth of Cascade Canyon.

images.altText: Hikers going up the trail to the popular Inspiration Point.
images.title: Inspiration Point
images.caption: Make the climb to Inpsiration Point - it's worth it!

data.bodyText:
The view from Inspiration Point draws thousands of visitors each year. Jenny Lake lies below to the east and the Teton Range towers to the west. On a clear day, you can see the Yellowstone Plateau to the north, the Absaroka and Gros Ventre ranges to the east, and the Snake River Range to the south. You feel as though you are high in the mountains, yet you are only 420 feet above the lake below. You are standing at the mouth of Cascade Canyon that slices through the heart of the Teton Range inviting you to explore.

Some hikers circle the north or south end of Jenny Lake to reach the west shore. Others take advantage of the Jenny Lake Shuttle Boat (fee charged) and shorten the hike by roughly 2 miles each way. From the west boat dock, the first half mile leads you to Hidden Falls, then the second half mile climbs steeply to Inspiration Point. 

Hike Information

5.7 miles round-trip, 3 hours, 870 ft total climbing. Moderate.
Via shuttle boat: 1.8 miles round-trip, 2.5 hours. 550 ft total climbing. Easy.

Name Origin

This viewpoint offers a spectacular panoramic view of Jenny Lake and Jackson Hole to the east and the Cathedral Group to the west.
data.audioDescription: The trail to Inspiration Point is the most strenuous in the park, with roughly 400 feet (120 m) of elevation gain. Be advised that along the way you will encounter a section of trail that hangs on a very steep ledge with no hand- or guardrails. The rocks can be slippery in this section, and the trail narrows as you climb, becoming progressively steeper, with many rocks and uneven surfaces. Exercise extreme caution along this stretch of trail. Along the trail, there are some outstanding views of the "Cathedral Group" towering above the canyon towards the west. This group includes 12,325-foot (3756 m) Teewinot Mountain, 13,770-foot (4197 m) Grand Teton and 12,928-foot (3940 m) Mt. Owen. From the lofty 7,200-foot (2194 m) perch of Inspiration Point, one may experience outstanding views of Jenny Lake, Jackson Hole, as well as the Gros Ventre Range towards the east, and the Gros Ventre Slide, a massive 1925 landslide. Turn around for views of Storm Point and Symmetry Spire to the west. As you stand at this viewpoint, imagine the massive glacier that flowed out of Cascade Canyon. When the glacier receded, it deposited the moraines (low ridges) that dam Jenny Lake.

data.title: Irrigation Ditch
data.listingDescription: The first homesteaders who settled on Mormon Row were dry-land farmers. They relied on snowmelt soaking into the soil and rainfall during the growing season to support their crops. The catastrophic flood of 1927 damaged many of the irrigation works from the Gros Ventre River. Around the same time, the Kelly Warm Springs began to produce more water. Homesteaders cut a ditch from the springs west to irrigate their dry lands.

data.title: Jackson Hole Airport
data.listingDescription: The Jackson Hole Airport is the only commercial airport within a national park in the country. As such, flying into the airport is an awe-inspiring introduction to the valley and park. Establishing the airport took many years and numerous locations were considered prior to settling on today's location. The airport began commercial operation in 1946 prior to park expansion and is now the busiest airport in Wyoming.

data.bodyText:
Location: Access the trailhead from the top of the aerial tram. Teton Village is about one mile south of Grand Teton National Park on the Moose-Wilson Road (WY 390).

Notes: Visitor services are extensive in Teton Village including motels, restaurants, shops and activities. Bears may be active any place and at any time-travel in groups, make noise and carry bear spray. Backcountry camping requires a permit-pick one up at a backcountry permits office.

For more information about the aerial tramway please visit the website.

Destinations

The aerial tram (fee charged) whisks hikers up 4,139 vertical feet in 15 minutes to the summit of Rendezvous Mountain at 10,455 feet. It is all downhill from there! Trails provide access the Teton Crest Trail and the southern Teton Range. The ski resort has several short loops hikes near the summit. Hikers looking for a longer day hike may continue down Granite Canyon and loop back to Teton Village. Backpackers can continue north toward Marion Lake or south toward Teton Pass.

 

Trails are not recommended for hiking until snow has melted, usually by late July. Fee charged.

Marion Lake
11.8 miles RT, 9 hours, 4000 ft total climbing, Strenuous.
Hike through alpine and subalpine terrain to Marion Lake and return to the tram.

Granite Canyon
12.3 miles total, 7 hours, 4200 ft total descent (with 450 ft climbing), Moderate.
Start at the top of the tram, hike into the park, down Granite Canyon and return to Teton Village.

Name Origin

Fur trappers called a mountain-ringed valley a "hole." Named Davey Jackson's Hole for fur trapper David E. Jackson who worked for the Rocky Mountain Fur Company. The name was later shortened to Jackson Hole.

data.title: Jackson Lake Dam Boat Launch
data.listingDescription: Informational panels on river safety are located at the launch area for you and your group to review. You will find resources like a map, things to do before going on the water, things to bring, and things to know.

images.altText: Paddleboards launch into the Snake River from boat ramp.
images.title: Jackson Lake Dam Boat Launch
images.caption: Jackson Lake Dam Boat Launch

data.bodyText:
The Snake River winds through the valley floor carrying snowmelt from the mountains westward toward the Pacific Ocean. This river is an artery of the park that offers stunning views of the Tetons. Many species of wildlife use the river, from the browsing moose to the industrious beaver. Whether you are fishing, viewing wildlife, or enjoying the scenery, floating on this river is an unforgettable experience. Jackson Lake Dam is the primary starting point for Snake River boating and floating trips in the park.

The course this river follows is not straightforward. It travels in and out of numerous channels that change every year. This is a powerful river that requires reading and navigation skills. Before you float, know what skills you need to float the river, where you are going, and what things you need. 

Informational panels on river safety are located at the launch area for you and your group to review. You will find resources like a map, things to do before going on the water, things to bring, and things to know.

For a complete overview of boating rules, regulations, and permit requirements, please review our webpage on boating and floating before getting out on the water.

Additional information about floating the Snake River, including an interactive map, is available too.

Permits and Regulations


To meet the permit requirements for Grand Teton National Park you must:

  • Have a Grand Teton Boat Permit
  • Have a valid Wyoming AIS Decal
  • Complete an AIS inspection

Grand Teton Boat Permit
 

All boats are required to have a Grand Teton Boat Permit before launching on any of the park’s waters. Permits are required for all motorized and non-motorized boats, including stand-up paddleboards (SUPs) and windsurfing boards. Privately owned vessels must register each year with Grand Teton National Park.Permits may be purchased on Recreation.gov or at the visitor centers in Moose or Colter Bay during summer operations. Boaters can also have their permit mailed directly to them within two weeks.

Wyoming AIS Decal


PREVENT THE SPREAD OF PATHOGENS - CLEAN. DRAIN. DRY.
All watercraft using Wyoming waters are required to display a Wyoming Aquatic Invasive Species decal.The decal can be purchased online at the Wyoming Game and Fish Department website or from a variety of local vendors. Additionally, all boats entering the park must stop for an Aquatic Invasive Species (AIS) inspection. By law, boats coming from out of state must be inspected or have valid proof of inspection before they launch on waters in Wyoming, including waters in the park. This includes motorized boats, rafts, drift boats, canoes, kayaks, stand-up paddle boards, and all watercraft 10 feet and longer. Aquatic Invasive Species, such as whirling disease and zebra or quagga mussels, are a serious ecological and economic threat to the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. Boats, waders, and anything else that comes in contact with a body of water has the potential to spread non-native plants, pathogens, and other invasive species among water bodies. Make sure to clean, drain, dry, all boating and fishing equipment after use.Learn more about preventing the spread of AIS.

Note: Non-motorized inflatable watercraft 10 feet or less in length, all solid and inflatable paddleboards regardless of length, and all devices defined as water sport toys are exempt from the Wyoming State AIS Decal requirement.
 

Stretches of River

Beginner
Jackson Lake Dam to Pacific Creek 5 miles
This stretch features scenic views, calmer water and few obstructions. At Pacific Creek landing the water is swift, boaters should scout this landing prior to launching.

Intermediate
Pacific Creek to Deadmans Bar 10 miles
his section drops significantly creating swift water and braided channels requiring careful route-finding.

Flagg Ranch to Lizard Creek Campground 10 miles
The braided channels make route-finding a challenge. The river winds for 6 miles before reaching Jackson Lake. Depending on the lake level, the trip is another 4 miles to Lizard Creek Campground. Strenuous rowing or paddling may be required. Afternoon thunderstorms and winds produce waves that may swamp canoes. Motors may be used on Jackson Lake.

Advanced
Deadman’s Bar to Moose Landing 10 miles
This is the most challenging stretch of river in the park, many accidents occur here. The river drops more steeply and the current increases. Complex braiding may obscure the main channel and strong currents can sweep boaters into side channels blocked by logjams.

Moose to Wilson 14 miles
This section of the river is as difficult as the preceding section. Advanced boating skills are required due to fast current, braided channels and logjams. The park extends 5 miles downstream from Moose on the west bank and 2 miles downstream on the east bank. There is no take out or access to the river at the park boundary. The next take-out is at the Snake River Bridge east of Wilson, WY, 14 miles downstream from Moose.

Use our advanced Snake River Map on our website for more route details.
data.audioDescription: At the end of the road and sidewalk of the Jackson Lake Dam area is the boat launch. Ten feet east of the in-ground concrete river sculpture and sidewalk switchback, to the south of the sidewalk, five three and half foot wide steps made of flat rocks lead you down to the river shoreline. Just past the steps, along the sidewalk, are two large metal brown bear boxes. They are approximately four feet high, 5 feet wide, and 3 feet in depth. There are two doors and two handles on each. The handle is bear-proof and requires you to stick your hand under a covering and push up to unlock the door. The sidewalk continues another thirty feet and is lined by simple log fencing to the south. Here, the sidewalk ends. Three panels to the south of the sidewalk provide safety information about the river. Two seven-foot-tall stained wooden posts stand upright and hold three vertical 32-inch by 48-inch informational panels, each encased in a brown metal frame with a few inches between each panel. About four feet by eight feet of paved sidewalk lies in front of the informational panels. The top third of the left panel is solid blue with title text that reads: Jackson Lake Dam Boat Launch Jackson Lake Dam to Pacific Creek Below the title text is a small white rectangle with a blue square and text that reads: Beginner skill level Next to the skill level marker are two paragraphs of text that read: Although this section of the Snake River looks like flat water, it’s moving steadily. Downstream, Oxbow Bend is a wonderful place to look for wildlife. After Pacific Creek, the river moves more rapidly with shifting channels and stronger currents. Know your skills, the capabilities of your watercraft, the weather forecast, and river conditions. The bottom two-thirds of the vertical panel is a map of the different sections of the Snake River and their difficulty level within Grand Teton National Park . The map is oriented north to south. You can see some of the glacial lakes, some topography of the landscape, and the Snake River. In the top left corner, a smaller, zoomed-out map, shows the area the large map is depicting. It is titled: Map Location. The main map shows the Snake River from Jackson Lake to Pacific Creek to Deadmans Bar and slightly beyond. The sections of river have symbols and are highlighted specific colors to indicate their difficulty level. Information in the bottom right corner explains the ratings. Beginner is indicated by a green circle and the river is colored light green. Jackson Lake Dam to Pacific Creek is rated as beginner. Intermediate is indicated by a light blue square and the river is colored light blue. Pacific Creek to Deadmans Bar is rated as intermediate. Advanced is indicated by a grey diamond and the river is colored light grey. Deadmans Bar to Moose is rated as advanced. Beneath the ratings is a reminder that: “In case of emergency CALL 911.” The middle panel focuses on River Safety. The top two-thirds of the panel discusses river safety, shows an image of a river hazard, and goes over things to do before going on the river. Small black and white graphics advise of steps to take before going on the river. Text reads: River Safety The Snake River—always changing and challenging. This river can be dangerous. River channels shift week to week, currents are fast, the water is cold, and blocking hazards appear overnight. Respect the river, be prepared, and take responsibility for your own safety. Things to do before going on the river Check the weather forecast. Tell someone where you are going and when you expect to be back. Always wear a personal flotation device (PFD). Know your skill level. The bottom third of the panel discusses things to bring. A large circle is filled with blue graphics of items recommended to bring on the river. Items listed are a throw bag, first aid, whistle, drinking water and snacks, knife, layers, proper footwear, and a PFD. It sits on top of a photograph of a raft on the river with the Tetons in the background. The right-side panel is split into two panels stacked on top of one another. The top panel discusses things to know before going on the river. Small graphics indicate regulations and prohibited actions. A photograph shows a kayaker paddling on the river with trees in the background. Text reads: Things to know Park boating permit is required for all watercraft floating the Snake River. Boat permits and Aquatic Invasive Species decals are required for watercraft including kayaks, canoes, rafts, and stand-up paddle (SUP) boards, inflatable or hard-sided. Permits may be purchased at the Craig Thomas Discovery or Visitor Center in Moose or Colter Bay Visitor Center. AIS decals may be obtained through Wyoming Game and Fish licensed sellers or on the web, check wgfd.wyo.gov/ais. Fish requires a Wyoming fishing license. Park regulations can be obtained from visitor centers. Help preserve high quality angling for native wild fish. This is only a partial list of regulations. For more information consult Title 36 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) and the Superintendent’s Compendium available at go.nps.gov/tetonlaws. Pets are not allowed on the river or on park trails. Where permitted, pets must be leashed. Drones are prohibited in the park. Launching, landing, or operating unmanned aircraft, such as drones, is prohibited within Grand Teton National Park. Motorboats and inner tubes are prohibited. Camping and fires are prohibited along the river. Prevent the transport of nuisance species. Clean all equipment and remove any visible mud, plants, fish, or animals before transporting equipment. The bottom panel on the right side is dedicated to park-related bulletins and has no text, graphics, or images. East of the informational panels the sidewalk continues past the boat launch ramp and curves north to connect to the three handicap accessible park spaces available. Just north of these handicap spaces is metal gate blocking a gravel service road. This is for authorized personal only. The boat ramp is roughly 40 feet wide with a steep decline to the river. Boaters can unload their boats here. To the north of the ramp, sidewalk, and informational panels, is a large, paved area where cars can turn around, use the handicap spaces, and rig boats before launching. North of the paved area and roadway is large marshy area full of trees, bushes, and beaver dams and lodges. This wet marshy area is perfect habitat for beavers, birds, and moose.

data.title: Jackson Lake Dam Overlook
data.listingDescription: Jackson Lake is a 400 foot-deep natural lake with a dam added on top. The original log-crib dam constructed in 1906-07, failed in 1910. In 1916, the Bureau of Reclamation completed a concrete dam raising the pool level by 39 feet. The increased water level flooded the surrounding forest, drowning many trees. Young men from the Civilian Conservation Corps helped to clear the shores of Jackson Lake and burn the slash piles during the Great Depression.

images.altText: Visitor standing near Jackson Lake Dam sign with Jackson Lake and northern Teton Range beyond.
images.caption: Jackson Lake Dam

data.bodyText:
Jackson Lake is a 400 foot-deep natural lake with a dam added on top. The original log-crib dam constructed in 1906-07, failed in 1910. In 1916, the Bureau of Reclamation completed a concrete dam raising the pool level by 39 feet. The increased water level flooded the surrounding forest, drowning many trees. Young men from the Civilian Conservation Corps helped to clear the shores of Jackson Lake and burn the slash piles during the Great Depression. Today, enjoy the views across Jackson Lake or fish in the Snake River below the dam.

History

A log crib dam first impounded water in 1906 with a storage capacity of 300,000 acre feet. The dam failed in 1910. An earthen dam replaced the log crib in 1916 to raise the natural lake level by 39 feet increasing the capacity to 790,000 acre feet. In 1917, the channel was dredged downstream to further increase the reservoir capacity to 847,000 acre feet. During the 1980s, engineers drained the reservoir and reinforced the dam to withstand a M7.5 earthquake.
data.audioDescription: This overlook is just south of Jackson Lake Dam, along the edge of the lake. As you face the lake, the dam lies to your right with the road crossing over it. From this angle you can see about 20 vertical concrete pillars supporting the roadway. The lake stretches out to your left. There are 5 wayside signs here. The first is on the edge of the lake near the road. The other four are in a covered pavilion along a paved path to the left.The first sign is titled, "Hoist Those Gates!" To the left and behind the sign is an actual historic gate hoist with its engine on a rolling cart. The cart is about 3 feet wide and 8 feet long, From the end nearest the lake, a gear shaft extends to the right connecting to multiple gears, the largest one being almost 3 feet in diameter. Feel free to touch this mechanism.Text on the sign reads, "Gates Control Flow. Fifteen 2.5-ton gates at the base of Jackson Lake Dam control the reservoir level by controlling the amount of water released. This is done by raising and lowering the gates. The reservoir is not filled when there is flood danger, leaving room to store water. During summer, water is discharged at a controlled rate to benefit agriculture and recreation."Hoisting the Gates. Modernized now, this type of gate hoist was manually operated from 1911 to 1986. The dam tender moved the engine cart along rails on top of the dam to the chosen gate. The drive shaft on the hoist engine and the drive collar on the reduction gears were engaged. This series of gears served to either raise or lower the gate."Imagine manipulating these immense gates by pushing the cart to the gate, starting the engine with the crank, engaging the shafts, then raising the gate and watching the water shoot out the tunnels below the dam."Above the text in the upper left of the graphic is an aerial photograph of the dam with four of the gates open, water rushing down the spillway. Along the right side of the sign are three other photographs. The top one is a picture of workers replacing the sluice gate hoists in 1941. We look along the top of the dam, the gear shafts over the first four gates in a line. After those four, workers stand on the right with a crane on the left.The middle picture shows an engine cart from winter 1975. It stands on rails in the snow along the edge of the dam, the gears just visible in the far right of the photo.The bottom picture from the same time period shows the shaft engaging the gears.The pavilion along the path to the left is surrounded by waist-high stone walls with openings on either side and is covered with a shingle roof. There is a small step up to the concrete floor. On the lake side are mounted 4 wayside signs. On the opposite side is a bench. From left to right, the first sign is titled, "Irrigating Idaho." Text down the left side reads, "Creating Farmland. The Reclamation Act of 1902 provided the means for the government to fund, design and operate irrigation projects. The Reclamation Service was created to implement the program. Most early irrigation projects were built by private businessmen. Many lacked engineering expertise and enough funding."Sagebrush Alchemy. Today the Minidoka Project provided irrigation water to southeast Idaho. Jackson Lake Dam is one of 9 dams that irrigate over 1.2 million acres. Land, now fertile, once was sagebrush flats. The annual value of irrigated crops exceeds $500 million. Jackson Lake Dam is farthest upstream. Irrigators rarely draw their full share of water allowing Jackson Lake Reservoir to remain above natural lake level."In the center of the sign is a round inset with a drawing of snowflakes. Text reads, "Snow Means Water. The biggest variable is unpredictable annual precipitation. Since 1919, snow surveys have helped predict the amount of water that will be available."The right side and bottom of the sign is filled with a map of the project, stretching westward from Jackson Lake Dam.The second sign is titled, "Depending on Water." Text down the left side reads, "Before irrigating downstream farm lands, Jackson Lake water provides great recreation. From power boating to sailing, recreation abounds. Fishing and rafting are popular below the dam. All activities are affected by the release of water."Fishing. Fish depend on insects for food year round. If winter water levels expose river gravels, insect populations can dry up. Winter reservoir operations help maintain flows supporting insects, fish and good summer fishing."Wildlife. The reservoir provides wildlife a reliable source of downstream water, even in dry years. Low water can expose beaver and muskrat dens or duck nests, making them accessible to predators."A large photograph filling most of the sign shows an aerial view of the dam taken in 1984. The dam itself lies at the bottom right of the picture with Jackson Lake extending out behind it to the base of the Teton Range.A small inset in the upper right shows a sketch of six people in a rubber raft. data.title: Jackson Lake Dam Parking and Picnic Area
data.listingDescription: Jackson Lake Dam Parking and Picnic area is below the dam on the north side of the Snake River. Large cottonwood trees shade several picnic tables. Minimal facilities include a vault toilet and trash receptacles. A short walk leads to the outwash from the dam. Many visitors launch non-motorized boats to float the river and fish in the turbulent outflow.

images.altText: Visitors enjoy a picnic with trees in the background.
images.title: Jackson Lake Dam Picnic Area
images.caption: Jackson Lake Dam Picnic Area

data.bodyText:
This picnic area sits beneath giant cottonwoods and features restrooms, trash disposal, interpretive information, and access to the river.  Accessible parking and picnic tables are available. Follow the paved path towards the river to find exhibits, fishing spots, the boat ramp, and views of the Dam and Teton Mountain Range. 

Use this parking area for vehicles and boat trailers if launching your boat from the Jackson Lake Dam, fishing, or just exploring the area. You can park trailers at any of the Snake River landings and launches, including this one, in the park for day use. Please park in designated areas only; illegally parked vehicles may be ticketed and/or towed. Do not park in the designated trailer parking areas if you do not have a trailer.
data.audioDescription: After turning off Teton Park Road, you will pass a one-way entrance to the parking lot (marked by a “Do Not Enter” sign), then a stop sign where you can either turn right into the parking lot or continue straight to the boat ramp. After turning right into the parking area, continue turning right to enter the north side of the parking lot where large buses, RVs, and boat trailers can park. There are roughly 15 trailer parking spaces in the 150-foot-long, 60-foot-wide lot. The south side of the lot has parking for regular vehicles, restrooms, trash and recycling, and picnic tables. Large, towering cottonwood trees surround the parking area. In the center, on the western side of the park lot, a sidewalk made of small, smooth rocks and concrete extends out semi-dividing the north and south sides of the lot. A large brown dumpster and a green recycling bin sit on the edge of the sidewalk. Just south, on the western side of the lot, are the restrooms. There are two doors to individual restrooms, for either gender, and handicap accessible. These are pit toilets. The building is brown, with wood siding and a green metal roof. Slightly north of the restrooms, just off the sidewalk, stand two six-and-a-half-foot-tall wooden posts holding a 32-inch by 48-inch vertical panel. The upper two-thirds of the panel displays a map of the lower Jackson Lake Dam area on the left side and information about the area with small black and white graphics on the right side. The bottom third of the panel is a black rubber material that is used to post announcements. The text on the upper right side of the panel reads: Grand Teton Jackson Lake Dam This stretch of the Snake River offers dramatic views of Jackson Lake Dam along with paddling, fishing, and wildlife viewing. Things to Know Always wear a personal flotation device (PFD). Black and grizzly bears live throughout the park. Keep your picnic area clean and put away all food in a bear box or vehicle. A Wyoming fishing license is required for fishing. Licenses are available at marinas, local outfitters, and online. Animals are drawn to the river. Stay at least 100 yards (91 m) away from bears and 25 yards (23 m) away from other wildlife. Report any bear sightings to a ranger. There are accessible fishing platforms available to people with limited mobility. The sidewalk continues south of the restrooms, down the western and southern side of the parking lot. Just south of the restrooms, the sidewalk extends towards the cottonwood trees so the first of six large wooden picnic tables can sit off the main pathway. The picnic tables are spaced out and continue as the sidewalk turns to border the southern edge of the parking lot. There is another entrance/exit point to the parking lot in the southeast corner. Near where the sidewalk turns south towards the plaza, boat ramp, and river, are two 32-inch by 48-inch informational panels, each supported by six and a half foot tall wooden beams. They stand roughly three apart and are oriented vertically. The northern panel is the same as the panel by the restroom, only slightly larger. It is split down the middle with the same map and information about the lower Jackson Lake Dam area. The southern panel provides education about Aquatic Invasive Species with rules, regulations, and photographs. The main text of the panel reads: Aquatic Invasive Species What Are They? Why Do Our Actions Matter? Aquatic Invasive Species (AIS) are non-native plants and animals that take over natural systems. Invasive species are a national problem. Below this text is a quote that reads: If these animals are detected in Wyoming waters, it could have catastrophic impacts to the water, the biodiversity of the area, recreation, and even water delivery systems within the state. —Alan Osterland, Chief of Fisheries, Wyoming Game and Fish Department, 2021 Next to the text is a photograph of a pipe, sawed open so the inside of the pipe is visible, and filled with zebra mussels. The zebra mussels are small, brown, shaped like a traditional mussel, and tightly compacted, blocking the pipe fully. Text above the photograph reads: Zebra mussels clog pipes in a South Dakota hydroelectric power plant. Any bit of water, mud, or plant matter can carry invasive species. The bottom third of the panel is divided into three photographs with instructions on the “Clean, Drain, Dry” process to prevent invasive species. The left photograph shows two women on the shore of a river cleaning a kayak off with a sponge and towel. It is titled “Clean” with instructions that read: Clean everything that comes in contact with water, removing any mud or plants. The center photograph shows the same two women tipping the kayak on its side to drain it of water. It is titled “Drain” with instructions that read: Drain any standing water out of your watercraft or fishing gear. The right-hand photo shows one woman unpacking a bag from a storage compartment on a kayak. It is titled “Dry” with instructions that read: Dry all your gear—including waders and fishing equipment. Beneath the three photographs is a long green bar with text that reads: Do your part. After each use clean, drain, and dry your gear to help protect Grand Teton’s water.

data.title: Jackson Lake Lodge
data.listingDescription: The historic Jackson Lake Lodge is one of two National Historic Landmarks in the park. With its concrete textured walls, this building was the first modern lodge built in a national park. Opening in 1955, the Rockefeller Lodge, as it was once known, inspires visitors with a wall of windows over-looking Willow Flats, Jackson Lake and the Teton Range beyond.Today, the great room is a place to relax and enjoy the view or escape from a rainy day.

images.altText: Walkway to the front of the Jackson Lake Lodge with grass lawn and large spruce trees
images.caption: Jackson Lake Lodge

data.bodyText:
The historic Jackson Lake Lodge is one of two National Historic Landmarks in the park. With its concrete textured walls, this building was the first modern lodge built in a national park. Opening in 1955, the Rockefeller Lodge, as it was once known, inspires visitors with a wall of windows over-looking Willow Flats, Jackson Lake and the Teton Range beyond.

Today, the great room is a place to relax and enjoy the view or escape from a rainy day. Other facilities in the lodge include a variety of lodging options, two restaurants, a lounge and gift shops. Outside, enjoy the swimming pool, horseback rides or hiking. The Grand Teton Medical Clinic is located in the area as is a service station.

For more information visit the Jackson Lake Lodge website.

Name Origin

Fur trappers called a mountain-ringed valley a "hole." Named Davey Jackson's Hole for fur trapper David E. Jackson who worked for the Rocky Mountain Fur Company. The name was later shortened to Jackson Hole.
data.audioDescription:
A wide paved sidewalk leads from the parking lot under the covered entrance drive that lines the front of the building. As you enter, into the main hall with stone flag flooring, the activity desk is to your left and the registration desk is to your right. The flooring changes to wood in front of the desks. Straight ahead at the end of the hall a wide staircase leads up to the huge, open upper lobby area. There is an elevator on the left at the end of the registration desk.

The upper lobby has a two-story high ceiling with dark brown wooden beam trusses. The upper walls are a beige color with stonework down below. In the front corners on either side of the entrance there are two curved fireplaces. The back wall of the lobby is glass, providing spectacular views of Jackson Lake with Mount Moran rising beyond and other central Teton peaks further south to your left. There are some benches in the back near the windows. On the left there are 2 restaurants.

At the top of the stairs, there are gift shops both to the right and left, as well as around the stairwell at the front of the building. In the middle of the open space are two square glass cases which hold a variety of woven baskets, pottery and other artifacts.

data.bodyText: The Jackson Lake Lodge gained recognition as a National Historic Landmark in 2003. The building broke with the National Park Service tradition of rustic log construction. Instead, designers constructed a "modern" lodge of concrete and steel that blended into the landscape. The great room with its wall of windows offers sweeping views across the valley toward the northern Teton Range. Step outside to the back deck and engage all your senses. Below is the Willow Flats area; a wet meadow where many species thrive. Across Jackson Lake, the northern Teton Range, dominated by Mount Moran, fills the skyline.
data.audioDescription: This wayside sits at the edge of a concrete aggregate patio behind the Jackson Lake Lodge. A ramp leads up to the lobby of the lodge. There are several benches around the patio, which is bordered by a rustic log rail fence. Beyond the sign is a large marshy meadow with Jackson Lake beyond. Behind the lake are the jagged peaks of the Teton Range. Mount Moran is almost directly in front of you with Grand Teton off to the left. Along the top of the sign is a computer-generated image of the range as it would look from 3500 feet above you. The peaks are labeled from left to right: Buck Mountain, to the south near Jenny Lake, then Teewinot Mountain, Grand Teton, Mount Owen, Mount St. John, Mount Woodring, Mount Moran, Bivouac Peak, Rolling Thunder Mountain, Eagles Rest Peak, and Ranger Peak at the far right. Text reads, "Grand Teton National Park. Welcome to Grand Teton National Park, an area of impressive scenery and abundant wildlife. The park consists of more than 300,000 acres, including the heart of the Teton Range and most of the valley called Jackson Hole. Grand Teton lies within the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, the largest nearly intact natural area remaining in the contiguous United States. Grand Teton and Yellowstone National Parks, seven national forests, and two national wildlife refuges contain millions of acres. Adjoining federal, state, and private lands increase the size of this ecosystem, which is essential to free-roaming wildlife." More text at the bottom left of the panel reads, "Help Protect Park Resources. Wild animals are wild. Do not feed or touch them. Give animals plenty of space. Walk on trails to avoid crushing plants and flowers. Store food and dispose of litter properly. Drive carefully. Watch for animals on the roads. Pets must be leashed. No pets are allowed on trails or in the backcountry." Along the bottom of the panel are line drawings of two ground squirrels, a crane and a beaver. The caption reads, "The wide variety of plants on the moist Willow Flats provide rich habitat for many species including Uinta ground squirrels, sandhill cranes, and beavers." On the right side of the panel is an historic photo of National Park Service Director Horace Albright speaking at the dedication of the national park in 1929.

data.title: Jackson Lake Overlook
data.listingDescription: The north section of US 89/191/287 hugs the eastern shore of Jackson Lake. Across the lake, notice the patchwork of burned forest. The 1974 Waterfalls Canyon fire was one of the first naturally ignited wildland fires allowed to burn. Today, wildland fire management is a critical part of park policy attempting to preserve all aspects of the park's ecosystem. The landscape we enjoy seems to change only with the seasons, but powerful geologic forces continue to shape the earth.

images.altText: Visitors at the north end of Jackson Lake looking south along the Teton Range
images.caption: Visitors at the Jackson Lake Overlook

data.bodyText:
The north section of US 89/191/287 hugs the eastern shore of Jackson Lake. Across the lake, notice the patchwork of burned forest. The 1974 Waterfalls Canyon fire was one of the first naturally ignited wildland fires allowed to burn. Today, wildland fire management is a critical part of park policy attempting to preserve all aspects of the park's ecosystem.

The landscape we enjoy seems to change only with the seasons, but powerful geologic forces continue to shape the earth. The Teton Range lies at a geologic crossroads surrounded by other mountain ranges built at different times at by different forces. Earthquakes, volcanoes and glaciers all played a role in the past and will again in the future.

Name Origin

Fur trappers called a mountain-ringed valley a "hole." Named Davey Jackson's Hole for fur trapper David E. Jackson who worked for the Rocky Mountain Fur Company. The name was later shortened to Jackson Hole.
data.audioDescription: This turnout is a narrow strip of asphalt at the northern end of Jackson Lake. The water stretches to your right with the larger area extending out to the distance on your left. Across the lake the mountain range rises with the higher peaks towards the left. The edge of the pavement is rough, with gravel and dirt extending down to the rock-covered water's edge a few yards away. There are two wayside signs along the turnout. The one on the right is titled "Geologic Crossroads." The background shows a color illustration of an aerial view of the region. The scale in the vertical direction has been exaggerated to clearly show the elevation differences of the different formations. A label marks your current location down in the valley at the northern end of Jackson Lake. Behind you to the east is the Absaroka Range, created by earlier volcanic activity. Across Jackson Lake the Teton Range rises. The caption reads, "The Teton Range towers over the valley called Jackson Hole. Motion on the Teton fault generated massive earthquakes that lifted the mountains skyward and caused the valley to slip downward." West of the Tetons another caption reads, "West of the Tetons, the Snake River Plain rises to meet the Yellowstone Plateau, concealing past volcanic explosions still evident in Yellowstone's landscape." At the upper left of the image is the Gros Ventre Range. The caption reads, "To the southeast, compression thrust up the Gros Ventre Range long before the Teton Range formed." Text in the bottom right reads, "Powerful geologic forces-including earthquakes, volcanoes, and glaciers-shaped this landscape. These mountain ranges formed in different ways, but ice-age glaciers scoured all of them and left behind lakes, U-shaped canyons, cirques, jagged ridges, and outwash plains." The wayside at the left end of the turn out is titled, "Recognizing the Value of Fire" It shows a photograph of large plumes of smoke billowing up over a conifer forest with mountain peaks in the background. The caption reads, "The Waterfalls Canyon fire burned 3,672 acres. Since 1974, many wildfires have burned on these slopes. Some were fought, but most have been allowed to run their course." A photo in the lower left corner shows a person wearing a hard hat and a harness slung with a variety of equipment and instruments, facing a fire in a forested area. The caption reads, "A fire-effects monitor collects weather data, documents fire behavior, and notes smoke dispersal-all important parts of managing a wildfire." Text at the top reads, "After more than 50 years of putting out all fires in national parks, the National Park Service realized that natural fires promoted healthier forests. When a bolt of lightning struck the hillside across from you in July 1974, rangers allowed the fire to burn. Months later, winter snowfalls put it out. "That summer-long Waterfalls Canyon fire sparked heated debates. People living near the Tetons called the new decision a "scorched earth" policy. Articles in The New York Times, Christian Science Monitor, The Philadelphia Inquirer, and Time drummed up controversy across the nation. Many people supported the science-based decision for natural fire. Allowing occasional natural fires opens the forest canopy and promotes plant growth. It removes dead trees and logs, and improves safety for people who live near places that are fire-prone."

data.title: Jackson Point Overlook
data.listingDescription: Signal Mountain rises almost 1,000 feet above the valley making it the highest point visitors can drive to in the park. On a clear day you may see several mountain ranges: Teton, Gros Ventre, Absaroka and Yellowstone Plateau. The valley floor records the passage of Pleistocene Ice Age glaciers that scoured the valley and carved lakes. The dimples in the landscape below you are potholes also known as kettles.

images.altText: A large landscape view up high of the valley floor and Teton Range with a couple visitors.
images.title: Jackson Point Signal Mountain
images.caption: Witness how geology shaped the landscape from the top of Signal Mountain.

data.bodyText: Signal Mountain rises almost 1,000 feet above the valley making it the highest point visitors can drive to in the park. On a clear day you may see several mountain ranges: Teton, Gros Ventre, Absaroka and Yellowstone Plateau. The valley floor records the passage of Pleistocene Ice Age glaciers that scoured the valley and carved lakes. The dimples in the landscape below you are potholes also known as kettles. These formed when ice broke free from retreating glaciers and was buried in sediment. The ice later melted and formed a depression. Enjoy the view but also appreciate the geologic forces that shaped this landscape.
data.audioDescription: This wayside stands in a dirt patch at the side of the roughly paved path that leads up from the parking area. To your right are views westward of the valley and distant mountains. The view over the sign is that of Grand Teton towards your right and the other peaks of the range stretching off in the distance behind Jackson Lake in the valley below. The background photograph on the sign is that of the view in front of you. Text reads, "Valley View. From this vantage point, notice how the landscape spreads before you. Geology controls the park's natural communities from valley wetlands to the mountain alpine. Ice-age glaciers periodically blanketed this landscape last retreating 14,000 years ago leaving behind river channels, outwash plains, glacial moraines, potholes, deep canyons and jagged peaks." "Glaciers act like conveyor belts depositing rocky debris as ridges called moraines that contain rocks ground to the consistency of flour. Rock flour retains moisture allowing lodgepole pine forests to flourish on these moraines." "As glaciers retreat, blocks of ice drop to the valley floor and become buried in outwash gravel. When the ice melts, the resulting depression or pothole forms a pocket of forest or wetland surrounded by a sea of sagebrush in the outwash plain." An inset photo in the bottom center of the panel shows a broad stream running over rounded river rocks through a meadow with the Teton Range in the background. The caption reads, "Melting glaciers washed away soil and left behind quartzite cobbles, gravel and sand forming the outwash plain where sagebrush thrives today. The meltwater carved channels into the outwash plain reflected in the wetlands along the Snake River."

data.title: Jenny Lake & Park Orientation
data.listingDescription: Plan your Jenny Lake and park experience by reading these informational signs.

images.altText: Informational panels about Jenny Lake and Grand Teton National Park
images.title: Jenny Lake and Park Information Panels
images.caption: Be prepared for your park experience.

data.bodyText: These informational signs will help you plan for your Jenny Lake experience and beyond. Only have a couple of hours? Planning to stay longer than four hours? These signs make suggestions about how to safely explore the Jenny Lake area no matter your time frame. You will find information about what to do in the entire park as well. Make sure you're aware of the park's rules and regulations and read about safety. A map is displayed to help orient you.
data.audioDescription: Located about 40 feet west from the park entrance station along the flat asphalt path, two large, six-foot wide, dual-sided information panels stand on a wide, flat, stone-paved plaza. They are spaced roughly 12 feet apart, and mounted between eight-foot tall double log posts. Moving to the first panel at the left, text at the top reads: Experience Jenny Lake The Jenny Lake area offers plenty of recreational options. View exhibits, grab a snack, or explore the trails and scenic views on this side of the lake. If you intend to hike on the other side of the lake, plan for a longer day and make sure you are prepared. Three color photographs in the middle show a ranger crouching before a young boy as part of the Jenny Lake Ranger Program, a couple picking their way across Rock Beach, and a view from the Jenny Lake shuttle boat approaching the back-country landing site. At the bottom left are several suggestions of what you can do if you have two hours or more, including exploring the Discovery Trail, joining a ranger-led program, or hopping on board the Jenny Lake shuttle boat, and hiking to Hidden Falls. Filling the right two-thirds of the panel is a map of the Jenny Lake Front-Country, with a black and white “You Are Here” label in the center. Black and white graphic icons with white text labels indicate the locations of the facilities, overlooks, and trailhead. At the lower left is a key to those icons, as well as a description of the characteristics of the paved trails of the Front-Country: the surface is paved flagstone, with a minimum width of 48 inches (1.2 m), a maximum five percent grade, and a maximum cross slope of three percent. About eight feet to the left of this map panel, note a low, wide granite boulder embedded in the ground with a tactile, bronze map of the area as shown on the panel. Touch the bronze map to get a feel for where you are . Moving to the back side of the first panel, text at the top left of a blue panel reads: Explore Jenny Lake and Beyond Backcountry adventures await you across Jenny Lake. If your visit allows four hours or more, take time to explore the Jenny Lake area more deeply. Trails wind up canyons, offering opportunities to explore the Grand Teton wilderness. If you prefer to stay in the front-country, bike, paddle, or drive to discover unique views of the rugged central peaks of the Teton Range. Three color photographs in the middle show hikers in Cascade Canyon, a family on bicycles enjoying a view, and a trout swimming at the water line, with snow-capped mountains above, and the lakebed below. At the bottom left are several suggestions of what you can do if you have four hours or more, including venturing into Cascade or Paintbrush canyon, discovering the vistas from the Jenny Lake Scenic Drive, or paddling a canoe, kayak, or paddleboard on Jenny, String, or Leigh Lake (permit required). A map fills the right two-thirds of this panel, showing a three-quarter, aerial perspective rendering of the Teton range. With Jenny Lake at the bottom center, each of the peaks above are labeled in black with their names and elevations. Likewise identified are other canyons, lakes, trails, and roads in the back-country area. A key at the bottom left of the map decodes the graphic icons of the facilities shown across the park. In a blue band across the bottom of the panel, more information about the Jenny Lake area trails is given. Text reads: Once you leave the pavement or take the shuttle boat across Jenny Lake, you will be on a wilderness trail system. Expect to encounter numerous rocks scattered throughout the trail surface, exposed tree roots, and multiple stairs. Stair steps vary from two to 11 inches high. Wheelchairs are welcome, but trails may be difficult to negotiate. Strollers, bicycles, and other wheeled vehicles are not allowed. At the right, information about seven different trails is provided, including the total length, approximate time to hike, total uphill climbing, trail difficulty, and where each leads. Moving back north to the front side of the second set of information panels, a map of the entire Grand Teton National Park fills the right half of the panel and shows all the roads, pathways, trails, and facilities. Text at the top of a blue panel at the left reads: Discover Grand Teton National Park Discover the magnificent landscape and wild communities of Grand Teton National Park, where the Teton Range rises abruptly from the high mountain valley known as Jackson Hole. From lush meadows and sage-covered floodplains to bare alpine rocks, the park is home to bald eagles, grizzly bears, river otters, and bison. Two color photographs in the middle show a wooden barn in front of the pink-tinged, snow-capped Tetons at sunset, and a hiker in Cascade Canyon. At the bottom left are several suggestions of what you can do if you have a day, or more than a day: take a float trip on the Snake River or a scenic cruise on Jenny or Jackson lakes; ride atop a horse to experience an elevated view; camp on Leigh or Jackson Lake (permit required); explore the interpretive exhibits at all four park visitor centers, each with different exhibits and focus. Moving to the back side of this panel, text at the top left reads, “Protect Yourself, Wildlife, and Your Park.” It lists several essential items to bring with you whenever you enter the backcountry, including a map, a first aid kit, bear spray, rain gear and layers, food and water, sun protection, and a flashlight. Note that while battery-powered devices, such as GPS units and smartphones, are useful, they may be unreliable in the park. Text at the lower left lists several things to know about park regulations and safety advisories. Visitors who plan to take a service animal into the backcountry should complete an acknowledgment form in a ranger station. Otherwise, pets are not allowed on park trails or in buildings. It is illegal to feed any wildlife, and one should always maintain a distance of at least 100 yards from bears and wolves, and 25 yards from other wildlife. The right two-thirds of this panel is divided into four sections, each with a large color photograph at the top and accompanying information below. Beginning at the top left, a couple people in long-sleeve jackets hike along a rocky, declined trail. Text below this photograph reads, “Have a Safe and Enjoyable Visit.” Note that you are responsible for your own safety, as rescue is not a certainty; mountain weather may change quickly; and you are to leave the park as you found it for others to enjoy. Do not pick wildflowers or collect any objects. At the top right, a photograph shows a person in full mountain-climbing gear, helmet, and gloves alone on a high, steep, rocky mountain face. Under the title, “Climbing and Mountaineering,” text notes that Teton route finding may be difficult; a permit is required for all overnight stays in the backcountry; climbing helmets are strongly recommended for al climbs; and you should ask a ranger for a list of current mountain guides if you need one. At the lower left is a photograph of a big black bear. Text reads: Be Bear Aware Grizzly and black bears thrive in the park. Reduce your risk and keep bears wild by following these guidelines: • Avoid surprising a bear • Hike in groups of three or more if possible. • Carry and know how to use bear spray. • Never approach a bear. • If you encounter a bear, STOP, and remain calm. Assess the situation. If you need to give the bear space, slowly back away while keeping your eyes on the bear. Never run from a bear as this could trigger the bear to chase you. • Follow food storage regulations. At the bottom right, the last photograph shows three people in a line hiking a flat, narrow trail across a wide mountain meadow. Text reads: Hiking and Backpacking All overnight stays require a backcountry camping permit. Get a permit at the Craig Thomas Discovery and Visitor Center in Moose, the Jenny Lake Ranger Station, or the Colter Bay Visitor Center. • Snow slopes are hazardous. Most mountain passes remain snow-covered into mid-summer. • Carry water or treat your water with a filter, purification tablets, or by boiling. • Vehicles, including bicycles and strollers, are prohibited on unpaved trails or off established roads or designated pathways. Wheelchairs and any type of assistive technology are welcome. • Keep park waters clean, pack out all trash, and stay on established trails. To the left of this last panel, note a roughly three-foot tall metal box with a hinged, sloping lid. Attached to the front, a small blue sign reads, “Visitor Guide.” A small blue sign attached to the lid reads: “$1 Donation, or Borrow and Return.”

data.title: Jenny Lake Boat Launch
data.listingDescription: Experience Jenny Lake from a new perspective--on the water! Launch your motorized and non-motorized (motor maximum: 10 horsepower) crafts from this boat launch. There are not facilities. Please review all boating regulations for the park prior to launch. Make sure you have all required permits.

images.altText: Jenny Lake Boat Launch with sign and views of Jenny Lake.
images.title: Jenny Lake Boat Launch
images.caption: Experience Jenny Lake from a new perspective--on the water!

data.bodyText:
Jenny Lake Boat Launch is accessible by vehicle from Lupine Meadows Road. Turn off Teton Park Road at Lupine Junction and follow signs to the small gravel parking area. From here, you can access the water. You cannot access the Jenny Lake Boat Launch by vehicle from the Jenny Lake Area. 

There are no facilities at this boat launch. Bring your own water and use a restroom before you arrive. Jenny Lake is open to non-motorized vessels such as kayaks and paddleboards, and motorized boats with motors that do not exceed 10 horsepower. Please do not park here if you are not launching a boat. 

Boating in the park requires planning, permits, and skill. Regardless of experience, recreating on the water poses significant risks. Know the regulations and safety requirements for boating in the park before you go. 
 

Permits & Decals

Grand Teton Boat Permit

All boats are required to have a Grand Teton Boat Permit prior to launching on any of the park’s waters. Permits are required for all motorized and non-motorized boats, including stand-up paddleboards (SUPs) and windsurfing boards. Privately owned vessels must register each year with Grand Teton National Park. Permits may be purchased on Recreation.gov or at the visitor centers in Moose or Colter Bay during summer operations. Boaters can also have their permit mailed directly to them within two weeks.

To fulfill the temporary permit requirements, you must:

  • Have a valid Wyoming AIS Decal
  • Have a boat sticker attached to the boat's port-side stern.

Wyoming AIS Decal

All watercraft using Wyoming waters are required to display a Wyoming Aquatic Invasive Species decal. The decal can be purchased online at the Wyoming Game and Fish Department website or from a variety of local vendors. Fees collected for the AIS decal will be used to fund the AIS program and inspections in Wyoming along with Game and Fish generated license sale funds.

Note: Non-motorized inflatable watercraft 10 feet or less in length, all solid and inflatable paddleboards regardless of length, and all devices defined as water sport toys are exempt from the Wyoming State AIS Decal requirement.

Aquatic Invasive Species

All boats entering Grand Teton National Park are required to stop for an Aquatic Invasive Species (AIS) inspection. By law, boats coming from out of state must be inspected or have valid proof of inspection before they launch on waters in Wyoming, including waters in the park. This includes motorized boats, rafts, drift boats, canoes, kayaks, stand-up paddle boards, and all watercraft 10 feet and longer. Boaters must also purchase an Aquatic Invasive Species (AIS) decal from the Wyoming Game and Fish Department.
data.audioDescription: The Jenny Lake boat launch is located about 100 feet (30 m) down a slight incline to the shoreline from a gravel parking lot, about 50 yards (45 m) to the south from the East Shore boat dock and shuttle boat launch. Note a park boat permit is required, and that motors only up to 10 horsepower are permitted. There is no swimming allowed in the lake at this location. Stands of pine trees line the sides of the road leading down to the launch, which crosses over the Jenny Lake loop trail just before the water’s edge. Note a line of boulders at your right as you approach the lake. The pristine waters of the lake act as a mirror, reflecting the surrounding peaks and evergreen forests that reach all the way down to the rocky shoreline. The crystal-clear water also makes it easy to see the rocky lakebed.

images.caption: Experience the top of the Tetons in the Jenny Lake Plaza.

data.bodyText:
Summit the Teton mountain peaks at this climbing exhibit. Learn about women alpinists, touch multiple elevation benchmarks, and scope out the different peaks. 

From Eleanor Davis to park search and rescue and recreational climbers, the Teton Mountain Range attracts folks to its highest peaks. Experience what it is like to summit a mountain on the large boulders where you will find USGS elevation benchmarks. Not sure what peak you're looking at? Look through the viewfinders to learn the names of the different peaks.
data.audioDescription: Outside the side entrance to the Jenny Lake Store, the asphalt sidewalk meets a wide, flat, plaza paved with large, irregularly shaped, granite stones, bounded by a three-foot tall granite stone wall at the back. Along the top of the low stone wall, a four-foot wide, inclined metal information panel sits mounted across two large boulders embedded in the wall. At the far left of the panel, two hikers stand on a high, craggy peak gazing over a rocky, snow-covered ravine below. Text in a blue field at the right reads: Grand Ascent Summitting the Grand Teton is an unforgettable accomplishment. It requires skill, preparation, climbing equipment—and some gumption. Most people take two days to summit the 13,775-foot peak. If the Grand is out of reach, there are still many opportunities for climbing and mountaineering. Visit the historic Jenny Lake Ranger Station in front of you to plan an ascent, obtain a permit, and check current conditions. Next to this text, a smaller inset color photograph shows a person strapped to a backboard surrounded by a team of people wearing helmets. A caption reads: Search and rescue incidents range from lost hikers and sprained ankles to more severe trauma. Always know your limits and be prepared. Continuing to the right, a black-and-white photograph at the top shows two women, one standing and one sitting, perched atop a large boulder. Text reads: Pioneer Woman Eleanor Davis (seated) was the first woman documented to summit the Grand Teton in 1923. Just one year later, retired school teacher Geraldine Lucas reached the summit. By the 1930s, more women followed suit. Any ascent of the Grand Teton takes strength and tenacity. These pioneering women climbed on, demonstrating their abilities and taking their place on the Teton’s peaks. At the far right of the panel, a few carabiners and rope lash across the face a small block of granite attached to the panel. Touch this climbing gear to get a feel for the equipment. Note the open field and slightly inclined landscape behind the stone wall, strewn with smaller boulders and hearty sagebrush, leading up to the permit office. In the distance, the mountain peaks rise high in the sky. Located outside the Jenny Lake Store at the far eastern end of the granite plaza is a boulder-strewn gravel area, ringed at the back with a rough line of additional boulders with smaller rocks in front. From the side entrance to the store, move right across the narrow asphalt walkway to the stone plaza, and a small cluster of boulders embedded in the gravel. Atop a roughly three-foot tall, flat-topped boulder in the cluster, touch a circular metal elevation benchmark embedded in the rock. Note a taller, nearly seven-foot tall boulder to its left with a second circular metal elevation benchmark embedded on its top. Touch a vertical groove cut in the taller rock. This groove makes it easier for agile climbers to scale the rock to get up to the benchmark. To the north, around these boulders, are two brown, metal viewing scopes perched side-by-side on four-foot tall metal poles. Move around the back of either scope to the right. On the top of each scope, a hollow, foot-long viewing tube sits mounted on a pivot in the center of a flat, metal circle, like a sundial. A roughly six-inch tall, vertical metal wall rings the edge of the circle at the left, with a series of half-moon cutouts along its top edge. Each cutout is labeled with the name of a particular peak. Rotate the hollow viewing tube, and rest the end into each of these cutouts to view the given peak through the tube.

data.title: Jenny Lake Donor Area
data.listingDescription: At this donor area, read the names of the supporters of the Grand Teton National Park Foundation and a brief history on the longstanding relationship between the park and its partners.

images.altText: Three bronze panels list out donors with visitors admiring the exhibit.
images.title: Jenny Lake Donor Wall
images.caption: Projects like the Jenny Lake Renewal are made possible with park partners and generous donors.

data.bodyText: Projects like the Jenny Lake Renewel would not be possible without the support of Grand Teton National Park Foundation and its donors. This is longstanding relationship between the park and its partners is one of the tenets of the National Park Service mission.
data.audioDescription: The Grand Teton Donor Area is located immediately to the south of Jenny Lake Visitor Center. A 15-foot wide walkway, flanked by several large boulders on either side and paved with flat, irregularly shaped, granite stones, leads 30 feet west from the asphalt walkway to a set of five, eight-foot tall by three-foot wide bronze panels. The panels are etched with the names of donors and supporters of the Grand Teton National Park Foundation. Three panels stand side-by-side at the end of the walkway, with two more panels at the left and right. Touch the panels to feel the thousands of small, circular holes that have been drilled into each panel, creating images of the mountains and park that surround the lists of donors.

data.title: Jenny Lake East Shore Boat Dock
data.listingDescription: Visitors began to flock to the shores of Jenny Lake even before the establishment of Grand Teton National Park. Early entrepreneurs started a boating business to shuttle hikers across the lake to the mouth of Cascade Canyon. Today, Jenny Lake Boating offers shuttle services to sightseers and hikers, and scenic cruises to those who wish to enjoy a quiet trip on the lake.

images.altText: Jenny Lake East Shore Boat Dock, boat, and passengers buying tickets. Mountains in the background.
images.title: Jenny Lake East Shore Boat Dock
images.caption: Take a ride across Jenny Lake on the shuttle boat.

data.bodyText:
The Jenny Lake East Shore Boat Dock is where you can purchase tickets and board the shuttle boat to the western side of Jenny Lake. Scenic cruises also depart from this location and require a reservation. Canoes and kayaks are available for rent. 

The shuttle boat only operates during the summer months and is not accessible during the winter. Jenny Lake Boating, an authorized concessionaire of the park, operates this shuttle service. There are also scenic cruises and canoe and kayak rentals.

As one of the most sought after activities in the park, expect lines in the peak summer months (June-August). There are no restrooms on the western side of the lake so please use the restroom beforehand.  

For more information visit the Jenny Lake Boating website.
data.audioDescription: The Jenny Lake East Shore Boat Dock and shuttle boat launch is located just east of the stone Jenny Lake Trailhead plaza. Moving south from the stone plaza, be mindful of the single large, granite boulder at the plaza’s far southwest corner, and the single step inside the boulder to the west as you move down from the plaza onto an eight-foot wide asphalt path with low, stone block walls on either side. On the far side of the south stone wall at the top of the path, a four-foot wide, inclined, rectangular metal information panel sits mounted between two granite boulders. A color photograph at the left shows a rocky canyon with sloped sides framing a high, snow-capped mountain peak in the background with the words “Enter the Wild” in the center. Text on a blue field at the right continues: The shuttle boat or the Jenny Lake Loop Trail will take you to the mouth of Cascade Canyon across Jenny Lake. Park lands across the lake are managed as a wilderness: trails are unpaved, services are not available, and vehicles and pets are not permitted. Instead, the forces of nature dominate, and humans are only visitors on the landscape. As you enter the Jenny Lake wilderness, lower your voice and silence your phone to allow yourself and others to enjoy the quiet solitude of this place. A second color photograph at the center right shows a burbling, mountain stream flowing down a rocky bed in the forest. A caption reads: Wilderness…is hereby recognized as an area where the earth and its community of life are untrammeled by man, where man himself is a visitor who does not remain. -Wilderness Act of 1964 At the far right, a third color photograph shows a female park ranger, Millie Jimenez, leaning against a vertical wooden post. A caption reads: Wilderness in My Heart “As a first-generation American growing up in New York City, I had no concept of wilderness until becoming a park ranger. Wilderness can be transformative: a person visiting wilderness leaves a part of their heart behind while retaining a part of wilderness in their heart.” The path to the shuttle launch leads west down a slight incline to a wooden footbridge with four-foot tall railings. Move about 20 feet across the bridge, then turn right and move about 10 feet to come to the boat launch ticket counter under the eaves of a 25-foot long, covered, wooden pavilion. Beyond the ticket counter, the queue for the shuttle boat winds back and forth in a series of rope-lined switchbacks across a wood plank floor to the dock. Note a wooden bench lines the periphery of the pavilion along the base of the walls. Once through the line, a 12-foot wide, inclined wooden ramp with four-foot tall railings on either side leads down to a floating metal dock. Staff on the dock will assist you in boarding the shuttle. Move up a small, three-foot wide ramp on the right side of the dock, and step over the side into the back of the boat.

data.title: Jenny Lake Gateway to Wilderness
data.listingDescription: Interpretive signs introduce the idea of "wilderness". As you head to the western side of Jenny Lake, the developed front country area slips away into an undeveloped, primitive world.

images.altText: Interpretive Signs on Wilderness
images.title: Gateway to Wilderness
images.caption: West of Jenny Lake is primitive, undeveloped, and primarily impacted by the forces of nature.

data.bodyText:
Interpretive signs introduce the idea of "wilderness". As you head to the western side of Jenny Lake, the developed front country area slips away into an undeveloped, primitive world. 

It was here in Grand Teton National Park where Margaret (Mardy) and Olaus Murie, along with Wilderness Society member Howard Zahniser, crafted the language that would become the basis for the Wilderness Act. 

Take some time to read these panels and ponder what wilderness means to you.
data.audioDescription: Heading east from the large restroom building at the far western end of the South Jenny Lake Visitor plaza, a 10-foot wide walkway, paved with large, flat, irregularly-shaped, granite stones parallels the main asphalt walkway. A three-foot tall granite block wall bounds the stone-paved plaza at the back. Note this stone-paved area widens and continues east along the entire plaza, nearly 300-yard (275 m) wide. About 30 feet east of the restrooms are two four-foot wide, inclined, metal information panels mounted across three large boulders embedded in the low, granite block wall. On the first panel at the left, a title across a photograph of a mountain canyon reads, “Gateway to Wilderness.” Text on a field of blue at the right continues: Where you stand, Jenny Lake is developed with buildings, parking areas, and concessions. But, head down one of the nearby paths to the lakeshore, and you will arrive at a gateway to a wider and wilder experience of Grand Teton. The land west of the lake is a world apart. It is a wild and natural world—primitive, undeveloped, and primarily impacted by the forces of nature. A second photograph in the middle of the panel shows a hiker in winter, standing beside a nearly frozen mountain lake at the base of a tall set of snow-capped peaks. Text at the right continues: Wild and Wonderful If you’ve ever wanted to sit still with the sounds of an alpine lake, watch wind whip through a mountain pass, or meditate on the silence of your footsteps on fresh snow—consider a trip to Grand Teton’s wilderness. The park preserves the wild, unrestrained nature of this public land by limiting human influence. Trails west of the lake are undeveloped, prohibit motorized recreation, and have no restrooms or other services. Moving to the right, beyond a central boulder embedded in the low stone wall, a photograph at the left of second inclined, metal information panel shows a rocky, verdant green hillside with a rushing stream. A quote at the top by Howard Zahniser, Principal Author of the Wilderness Act, reads: “We have a profound fundamental need for areas of the earth where we stand without our mechanisms that make us immediate masters over our environment.” Text on a blue field at the right continues: Roots of Wilderness The Wilderness Act of 1964 preserves the “wilderness character” of public lands by restricting human influence and activities to lands designated as Wilderness. Conservationists Margaret (Mardy) and Olaus Murie believed strongly that wilderness lands should remain undeveloped. The Muries, along with Wilderness Society member Howard Zahniser met regularly at the Murie Ranch—here in what is now Grand Teton National Park—over two decades to craft language that would become the basis for the Wilderness Act. A second black-and-white photograph at the right shows a small group of men and women in a cozy, log-cabin room beside a roaring, stone fireplace. A caption reads, “Olaus and Mardy Murie, along with Howard Zahniser, and friends at the Murie Ranch.” Text at the far right reads: The Wilderness Act Defines Wilderness as: UNTRAMMELED: Retains its primeval character and influence UNDEVELOPED: Affected primarily by the forces of nature NATURAL: Persists without permanent improvements or human habitation PRIMITIVE: Affords solitude or a primitive and unconfined type of recreation VALUABLE: Contains features of scientific, educational, scenic, or historical value Behind the panels, a field of sagebrush and pine trees slopes gently uphill, framed by towering mountains rising high into the sky. About 10 feet to the right of the last panel, note a 10-foot wide opening in the stone wall. Framed by two large boulders, a four-foot wide asphalt path leads north up a slight incline, away from the plaza. A sign mounted on the face of the right-hand boulder identifies this as the Discovery Trail, and indicates the Lakeshore is about 250 yards (229 m) to the right.

data.title: Jenny Lake Lodge
data.listingDescription:
The Jenny Lake Lodge was once known as the Danny Ranch. Today, the lodge exemplifies rustic elegance. Individual and duplex cabins are set back in the trees behind a small lodge. Guest amenities include breakfast, dinner, horseback riding and bicycling. Meals are available to all visitors. Although the lodge is near Jenny Lake, the lake itself is hidden from view.
For more information visit the Jenny Lake Lodge website.

images.altText: Approach to Jenny Lake Lodge front door. Brown log cabin with wooden chairs on walkway and small patio. Flower baskets hang from eaves.
images.caption: Entrance to Jenny Lake Lodge

data.bodyText:
The Jenny Lake Lodge was once known as the Danny Ranch. Today, the lodge exemplifies rustic elegance. Individual and duplex cabins are set back in the trees behind a small lodge. Guest amenities include breakfast, dinner, horseback riding and bicycling. Meals are available to all visitors. Although the lodge is near Jenny Lake, the lake itself is hidden from view.
For more information visit the Jenny Lake Lodge website.

Name Origin

Jenny was the Shoshone Indian wife of a British expatriate named Richard "Beaver Dick" Leigh. He moved to the Teton area in 1863 as a fur trapper. Jenny and Beaver Dick assisted the 1872 Hayden expedition - he as their guide, she with camp logistics. The Hayden Expedition named Jenny and Leigh lakes in their honor.
data.audioDescription: Jenny Lodge has paved parking areas on either side of a central grassy median. The roadways on either side lead to the cabins located toward the rear of the property and on either side of the parking lot. On the left side of the parking area is a log building which contains a dining room on its left side and a gathering area and a gift shop on the right. A gently sloped cement sidewalk leads from the parking lot up along the left side of the building onto a wooden deck. The deck extends along the building with a porch area to your right. The entrance is on the wall on the left side of the porch.
