data.title: Jenny Lake Overlook
data.listingDescription: Jenny Lake is the most popular destination in the park. The view across the lake toward Cascade Canyon is stunning. Pleistocene glaciers carved the U-shaped canyon and the basin filled by the lake today. Many people have visited in the past-American Indians, fur trappers, survey expeditions, dude ranchers, car campers and adventurers. The lake is named for a Shoshone Indian woman named Jenny who married a British fur trapper named Richard "Beaver Dick" Leigh.

images.altText: A view across Jenny Lake looking toward Inspiration Point at the mouth of Cascade Canyon with the Cathedral Group peaks to the left and Mt. St. John to the right.
images.caption: View Across Jenny Lake

data.bodyText:
Jenny Lake is the most popular destination in the park. The view across the lake toward Cascade Canyon is stunning. Pleistocene glaciers carved the U-shaped canyon and the basin filled by the lake today. Many people have visited in the past-American Indians, fur trappers, survey expeditions, dude ranchers, car campers and adventurers. The lake is named for a Shoshone Indian woman named Jenny who married a British fur trapper named Richard "Beaver Dick" Leigh. Richard and Jenny assisted the Hayden Survey of 1872 as they mapped and explored the valley. Notice these names as you travel around the park.

Name Origin

Jenny was the Shoshone Indian wife of a British expatriate named Richard "Beaver Dick" Leigh. He moved to the Teton area in 1863 as a fur trapper. Jenny and Beaver Dick assisted the 1872 Hayden expedition - he as their guide, she with camp logistics. The Hayden Expedition named Jenny and Leigh lakes in their honor.
data.audioDescription: Along side the paved parking lot at this turnout is a wide aggregate sidewalk bordered by a three-foot high stone wall. On the far side of the wall the land falls steeply down through dark green conifers to the edge of the lake. The lake here is small and oval-shaped, the water a bright blue on clear days. It nestles at the base of the Teton Range, with the mountains seeming to rise directly out of the water. Directly across the lake is a deep canyon extending back between Teewinot Mountain on your left and Mount St. John on your right. Towards the right end of the sidewalk is a wayside sign. About mid-way along the wall is an opening where paths lead to a lower walkway. In the sidewalk pavement at this point are footprints left by a wandering moose. The path down the bank splits into two paths. The right hand fork descends in broad, shallow steps. The fork to the left descends a long ramp. Both lead to a stone-edged sidewalk overlooking the lake with log benches along the side away from the lake. The background image on the wayside sign is a color photograph of the canyon and mountains in front of you. Text on the left reads, "Jenny Lake. Across Jenny Lake from here, Cascade Canyon slices through the heart of the Teton Range. Before Pleistocene glaciers carved out the U-shape canyon we see today, streams initially cut a V-shaped canyon. Glaciers act like belt-sanders. Glacial ice flowing downhill picks up rocky debris that grinds away the bedrock broadening and deepening the canyon. "Around 20,000 years ago, the last glacier flowed out of this canyon onto the valley floor bulldozing out a depression. As the ice melted, rocky debris carried by the glacier deposited as ridges called moraines. Today, moraines form the natural dams around lakes such as Jenny, Leigh and Jackson fed by remnant glaciers and snowmelt." Below the text is an historical photograph showing a man standing in front of a teepee on the left. He wears a beard and holds a long rifle. A dark-haired woman sits on the ground by the teepee along with three young children. An older child sits on one of a pair of donkeys at the right. The caption reads, "Jenny was the Shoshone Indian wife of Richard "Beaver Dick" Leigh, a trapper who served as guide for the 1872 Hayden Expedition." At the bottom right corner of the panel is a drawing showing a three-dimensional cross section view of a mountainside with a glacier. At the right side a circular ice field below higher peaks is labeled a cirque. Further down to the left is a glacier shown as an icy river. Around its lower edge is a line of debris labeled as a moraine. Still further at the left edge of the drawing is a flat area showing branching water flow from the melting ice on the outwash plain. The caption reads, "Jenny Lake is more than 250 feet deep indicating the power of glaciers to sculpt the landscape."

data.title: Jenny Lake Pathway Hub
data.listingDescription: The Jenny Lake Pathway Hub is the most northern point of the multi-use pathway. Read our informational sign about biking and use the bike rack to store your bike while you explore the Jenny Lake area.

images.altText: Information panel on Jenny Lake Pathway Hub described in the audio description
images.title: Jenny Lake Pathway Hub Sign
images.caption: Bike, walk, and ride at the base of the Tetons.

data.bodyText:
Start or end your bike ride at the Jenny Lake hub. You will find a bike rack and informational panels about biking and the multi-use pathway. Biking south will take you towards Moose. The multi-use pathway ends here so if you bike north, be prepared to bike on Teton Park Road. Biking north will take you to the Jenny Lake Scenic Drive where there is a dedicated two-way bike lane. If exploring the Jenny Lake front country area, please use the bike rack or walk your bike. Take some time to read the informational panels so you can have a fun and safe bike ride. 

For a complete overview of biking in the park and an interactive map, please check out our biking page on our website.
data.audioDescription: The bike rack is located just north of the south parking lot, across the street from the drop-off pullout in front of the Jenny Lake Entrance Station. A crosswalk leads from the top of the lot into the roughly rectangular bike rack area surrounded by a wooden fence: a series of single, inclined logs supported by vertical wooden posts, spaced eight feet apart. Two rows of three-foot high, tubular steel arches run north-to-south along either side of a central asphalt strip, parallel to the road. One line of racks runs along the tree line away from the road, the other inside the log fence next to the road. Just off the asphalt surface under the trees, to the west of the bike racks, note a set of three park information panels mounted in an eight-foot tall by ten-foot wide log frame structure, beside a low, backless, wooden park bench. Facing the panels, text at the top of the left-hand panel reads: “Jenny Lake Hub Pathway. Bike, walk, and ride at the base of the Tetons. Explore the park at your own speed while experiencing the grandeur of the Tetons. Travel through the vast sagebrush steppe and feel the exhilaration of the elements.” Below that text is a curvy line with small human figures biking, skating, and rollerblading. Beneath the line, on the left, is a header that reads: “How to Ride” Beneath “How to Ride” are three bulleted points marked with small circle graphics. The first bullet point is titled: “Ride Responsibly” Beneath “Ride Responsibly”, the text reads: “Be visible and be predictable. Obey all traffic laws and posted signs.” The second bullet point is titled: “Share the Path” Beneath “Share the Path”, the text reads: “Say “hi” when approaching other users. Keep right while moving and allow others to pass on the left. Move to the right when you stop.” The third bullet point is titled: “Stay Vigilant” Beneath the title, the text reads: “Keep your bear spray within reach and always yield to migrating animals.” Next to the column titled “How to Ride” is a header that reads: “What to Bring” Beneath “What to Bring” are 8 bullet points marked by small graphics. The bullet points read: “Food and Water. Bring two liters of water and a high energy snack.” “First Aid. Travel with a basic first aid kit and know how to use it.” “Layers. Be prepared for sudden weather shifts.” “Helmet. Protect your head and wear bright colors.” “Repair Kit. Your kit should include a bike tool, spare tube, and a pump.” “Sun Protection. Sunglasses, sunscreen, and a hate will go a long way.” “Navigation. Know your route and how far you’re going.” “Bear Spray. Keep it within reach and know how to use it.” Moving down the panel, the next header reads: “Where to Ride” Below the header are three rectangular photos arranged next to each other with text on the image. Directly below the photo is a rectangular text box. The first photo on the left hand side is of a lake and mountains. The mountains slope down to a lake shore and a portion of a lake. There are trees close to the viewer and along the lakeshore. It appears sunny with some clouds in the sky. The text at the bottom of the photo reads: “Jenny Lake to String Lake” Below the image is a text box describing the route. It reads: “Travel north through the Jenny Lake Campground to connect with the Scenic Drive. Use the bike lanes to reach String Lake. 3.0 mi / 4.8 km one way. This route uses unprotected bike lanes.” The next photo in the middle has a man on a bike with a helmet and backpack. He is riding the bike away from the viewer and looking back. He is on a paved bike path next to a field of sagebrush with some mountain peaks in the background. It appears sunny with some wispy clouds in the sky. The text at the bottom of the photo reads: “Jenny Lake to Moose” Below is a text box describing the route. It reads: “Follow the pathway through the sagebrush to Moose Bike Hub. Visit the Craig Thomas Discovery and Visitor Center in Moose. 7.2 mi / 11.6 km one way. There is a steep hill (5% grade) north of the Moose Entrance Station.” The third and final photo on the right hand side of the panel shows two adults on skateboards with helmets riding on a paved pathway away from the viewer. One person has a backpack. The pathway is next to a field of sagebrush and there are mountains in the distance. It is sunny with no clouds in the sky. The text at the bottom of the photo reads: “Jenny Lake to Jackson” Below is a text box describing the route. It reads: “Head south to the town of Jackson for a longer ride. Enjoy panoramic views of the Tetons and the Gros Ventre Mountain Range. This route connects to the Jackson Community Pathways. 20.1 mi / 32.3 km one way” Moving about three feet to the right, the middle panel displays a map of the park. At the top of the panel is a black bar with white text that reads: “Grand Teton Pathway” The map shows Grand Teton National Park. The map shows as far north as Leigh Lake, as far south as the town of Jackson, as far west as the border of Grand Teton National Park and National Forest Land, and as far east as the border of Grand Teton National Park and Bridger Teton National Forest. Roads, waterways, lakes, peaks, trailheads, amenities, and pathway hubs are displayed on the map. The Jenny Lake hub has a zoomed in map in the shape of a circle showing the south Jenny Lake area. Beneath the header “Jenny Lake Hub” it says, “You Are Here”. The pathway routes are highlighted in bright green. The routes highlighted correlate with the routes described on the left-hand panel. In the lower right-hand corner, a legend defines features used on the map. Moving about three more feet to the right is the third and final panel. The far-right panel has a large photo banner at the top. The photo shows a group of 7 male and female bicyclists stopped on the side of the road looking away from the viewer up the road where a herd of bison are grazing in the field and standing in the roadway. At the bottom left of the photo banner, large text reads: “Things to Know” Below the photo banner are various safety rules and regulations related to the pathway and biking. Two columns with three points each are bulleted with small graphics. The bulleted points read: “E-bikes are considered bicycles if they have fully operable pedals and an electric motor of less than 750 watts (1hp).” “The multi-use pathway is closed from dusk to dawn for wildlife and public safety.” “Leave what you find. Keep items in their natural setting for others to enjoy. Picking wildflowers and collecting historic objects, archaeological artifacts, or antlers is prohibited.” To the right is another column of bulleted points with “no symbol/prohibition” symbols. The first no-symbol has a dog graphic. Next to the symbol, the bulleted points read: “Pets are not allowed on the pathway. Elk, deer, and pronghorn frequently cross the pathway during migration. Follow food storage requirements and never leave food unattended.” Moving down the panel is a graphic that displays how far away to be from wildlife. From the left of the panel to the right of the panel runs a thin line. There are skating and bicycling human figures on the left side. Moving to the right, marked as twenty-five yards away is a bison, bull moose, and bull elk graphic symbol. Text beneath the symbols read: “Bison, moose, elk, and all other wildlife Keep 25 yards (23 m) away” Moving further right along the line, marked as 100 yards away are a bear and wolf graphic symbol. Beneath the symbols, the text reads: “Bears and wolves Keep 100 yards (91 m) away” At the bottom of the panel is a photo of bicycles lined up. The photo fades out at the top. On top of the faded photo are two large text boxes. One is titled: “Where can I take my pet?” It has a small dog on a leash graphic. Beneath the header, the text reads: “In the park, leashed pets may go anywhere a car may go—roads and road shoulders, campgrounds, picnic areas, and parking lots. Pets are not allowed on the pathway. Outside of the park, check out the Jackson Hole Community Pathways or nearby US Forest Service lands.” To the right of the first text box is a second text box titled: “Riding on the Road” It has a small bicyclist graphic. Beneath the header, the text reads: “Sharing the road with cars requires special safety considerations. Traffic is heavy during the summer, with daily peaks midmorning to late afternoon. Road conditions vary in the park. Some roads have paved marked shoulders, other roads have very narrow shoulders or lack them altogether. Expect to see vehicles parked on the shoulder, especially near popular destinations. Use caution when riding by cars parked on roadways.”

data.title: Jenny Lake Plaza

data.bodyText:
Dive deeper into the history of Grand Teton National Park. Interpretive signs introduce topics like the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, grizzly bear research, geologic forces and features, glaciers, and the Hayden Survey.

A large bronze tactile relief map will help orient you in relation to where you are in the park. Different peaks, canyons, lakes, falls, and other park features are labeled throughout the map.
data.audioDescription: Outside the Jenny Lake Visitor Center, the asphalt portion of the plaza widens to meet a nearly 100-foot (30 m) wide, flat triangular area paved with large, flat, irregularly-shaped, granite stones, bounded by a three-foot tall granite stone wall at the back. A large, bronze tactile map stands in the center of the plaza. Along the top of the low stone wall, behind the map, is the first of a set of three, four-foot wide, inclined metal information panels mounted across two large boulders embedded in the wall. At the far left of the panel, a map of northwest Wyoming shows Yellowstone and Grand Teton National Parks in light green, surrounded by a larger blue area extending further south into Wyoming and into parts of Idaho to the west, and Montana to the north. Text in a blue field at the right reads: Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem Covering 20 million acres, the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem is one of the largest intact temperate-zone ecosystems on Earth. Intact ecosystems are extremely rare today, but this ecosystem has not lost a single species of plant or animal since explored by fur trappers. A photograph in the center shows two grizzly bears foraging in a rocky, mountain meadow. A third photograph to the right shows two men attaching a neck collar to a grizzly bear that is lying on the ground. Text reads: Worthy of Protection Biologist Frank Craighead, Jr., first used the term “Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem” in 1979 to describe the vast area then occupied by grizzly bears. Frank (left) teamed with his brother John (right) to expand their studies beyond grizzly bears. They wanted to understand the ecosystem as a whole and recognized that the entire ecosystem was worthy of protection. The brothers pioneered the use of radio collars in grizzly bear research during their 1959–1970 study. At the far right of the panel is a life-sized cast paw of the first grizzly bear radio-collared by Frank and John Craighead in Yellowstone in 1959. Touch the cast to feel its claws, size, and texture. Moving about 15 feet to the right, two more inclined, metal panels sit atop the low stone wall, supported by three more large boulders in the wall. Text at the left of the first panel reads: A Restless Earth Powerful geologic forces are uplifting the steep Teton Range in front of you and dropping the valley of Jackson Hole. The same subterranean heat that fuels Yellowstone’s geothermal features helps lift and stretch the entire region, producing the Teton fault and the Yellowstone Plateau. A photograph shows the steep, sheer, rocky faces of the Teton Range, dusted with snow. Three more photographs on a blue field fill the right side of the panel. The first shows a low portion of a rocky hillside with a dark band across the center with the words, “Fault Scarp.” Text explains this is the: Teton Fault About ten million years ago, the Earth’s crust began stretching and cracking, generating many earthquakes on the Teton fault. Each earthquake tipped the Teton Range steeply upwards, while the Jackson Hole valley hinged downward. Steep slopes along the base of the mountains—called fault scarps—provide evidence of this process. The second photograph in the center shows a portion of the mountain range completely buried in snow. Text reads: A Sea of Ice About two million years ago, glaciers began flowing off the Yellowstone Plateau and down from mountain canyons. Like slow-moving rivers, these glaciers buried the Jackson Hole valley under several thousand feet of ice. From this vast, icy expanse, the highest Teton peaks jutted up like jagged islands. The third photograph shows a large boulder sitting by itself beside a trail in the summer. Text reads: Out of Place Ever notice large boulders out of place on the landscape? These may be glacial erratics—rocks that fell on the ice or were plucked from canyon walls. As glaciers move, they carry debris for miles along a conveyor belt of ice. Glacial erratics are deposited across the landscape as the ice melts. Move about a foot to the right, around a second boulder, to the second information panel. At the far left, a reproduction of a survey map of the Tetons from the 1870s is shown. Text on a blue field at the right reads: An Unmapped Range In the early 1870s, explorers Ferdinand Hayden and James Stevenson led a team to survey and map the Teton Range. While American Indians, fur trappers, and prospectors were familiar with the Tetons, Stevenson’s division of the Hayden Survey built upon this knowledge to produce a detailed map of the territory. In the center of the panel, a black-and-white photograph shows four men sitting and standing in front of a canvas tent on a wide, mountain plain. A caption at the lower right reads: Stevenson’s team included geologists, botanists, map-makers, and artists to study and map the region. At the far-right, several surveying instruments from around 1870 are mounted to the panel’s face, including a hammer, compass, and viewing scope. Text beside these instruments reads: Tools of the Trade The expedition used tools like these to collect scientific specimens, and to survey and measure the landscape. Touch these instruments to feel their shape, size, and features. About 30 feet to the right, note another 10-foot wide gap in the stone wall where an asphalt path leads north along another portion of the Discovery Trail to the Lakeshore. Located in the middle of the granite plaza outside the Crandall Studio is a nearly 12-foot wide by six-foot deep bronze, three-dimensional tactile map of the Teton Range. Raised letters and words identify the different peaks, canyons, lakes, and falls. A raised star towards the front right, labeled “You Are Here,” indicates your current position alongside Jenny Lake. A raised-letter key at the right associates the letters A through Q with the specific park feature identified on the map’s surface. Wander around all sides and touch the map to feel the topography of the Tetons. Note a smaller touch map is available inside the Visitor Center. It can also be brought outside to this larger bronze map for clarity and comparison. Please ask a ranger inside the Visitor Center if would like to experience this smaller map.

data.audioDescription: There are two restroom buildings at the far western end of the Jenny Lake Visitor Center plaza. The first restroom building is located west from the Crandall Studio, just past the Donor Wall walkway along the main asphalt path. The men’s room is to the left, and the women’s room is to the right. There’s a family restroom in the center. Facing the restroom building, note two wooden park benches with armrests and backs outside the front of the building at the left. Immediately to the right of the building, an asphalt path leads south back to the south parking lot. A third, backless, wooden park bench sits directly opposite the path to the parking lot, on the north side of the plaza, along the main asphalt walkway. A second, larger restroom building is located at the very far western end of the plaza. Once again, the men’s room is to the left, the women’s room is to the right. There’s a family restroom in the center. Note there is a water fountain and water bottle filling station on the outside, front left wall of this building.

data.bodyText: The Jenny Lake store is a convenient option if you're looking to buy firewood, ice, clothing, souvenirs, and snacks. This store is located right next to the Jenny Lake Visitor Center and a five minute walk from the Jenny Lake Campground making it an easy stop while you explore the area.
data.audioDescription: About 40 feet west of the Jenny Lake Entrance area, beyond the bronze tactile park map and information panels, a roughly 15-foot wide asphalt walkway at the right leads about 15 feet up a slight incline to the Jenny Lake Store, a one-story log cabin structure. There’s a set of double wood and glass store entry doors in the center, and an eight-foot-wide, covered wooden deck wraps the front and left sides of the building. Note additional granite boulders along the edges of the walkway leading to the store. Moving across the threshold into the store, note the cash register is to the right. The store sells camping and hiking supplies, groceries, gifts, postcards and souvenirs, books, hot dogs, snacks, ice, water, and soft drinks. You may also purchase jewelry, clothing, puzzles, and other knick-knacks. Outside, to the right of the doors, note a water fountain and water bottle filling station mounted on the exterior log wall. Just beyond the filling station to the left is a low, wooden bench, next to a pay phone mounted on the wall. In front of the filling station, a roughly 15-foot wide by 20-foot long porch extends out from the building towards the main walkway, ringed with a four foot tall log fence. There are three wooden picnic tables in the center, and several metal garbage cans at the far east side of the porch, away from the store doors. To the left of the doors, the covered porch continues past a second long, low wooden bench to the corner of the building, then turns right. Two more low wooden benches along this exterior side wall flank a pair of double wood and glass side doors leading west from the store out onto the larger plaza area.

images.caption: Your Teton backcountry adventure starts here.

data.bodyText:
Hikes

There are numerous hiking options from this trailhead. You can do the Jenny Lake Loop, Hidden Falls and Inspiration Point, Forks of Cascade Canyon, North Fork or South Fork Cascade, Moose Ponds, or link to the String Lake and Paintbrush Canyon trails. 

You can use the Jenny Lake Boat Shuttle one-way or round-trip to shorten any hike. The shuttle boat goes from the East Shore Boat Dock to the West Shore Boat Dock. There is a fee to use the shuttle. 

Jenny Lake Loop

7.1 miles round-trip, 4 hours, 1,040 ft total climbing. Moderate.
Rolling trail that alternates between the lakeshore and glacial moraine.

Hidden Falls 

4.9 miles round-trip, 2.5 hours, 620 ft total climbing. Moderate.
Via shuttle boat: 1.0 mile round-trip, 1.5 hours, 300 ft total climbing. Easy.
Popular trail climbs to a view of a 200-ft cascade.

Inspiration Point

5.7 miles round-trip, 3 hours, 870 ft total climbing. Moderate.
Via shuttle boat: 1.8 miles round-trip, 2.5 hours, 550 ft total climbing. Easy.
Popular trail climbs to view point of Jenny Lake.

Forks of Cascade Canyon

13.3 miles round-trip, 8 hours, 1,720 ft total climbing. Strenuous.
Via shuttle boat: 9.2 miles round-trip, 6 hours, 1,480 ft total climbing, Moderately strenuous.
Popular trail leads into Cascade Canyon with views of the Grand Teton, Mt. Owen, and Teewinot.

Lake Solitude - North Fork

18.3 miles round-trip, 11.5 hours, 2,910 ft total climbing. Strenuous.
Via shuttle boat: 14.4 miles round-trip, 10 hours, 2,670 ft total climbing. Very strenuous.
Follow Cascade Canyon trail. North Fork leads to Lake Solitude and views of the Grand Teton and Mt. Owen.

Hurricane Pass - South Fork

23.9 miles round-trip, 15 hours, 4,370 ft total climbing. Very strenuous.
Via shuttle boat: 20 miles round-trip, 13.5 hours, 4,370 ft total climbing. Very strenuous.
Follow Cascade Canyon trail. South Fork leads to Schoolroom Glacier and Hurrican Pass. 

Location

The Jenny Lake Trailhead is eight miles north on the Teton Park Road from Moose Junction. The trailhead is located next to the east boat dock and provides access to the core of the Teton backcountry.

Notes

Visitor services include a visitor center, restrooms, water, store, ranger station, shuttle boat, boat rentals and campground. The parking lot is often full from 9am-4 pm. Arrive early to secure your space. Bears may be active any place and at any time--travel in groups, make noise and carry bear spray. Backcountry camping requires a permit--pick one up at a backcountry permits office.

Name Origin

Jenny was the Shoshone Indian wife of a British expatriate named Richard "Beaver Dick" Leigh. He moved to the Teton area in 1863 as a fur trapper. Jenny and Beaver Dick assisted the 1872 Hayden expedition - he as their guide, she with camp logistics. The Hayden Expedition named Jenny and Leigh Lakes in their honor.
data.audioDescription: The Jenny Lake Trailhead is located next to the East Boat Dock on a wide, open area paved with flat granite stones. A low, three-foot tall granite block wall runs along the entire 50-foot length of the trailhead plaza at the back. In the center of the plaza, spaced roughly 25 feet apart, are two large, four-foot wide, dual-sided information panels mounted between eight-foot tall double log posts. Between the two sign panels, just off the asphalt path, note the first of three, large granite boulders embedded in the ground, the remaining two being located at the far southern end of the plaza. From a position at the south end of the plaza facing the first information panel, text along the left-hand side of the panel identifies this as the Jenny Lake Trailhead. Information on how to protect yourself, wildlife, and your park is presented. Text advises that you always bring a map, as battery-powered devices may be unreliable in the park. Bring along a first aid kit, bear spray, and rain gear. Carry extra water to avoid dehydration, high-energy snacks to prevent fatigue, and protect yourself from the sun. Visitors who plan to take a service animal into the backcountry should complete an acknowledgment form in a ranger station. Otherwise, pets are not allowed on park trails or in buildings. It is illegal to feed any wildlife, and one should always maintain a distance of at least 100 yards from bears and wolves, and 25 yards from other wildlife. Information on the right-hand side of this panel provides tips on how to have a safe and enjoyable visit. Text implores you to be responsible for your own safety, as rescue is not a certainty. Keep your group together, especially children, monitor weather changes, know when to turn around, and leave the park as you found it. Be bear aware. Avoid surprising a bear, hike in groups, carry and know how to use bear spray, and never approach a bear. Follow all food storage regulations, and if you do encounter a bear, stop, and remain calm. Never run from a bear, rather slowly back away while facing the bear. Information at the bottom right-hand side of the panel provides tips on safe hiking, backpacking, climbing, and mountaineering. Moving to the back side of this first sign, a map of the greater Jenny Lake area fills the top of the panel, with a black and white “You Are Here” label at the lower left. Black and white graphic icons with black text labels indicate the locations of the facilities, overlooks, and trailheads. At the lower left is a key to those icons. Text on a blue field at the bottom of the panel reads: Explore Jenny Lake and Beyond Backcountry adventures await you across Jenny Lake. If your visit allow four hours, take time to explore the Lenny Lake area more deeply. Trails wind up canyons, offering opportunities to explore the Grand Teton wilderness. If you prefer to stay in the front-country, bike, paddle, or drive to discover unique views of the rugged central peaks of the Teton Range. Three color photographs at the bottom right show hikers in Cascade Canyon, a family on bicycles enjoying a view, and a trout swimming at the water line, with snow-capped mountains above, and the lakebed below. Text underneath these photographs suggest various activities if you have four hours or more. To the left of this last panel, note a roughly three-foot tall metal box with a hinged, sloping lid. Attached to the front, a small blue sign reads, “Visitor Guide.” A small blue sign attached to the lid reads: “$1 Donation, or Borrow and Return.” About eight feet to the east of this panel, near the edge of the stone plaza, a four-foot wide bronze tactile map of the park and its trails sits mounted on top of a granite boulder. This three-dimensional map covers the same area as the map on the panel. Wander around all sides of this exhibit to feel the mountain peaks, canyons, roads, and trails within the park, all identified with raised letters and words. A raised star towards the front right, labeled “You Are Here,” indicates your current position alongside Jenny Lake. A raised-letter key at the front left associates the letters A through J with the specific park feature identified on the map’s surface. Note a granite boulder embedded in the ground about ten feet south of this map at the corner of the stone plaza. Just to the west of this boulder, note the only step in this whole front-country area where the stone plaza re-joins the asphalt path leading to the shuttle boat launch. Moving to the second information panel towards the north end of the plaza, a chart on a blue field covering the left-hand side of the sign provides information about wilderness trails. Text reads: Once you leave the pavement, or take the boat shuttle across Jenny Lake, you will be on a wilderness trail system. Expect to encounter numerous rocks scattered throughout the trail surface, exposed tree roots, and multiple stairs. Stair steps vary from 2 to 11 inches high. Wheelchairs are welcome, but trails may be difficult to negotiate. Strollers, bicycles, and other wheeled vehicles are not allowed. At the left, the chart lists the various trails in the Jenny Lake Loop, Hidden Falls Loop, Inspiration Point Loop, and the Moose Ponds Loop, along with each of their lengths, grades, width, cross slopes, and obstacles. A few posters at the right entreat visitors to not feed the foxes, be bear aware, and to be careful of sparks from vehicles which could cause wildfires. Moving to the back side of this second sign, text on a blue field on the left side of the panel reads: Ancient Trails Your path around Jenny Lake follows in the footsteps of many who came before you. The first evidence of human activity here dates to more than 10,000 years ago. This special place has been a destination for tribes, trappers, explorers, homesteaders, and modern travelers. Today, trails around the lake and into the canyons remain primitive, providing a glimpse into the same mountain landscape experienced by those before you. At the right, a large color photograph fills the top half of the panel showing the rocky shoreline of Jenny Lake. Along the bottom half are a series of four images. The first shows a black-and-white photograph of an American Indian on horseback in winter representing First Peoples. A caption reads: The earliest evidence of human activity in the area near Jenny Lake dates to more than 10,000 years ago. American Indian peoples hunted, fished, and gathered plants here as part of their regular, seasonal migration route. Spiritual ties to the land, water, plants, and animals still persist in Indian people today. The second image shows a color illustration of a trapper clad head to toe in leather. A caption reads: Trappers on the Creek Jackson Hole was once a destination for fur trappers. Few records were kept among the diverse bands of trappers that included recent immigrants from Europe, former slaves, native Hawaiians, and American Indians from eastern and western tribes. Trappers in this area moved along streams like Cottonwood Creek seeking beaver pelts. Next, a black-and-white photograph shows a couple men on horseback dwarfed by a stand of trees and the Teton Range above them, with the caption: Presidential Trail Guides Jackson Hole was a vacation destination of President Chester A. Arthur, who traveled here to fish in Jackson Lake and the Snake River. Pictured above are the president’s American Indian guides in front of Teewinot Mountain in 1883. A final black-and-white photograph shows a group of men standing, kneeling, and sitting in several lines in a field. A caption reads: Trail Builders During the Great Depression, many young men found work in national parks through the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC).

data.title: Jenny Lake West Shore Boat Dock
data.listingDescription: The west shore boat dock is where the shuttle boat drops off passengers who boarded on the eastern side. You can also board the shuttle boat here for a one-way trip back to the eastern side. You can pay for the one-way trip at the East Shore Boat Dock.

images.altText: Passengers loading the Jenny Lake Shuttle Boat at the West Shore Boat Dock.
images.title: Jenny Lake West Shore Boat Dock
images.caption: Access numerous Jenny Lake backcountry trails from the West Shore Boat Dock.

data.bodyText:
The west shore boat dock is where the shuttle boat drops off passengers who boarded on the eastern side. You can also board the shuttle boat here for a one-way trip back to the eastern side. You can pay for the one-way trip at the East Shore Boat Dock. 

From the boat dock, take the trails to Hidden Falls, Inspiration Point, Cascade Canyon, and the Jenny Lake Loop. There are no bathrooms or other facilities on the western shore. This is a popular service during the peak summer months (June-August) so expect lines. It is 2.5 miles to hike back to the eastern shore on the Jenny Lake Loop trail along the southern edge. 

Please read below for more details on services offered from Jenny Lake Boating. 

Shuttle Service

Jenny Lake Boating

Jenny Lake Boating provides shuttle services across Jenny Lake at the base of Mount Teewinot. On the West side of the lake you will find the Cascade Canyon trailhead. There are trails from the boat dock to Hidden Falls (1/2 mile each way), Inspiration Point (1 mile each way) and into Cascade Canyon that leads North to Solitude Lake or South to the South Fork of Cascade Canyon, and beyond to Hurricane Pass and Schoolroom Glacier.

Reservations are not taken as the boats run continuously throughout the day. Come to the East Boat Dock, purchase the fare, and board the boat.

The shuttle boat eliminates a 2-mile hike (each way) to the Cascade Canyon trailhead, thereby saving time and energy for your hiking day.

Shuttles run every 10-15 minutes throughout the day. The last boat will leave the dock at the posted closing time.

Options are available to take the shuttle round-trip (over and back with hiking time between); One-way from either East or West dock (ride the boat one way and hike one way). It is possible to hike to Hidden Falls and then take the shuttle to return to the East side of the lake. Simply hop on the next boat and pay at the counter on the East Dock.

Prices:

$ 20.00 – Adult Round-trip (12 yrs to 61 yrs)

$ 12.00 – Adult One-Way

$ 12.00 – Child Round-trip (2 yrs to 11 yrs)

$ 10.00 – Child One-Way

$ 17.00 – Senior Round-trip (62 yrs and over)

No Senior One-Way rate

FREE Under 2 years of age and over 80 yrs.
data.audioDescription: The shuttle boat makes the nearly mile-long trip across Jenny Lake to the West Shore boat dock. Staff on the boat and dock will assist you in disembarking from the shuttle boat onto a wide, floating dock with wood planking. Move up a three-foot wide, inclined metal ramp to a wide, wooden dock waiting area, ringed with four-foot tall wooden railings. Note several wooden benches on the dock at the right. Move up a set of stairs from the dock to a gravel loop trail, and proceed left, or west, up along a relatively steep incline along a trail that leads along Cascade Creek towards Hidden Falls and Inspiration Point. Note the abundance of huckleberry bushes lining the sides of the trail. During the summer, feel free to pick and taste the ripe, deep purple fruit, but always be bear aware as you do so.

data.title: John & Bartha Moulton Barn
data.listingDescription: The John Moulton barn is an iconic structure in Jackson Hole. The sunrise view with the barn in the foreground and the Teton Range as the backdrop is one of the most photographed structures in the valley. The remaining fences and corrals add character to the view. John Moulton and his brother Thomas Alva (T.A.) homesteaded on Mormon Row in 1908. John dry farmed grain until the state built irrigation ditches to the Mormon Row area in the late 1920s.

images.altText: A historic log barn with snow covered mountains in the background.
images.title: John & Bartha Moulton Barn
images.caption: John & Bartha Moulton Barn

data.bodyText:
The John Moulton barn is an iconic structure in Jackson Hole. The sunrise view with the barn in the foreground and the Teton Range as the backdrop is one of the most photographed structures in the valley. The remaining fences and corrals add character to the view.

John Moulton and his brother Thomas Alva (T.A.) homesteaded on Mormon Row in 1908. John dry farmed grain until the state built irrigation ditches to the Mormon Row area in the late 1920s. Around that same time, John switched to dairy farming and sold his milk, cream and butter to nearby dude ranches.
data.audioDescription: To the right of the house is the barn, set closer to the road with a log-railed fence enclosing a paddock in front. The building is a traditional barn-shape with a one story winged addition on either side. The barn is built of dark-stained log with white chinking. The roof is covered with wood shingles. The side facing the road has no main door, although there are small doors into the one story winged additions on the outer edges of the front.

data.title: John & Bartha Moulton Residence
data.listingDescription: The "Pink House" as it is locally known was once the residence of John and Bertha Moulton. For the first 17 years of their marriage, the couple lived in a small log cabin. Around 1934, they built the pink stucco house. John and his brother T.A. homesteaded on Mormon Row around 1908. Their iconic homesteads provide a glimpse into communal life in Grovont in the early 1900s.

data.audioDescription: This small house has an outer stucco-like finish painted pink, which has softened to almost a peach-color. data.title: John D. Rockefeller, Jr. Memorial Parkway North Turnout
data.listingDescription: The north boundary of the John D. Rockefeller, Jr. Memorial Parkway abuts Yellowstone National Park. The headwaters of the adjacent Snake River are east along the Yellowstone, Teton Wilderness Boundary. Lodgepole pines regenerated after the 1988 Yellowstone fires cover the landscape. The parkway is the northern-most parcel of land managed by Grand Teton National Park. Stop at the wayside to learn about activities in the park, the Rockefeller Legacy and a map.

data.audioDescription: This turnout is on the boundary between Yellowstone National Park to the north and the John D Rockefeller Memorial Parkway to the south. Young conifer woods and open meadows lie on either side of the road. The Snake River can be seen to the east of the road. At the edge of the sidewalk bordering the turnout is a large, three-panel wayside sign hanging in a wooden post structure. The left hand panel shows a photo of mountain peaks at the top. Text reads, "Explore Teton Country. Discover the magnificent landscape and wild communities of Grand Teton National Park. Here the Teton Range rises abruptly from the high mountain valley known as Jackson Hole. From bare alpine rocks to lush meadows and floodplains, the national park is home to bald eagles, grizzly bears, river otters, and bison." Underneath the photo is a quote: "Today, come to this national park with an open mind, open eyes, and an open heart ... walk the trails ... canoe ... you may see a moose or two ... a great blue heron, a pair of trumpeter swans ... These quiet adventures will remain with you always.-Margaret E. "Mardy" Murie" A band of photos across the middle of the panel show, from left to right, several canoes being paddled on smooth water with reflections of autumn trees, a group of schoolchildren in a meadow with a park ranger, a mother elk with her calf and a bright blue tent near a lake. Below these an inset photo shows a large moose crossing a road and at the bottom two hikers in a meadow with the mountain range in the distance. Additional text blocks read, "Plan Your Visit. Pick up a map and newspaper at any entrance station or visitor center to help plan your trip. Stop at visitor centers for orientation information, ranger-led activities, and interpretive exhibits. "Be Extra Careful. Drive carefully, obey speed limits, and watch for wildlife on roads. Drivers hit and kill more than 100 large animals on park roads each year. Animals are wild. Do not feed or approach them. Stay more than 100 yards away from all large animals. Be "Bear Aware." Black and grizzly bears can be anywhere in the park. Protect your food and toiletries from bears, even toothpaste and sunscreen. It all smells to a bear. Please be careful. Follow food storage regulations. Do not leave food unattended. Keep pets on a leash six feet long or less. Pets are not allowed on unpaved trails, the multi-use pathway or in the visitor centers." At the top right is a photo of a bald eagle in flight. At the bottom right is a photo of an elk. At the top right of the third panel is a photograph of John D. Rockefeller and his first wife Abby with the Tetons in the background on a visit in 1931. At the bottom of the panel is a photo of the mountains with a small wooden building in the foreground. Text on the panel reads, "Enjoy Rockefeller's Legacy. Had it not been for John D. Rockefeller, Jr., this park would not include much of the Jackson Hole valley. He donated over 33,000 acres, bringing Grand Teton National Park to 310,000 acres of land preserved for all to enjoy. "Concerned that development threatened the spectacular views of the Tetons and lakes, Rockefeller formed the Snake River Land Company to buy property in the valley to donate to the National Park Service. His gift served as a catalyst for Grand Teton National Park's expansion in 1950. In recognition of his philanthropy here and at other national parks, the U.S. Congress created the John D. Rockefeller, Jr. Memorial Parkway, which links Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks. "The marvelous scenic beauty of the Teton Mountains and the Lakes at their feet ... this valley is the natural ... feeding place for the game which inhabits ... the surrounding region. - John D. Rockefeller, Jr.'s "two reasons" for purchasing lands in the valley." Across the middle of the panel is a band of historic photos. The first one on the left shows a long ranch house of log construction. The caption reads, "The Snake River Land Company purchased the Hogan ranch in 1930 and used it as its local headquarters and residence." Next is a photo of National Park Service Director Horace Albright, who worked closely with Rockefeller, speaking at the dedication of the national park in 1929. The third photo shows two men and a woman, sitting on the ground, roasting bits of food over a camp fire. The caption reads, "Mr. and Mrs. Rockefeller enjoy a picnic in 1931 with Samuel Woodring, Grand Teton's first superintendent."

data.title: Journeying to the Bar BC
data.listingDescription: Early visitors arrived at the Bar BC after a several-day journey by train and wagon. Because the trip took so long and was so expensive, visitors tended to stay at dude ranches for weeks, if not the entire summer. Often, the same families would return year after year. However, with the growing popularity of the automobile in the 1930s and 40s and the advent of the "tin can dude" or automobile tourist, more people wanted to stay for just a few days.

images.altText: Six people stand on the porch of a log cabin in the trees, next to an antique car.
images.caption: A family stands on the porch of their cabin, with their automobile parked outside (courtesy of Jackson Hole Historical Society and Museum, 1992.4413.001).

data.bodyText: Early visitors arrived at the Bar BC after a several-day journey by train and wagon. Because the trip took so long and was so expensive, visitors tended to stay at dude ranches for weeks, if not the entire summer. Often, the same families would return year after year. However, with the growing popularity of the automobile in the 1930s and 40s and the advent of the "tin can dude" or automobile tourist, more people wanted to stay for just a few days and visit more locations-similar to the way people vacation today. A growing middle class also meant that more people had the means to travel, though generally not the freedom to take the entire summer off. These shifts changed the unique culture and camaraderie that once existed among the longtime guests and their hosts at dude ranches, and many ranches ceased operating altogether.
data.audioDescription:
Host: Early visitors arrived at the Bar BC after a several-day journey by train and wagon. Because the trip took so long and was so expensive, visitors tended to stay at dude ranches for weeks, if not the entire summer. Often, the same families would return year after year. However, with the growing popularity of the automobile in the 1930s and 40s and the advent of the "tin can dude" or automobile tourist, more people wanted to stay for just a few days and visit more locations-similar to the way people vacation today. A growing middle class also meant that more people had the means to travel, though generally not the freedom to take the entire summer off. These shifts changed the unique culture and camaraderie that once existed among the longtime guests and their hosts at dude ranches, and many ranches ceased operating altogether.

Excerpt from "Jackson Hole Journal": "The journey took about six days on a train through the summer Middle West with no air conditioning, and windows that opened to the blasts of baked prairie heat and cinders from the steam engines. ... Finally, we boarded [another] train up to Victor, arriving in the morning for the total excitement of the Teton Range emerging, turned backwards, over the Idaho foothills; and then at last came the disembarkation to the waiting wagon, or, later on, the truck. The trip was miserable, enthralling, exhausting-an experience. And finally, the blessed clean, cool quietness of the ranch, loud at night with the sound of the river, brilliant by day with flowers and butterflies. No wonder that when Easterners went through all that, they felt that they had gotten somewhere-somewhere important, exotic, isolated and special, well worth the trip-but on the other hand, made worthwhile by that trip."

Name Origin

Founded by William Kelly when he built a sawmill in 1907. The town was nearly voted the county seat for Teton County in 1925. That same year a massive landslide dammed the Gros Ventre River forming Lower Slide Lake. Two years later the natural dam failed, flooding the town and killing six people. Only two buildings remained standing.

data.bodyText:
The spring averages only 80 degrees Fahrenheit, cool compared to hot springs. Families often picnic on the grassy meadow surrounding the pool. Entering the warm spring is not recommended. In spring, bison and elk linger by the pool since the grass greens up early. Over the years, people have released their unwanted tropical fish into the pool disrupting the ecosystem. Some of these non-native species thrive and out-compete native species. Please do not release non-native fish into the spring. Be aware the pool contains high levels of E. coli and the presence of Naegleria fowleri .

data.audioDescription:
This wayside sits at the edge of a gravel parking area separated from the road by round logs. As you face the sign, the pond is across the road in front of you. The narrow, two-laned road is paved, with no curbs. On the other side of the road a grassy path leads through a split-rail fence down a gentle slope to the water. Large patches of algae grow on the surface.

The background image on the sign is a photograph of the pond showing the algae growth. Text reads, "Protect Kelly Warm Spring. Kelly Warm Spring is a relatively new feature on the Jackson Hole landscape. While the source of the thermal water is geologically quite old, the pools came into existence during the past century. When the dam created by the Gros Ventre slide failed in 1927 and flooded the town of Kelly, the hydrology of this area drastically changed.

"In recent years, non-native species-including pet fish and amphibians such as bullfrogs-have been released into Kelly Warm Spring. Non-native species may seem innocuous, but they damage much more than the water feature in front of you. Kelly Warm Spring flows directly into Ditch Creek-a tributary of the Snake River and home to the ecosystem's only native trout, Snake River cutthroat trout. Non-native aquatic nuisance species can out-compete native organisms, introduce diseases, degrade habitat, and prey on eggs and larvae of native species. As non-native species spread into other waters, they threaten the existence of the Snake River cutthroat trout and other native plants and wildlife.

"The National Park Service is committed to protecting the Kelly Warm Spring and other thermal features for generations to come. Federal law prohibits the introduction of non-native species. Please help protect these waters by never releasing exotic species here.

"Warning: Periodic water tests at this location have shown high levels of the bacteria E. coli. Swim at your own risk."

A photograph to the left of the text shows a gold fish that measures 12 inches long. The caption reads, "When released into the wild, aquarium fish grow to enormous sizes and become unwanted predators on native fish."

data.bodyText:
Lake Creek flows south from Phelps Lake as a clear mountain stream. Early season the stream is high and cold with snowmelt. As summer days warm, the flow diminishes but is still shockingly cold! Visitors of all abilities may reach this picturesque spot.

You may notice the brownish yellow or white mats clinging to the rocks in the water. This algae bloom, called "didymo" or "rock snot," has spread quickly in the Lake Creek drainage as visitors inadvertently transported the algae from another place. Help stop the spread! Clean-Drain-Dry your gear before and after visiting a new waterway.
data.audioDescription:
This section of trail leads to a wooden section that extends out to Lake Creek. Low wooden edges outline the platform. It curves gently to the left. Near the end, a section extends to the right with a long, wooden block bench for sitting. The creek flows from right to left, curving away from you, past woods towards the more open meadows beyond.

A small sign at the entrance to the wooden path reads, "Do you see the brownish yellow or white mats clinging to the rocks in Lake Creek This algae bloom, called "didymo" or "rock snot," has spread quickly through Lake Creek in the Laurance S. Rockefeller Preserve. Stop this aquatic nuisance from hitching a ride on your gear to another stream. Clean - Inspect - Dry. Did you enter Lake Creek? Protect streams by decontaminating your gear before and after entering waterways. Use the wash station near the Preserve's parking lot." A photograph shows a rock in a streambed covered with algae.

data.title: Laurance S. Rockefeller Preserve Trailhead
data.listingDescription: Location: Access the Laurance S. Rockefeller Preserve Trailhead from the Moose-Wilson Road. The Preserve provides access to the last piece of land donated by the Rockefeller family to Grand Teton National Park. This area is not accessible to vehicles over 23.3 feet long or trailers. The 50 vehicle parking lot is often full from 9 am-4 pm, and parking is prohibited along the Moose-Wilson Road. Arrive early to secure your space. Notes: The Preserve Center offers visitor info

images.altText: Hikers viewing a lake with mountains reflected into it.
images.title: Phelps Lake
images.caption: Hikers viewing Phelps Lake

data.bodyText:
General Description


The Laurance S. Rockefeller Preserve contains a trail network, a unique visitor center, and the opportunity to connect with nature on a deeper level. This 1,100 acres of land was once known as the JY Dude Ranch. Eventually, John D. Rockefeller and his family—who had great influence on the creation of the park—eventually purchased the ranch and it became a family retreat. Laurance, the son of John D. Rockefeller, announced in 2001 that this privately owned parcel of land would be donated to the park and in 2008, the preserve opened to the public. Laurance's vision of creating a place that fostered a deeper connection with the natural world continues today.

Location

The Laurance S. Rockefeller Preserve Trailhead and Visitor Center is accessed by turning off Moose-Wilson Road. Please note that no vehicles over 23 feet long, 8 feet wide, or trailers are allowed on Moose-Wilson Road. After turning into the preserve, short drive will take you to a small parking lot that holds 50 vehicles. The parking lot is usually full from 9am-4pm during peak summer months; a queue is formed once filled. There are restrooms in the parking lot, up by the visitor center, and by the lakeshore. 

The Preserve Center offers visitor information, water and restrooms.

Backcountry camping requires a permit-pick one up at a backcountry permits office. Backcountry campers may not leave a vehicle at the Laurance S. Rockefeller Preserve parking lot.

Notes

Unlike most hikes in Grand Teton, there is a restroom (with no potable water) right before the lakeshore. Due to the unique and serene design of the preserve, it is recommended to keep group size to a max of ten people. Please note that no vehicles over 23 feet long, 8 feet wide, or trailers are allowed on Moose-Wilson Road. The parking lot holds 50 cars is usually full from 9am-4pm during peak summer months; a queue is formed once filled

Hikes

A short pathway leads you from the parking lot to the visitor center. Here, you can tour the center and its exhibits, use the restrooms, and begin your hike. An informational kiosk outside the center marks the beginning of the preserve's trail system. Rangers are present at the visitor center during the summer months and can answer questions. Black bears frequent this area so remember to bear aware while hiking. 

Lake Creek-Woodland Trail Loop
3.0 miles round-trip, 1.5 hours, 300 ft total climbing. Easy.
Trail follows Lake Creek to several scenic views across Phelps Lake, then loops back through a mature forest on the Woodland Trail.

Aspen Ridge-Boulder Ridge Loop
5.8 miles round-trip, 3 hours, 550 ft total climbing. Moderate.
Hike a forested loop with views of Phelps Lake and the valley. Optionally, hike through a boulder field.

Phelps Lake Trail Loop
6.3 miles round-trip, 4+ hours, 600 ft total climbing. Moderate.
Hike around Phelps Lake crossing the wetland boardwalk.

Name Origin

Laurance S. Rockefeller was the fourth child of John D. Rockefeller, Jr. and Abigail Rockefeller. Laurance was a businessman, philanthropist and conservationist. He transferred the family retreat (formerly the JY Dude Ranch) to Grand Teton National Park in 2001. After the removal of ranch infrastructure, and the construction of trails and a LEED Platinum certified visitor center, the Laurance S. Rockefeller Preserve opened to the public in 2008.
data.audioDescription: This trailhead is located at the end of the porch along the front of the visitor center here at the preserve. There is an open space here with a dirt and gravel surface and a 3-foot boulder in the middle. If you stand at the boulder with the visitor center on your right, the restrooms are to your left in a small building with the women's on the right and the men's on the left. The accessible trail is directly in front of you, heading off through huckleberry thicket with an open, sagebrush-covered meadow to the right. On the right at the start of the trail is a covered sign showing a map of Phelps Lake with the preserve just to the south of it. Information on hikes to and around the lake and along ridges in the vicinity is provided.

data.bodyText:
Location: Access the marina about one-mile north of Colter Bay Village west of US 89/191/287. Follow the paved road to the east shore of Jackson Lake where you will find the marina and Leeks Pizzeria.
Notes: Leeks Marina services private boats. The marina runs shuttle boat from the small dock to boats moored on the lake. There are no boat rentals at this location.

Regulations

All boats including paddleboards launched in Grand Teton National Park must have a park permit. Purchase permits at the permits desk in the Craig Thomas Discovery & Visitor Center in Moose or the Colter Bay permits office. More information on park boat regulations .

Boat inspections required for all boats entering Wyoming between March 1 and November 30 for Aquatic Invasive Species (AIS). AIS inspection stations near Moose and Moran. Boat owners must buy a decal to support this program. Decals available at Snake River Anglers in Dornans or at the Colter Bay Marina; and other Wyoming Game and Fish outlets. More information on state boat regulations.

Name Origin

Stephen Leek was a cattle rancher, conservationist and entrepreneur. He settled in the south part of the Jackson Hole valley in the 1880s. Before 1900, he established Leek's "clubhouse" on the north end of Leigh Lake and then Leek's Camp on the east shore of Jackson Lake as hunting and fishing camps. Later, Leek took photographs of starving and dying elk during the winter of 1908-09. He used these images in lectures, articles and tours to help publicize the dilemma. In 1912, Congress established the National Elk Refuge to provide wintering grounds for elk.

data.bodyText:
Leigh Lake Trailhead provides hikers a wide variety of options from easy level trails to access to mountain passes. Some may opt for the relatively level trail that begins along the east shore of String Lake and extends north to Leigh, Bearpaw and Trapper lakes. Others may enjoy a loop around String Lake with views of the Jackson Hole valley. For those looking for a longer hike, venture up Cascade or Paintbrush canyons to reach the alpine lakes such as Lake Solitude or Holly Lake.

Suggested Hikes

Leigh Lake
1.8 miles RT, 1 hour, 40 ft total climbing, Easy.
Hike along the east shore of String Lake, pass the bridge across a stream and climb to Leigh Lake.

Trapper Lake
9.2 miles RT, 5 hours, 400 ft total climbing, Easy-Moderate.
From String Lake, follow forested shore of Leigh Lake to smaller lakes with views of Mount Moran.

Holly Lake
13.0 miles RT, 9 hours, 2600 ft total climbing, Strenuous.
Follow Paintbrush Canyon trail through forests and wildflowers meadows to an alpine lake.

Location

Access the Leigh Lake Trailhead from the Jenny Lake scenic loop drive. Turn west at North Jenny Lake Junction, bend north where the road splits and choose from a series of parking lots. The first parking lot is the String Lake Trailhead. The second lot serves as a boat launch for String Lake. The third lot provides access to the Leigh Lake Trailhead and the String Lake Picnic Area. Check the parking page for additonal information.
Note, the Teton Park Road is seasonally closed to this destination from November 1-April 30. 

Things to Know

This area is popular for picnicking and water sports. Parking is often congested mid-day especially on weekends. Restrooms are located near the Leigh Lake trailhead. Remember to bring water with you.

Bears may be active any place and at any time-travel in groups, make noise and carry bear spray.

Backcountry camping requires a permit-pick one up at a backcountry permits office. Overnight parking is only allowed with a backcountry permit, no camping in parking lot.

Name Origin

Richard "Beaver Dick" Leigh was a British expatriate who moved to the Teton area in 1863 as a fur trapper. He married Jenny a Shoshone Indian and they had five children. Jenny and Beaver Dick assisted the 1872 Hayden expedition - he as their guide, she with camp logistics. The Hayden Expedition named Jenny and Leigh lakes in their honor.

data.title: Looking Forward
data.listingDescription: Stop 7 (Grassy Lake Road): How is climate change affecting fire behavior, and how will that change forests in Greater Yellowstone? Hear what scientists have to say.

images.altText: Burning trees emit ribbons of smoke, while an unburned tree stands in the foreground.
images.caption: Burned trees continue to smoke, while unburned trees are visible in the foreground and background.

data.bodyText: Stop 7 (Grassy Lake Road): How is climate change affecting fire behavior, and how will that change forests in Greater Yellowstone? Hear what scientists have to say.
data.audioDescription:
Host: Over the past ten or so years, fire managers across the West have been seeing larger fires and more extreme fire behavior. This is largely driven by a changing climate, which brings hotter temperatures, drier summers, and longer fire seasons. Here in Greater Yellowstone, we are see not only larger, but more frequent fires. Earlier in this century, managers could rely on areas that had burned in the last 50 years or so to stop or slow the progression of a new fire. But now, they're observing that forests that burned just 10-30 years ago can carry fire, under the right conditions-and we're getting those conditions more and more often. Here's Monica Turner, a fire ecologist from the University of Wisconsin who's studied these forests since 1988, to tell us what this may mean for the future:

Monica: Why would more frequent fires be a problem for forests in Grand Teton? It takes some time for the trees to grow big enough to start producing the cones that provide the seeds that allow forests to recover after a wildfire. If the forest burns again before it has had enough time to grow big enough and produce enough of a cone crop, we might not have enough seeds to regenerate the forest. We've seen the effects of that in the 2016 Berry Fire in Grand Teton, where it re burned areas of the Glade Fire. We've seen a drastic reduction in the number of seedling trees that have come back into those areas where we had only 16 year old trees burn, primarily because they haven't had enough time to build up that seed crop.

Host: Another factor that Monica has observed is that in some locations, even when a mature forest burns and there are plenty of seeds, it's becoming too hot for those seedlings to germinate and survive.

These changes will not only impact these ecological processes, but also how we manage fires, and how we understand the presence of past fires on the landscape. Here, Ron Steffens, a fire analyst for the park, discusses how the Berry Fire, in 2016, interacted with areas that had burned in 1988. Up until that year, very few fires had re-burned any of the regrowth from â€˜88.

Ron: We learned on the berry fire that our ability to utilize past fires as areas that slow a fire can sometimes be overcome by the intensity of the weather conditions and the fuel. So in that case some of the prior burned areas were burned through again, and this was with multiple days of high winds of 25-35 miles per hour, and fires that were crossing parts of the Snake River, burning into particularly the 1988 fires and slowing there, but in areas that had burned more recently the fire did not slow down. And it became a different type of fire when it was burning in younger fuel. But it slowed some but it did not stop. So we're seeing now. At a time when we're tracking and monitoring change in the climate that we may be seeing more frequent fire potential in our ecosystem and our bio region because we have more days that are drier. The days may stay drier at night and less humidity recovery, so that the fires are burning further into the night than we've seen in the past. And that may be one of the effects of a change in the climate.

Host: As the way fires behave on the landscape changes, that will affect the way staff make decisions about how to manage them. Here's Diane Abendroth, the park's fire ecologist, reflecting on what they might look like:

Diane: When I started my career in western Wyoming in fire, we used to think that fire was scarce, and in order to have a properly functioning ecosystem we needed to introduce more of it on the landscape. That maybe we'd been suppressing it too much and changing the vegetation to the point where there's just not enough of that early forest out there. And so in my work, we really encouraged people to allow some fires to burn where it was safe to do so, and also we did a lot of prescribed fire. And 20 to 25 years later, it seems like with the climate and with the way fires are burning, maybe we need to start thinking about the unburned forests being the rarity on the landscape. And I think that's a...kind of interesting but daunting change.

data.bodyText:
The Willow Flats area offers excellent wildlife and scenic viewing opportunities. Elk rear their calves in the protection of the willow-shaded meadows below. Grizzly bears forage on grubs and bulbs and hunt elk calves. Sandhill cranes frequent the open grasslands.

The view across Jackson Lake toward the Teton Range highlights the dramatic rise of the mountains above the valley floor. No foothills block your view because uplift along the Teton fault hinges the crustal block skyward while dropping the valley floor. The lodgepole pine-covered ridges are not foothills, but glacial moraines. As glaciers retreated, they left behind ridges of rocky debris that now support forests on the valley floor.

images.altText: Wooden log cabin with a porch with mountains in the background
images.caption: Lucas-Fabian Cabin

data.bodyText:
Geraldine Lucas bucked tradition by leaving her husband, returning to college as a single mother, and teaching school. Upon retirement in 1913, she joined her siblings in Jackson Hole and homesteaded south of Jenny Lake. In 1924, she met 16-year-old Paul Petzoldt as he set out for his first climb of the Grand Teton. Later that year, Petzoldt guided Lucas, who at age 58 became the second woman to reach the summit of the Grand Teton.

Today, eleven of the old homestead buildings still stand at the base of the Grand Teton inspiring all who visit with the spectacular views that Geraldine saw.

In 1998, the Geraldine Lucas Homestead and Fabian Place were listed on the National Register of Historic Places as an Historic District.

data.bodyText:
Most hikers and climbers approaching "Les Trois Tétons" depart from the Lupine Meadows trailhead. Conifers canopy the first part of the trail giving way to shrub-covered slopes with views of the valley. The trail splits three miles up from the trailhead. The north fork climbs to Surprise and Amphitheater lakes at the base of Disappointment Peak. The south fork wraps around into Garnet Canyon with a stunning view of the Middle Teton. Garnet Canyon trail is the primary access route for climbing the Grand Teton.

Suprise and Amphitheater Lakes
10.1 miles roundtrip, 7 hours, 3000 ft total climbing, Strenuous.
Hike to glacial lakes surrounded by meadows. Disappointment Peak towers above.

Garnet Canyon
8.4 miles RT, 6 hours, 2650 ft total climbing, Strenuous.
Trail climbs into Garnet Canyon offering spectacular views of the Middle Teton.

Location

Access the Lupine Meadows Trailhead from the Teton Park Road one mile south of South Jenny Lake Junction. Turn west and follow a gravel road for about one and a half miles.

Things to Know

Visitor services include gravel parking lot, a vault toilet, bear food storage boxes and a trailhead sign. Remember to bring water with you.

Bears may be active any place and at any time-travel in groups, make noise and carry bear spray.

Backcountry camping requires a permit-pick one up at a backcountry permits office. Overnight parking is only allowed with a backcountry permit, no camping in parking lot.

Name Origin

Silver lupine blooms in the meadow during early summer.

data.title: Maud Noble Cabin
data.listingDescription: Maud Noble's cabin provides a glimpse into the past. Learn about early homesteaders, dude ranchers, and the historical importance of this central meeting place in the Jackson Hole valley.

images.altText: A ranger talking to visitors inside a historic log cabin.
images.title: Inside Maud Noble's Cabin
images.caption: Learn about the history of the park through Maud Noble's Cabin.

data.bodyText:
Maud Noble came to the valley as a dude rancher at the Bar BC Ranch summer of 1915. She moved to the valley permanently in 1916 and contracted a cabin on the east side of Cottonwood Creek. She purchased the Menor homestead in 1918 and had her cabin moved to the homestead. With her partner Frederick Sandell, she ferried increasing numbers of visitors across the Snake River and ran the Ferry Ranch Store.

In 1923, a group of local residents and Horace Albright, Superintendent of Yellowstone National Park, met at Noble's cabin to discuss their concerns over commercial development along the base of the Teton Range. The alarmed meeting participants discussed ways to save the valley from tawdry exploitation. They agreed that some sort of preserve would be necessary to protect the "Old West" character of the valley, though their concept of a preserve was different from a national park. The group decided to seek a wealthy individual who would be willing to buy private land to donate to the preserve -- that person was John D. Rockefeller, Jr.

In 1927, a steel truss bridge was built just south of the ferry, making it obsolete. Maud Noble sold the property to the Snake River Land Company in 1929.
data.audioDescription: This log-and-white-chinked building is a rectangle with the front door in the long side. An extension is built out from the left back. A stone chimney sits outside the left hand wall. A small lean-to roof shelters the front door. Two wooden benches flank the door. Near the path to the left of the door a small sign reads, "Park Takes Root. On July 26, 1923, Maud Noble hosted a landmark meeting in this cabin. Yellowstone National Park Superintendent Horace Albright joined a small group of locals here. They launched a plan that planted the seed for the creation of Grand Teton National Park." Hanging on the wall to the right of the front door is a bronze plaque which commemorates that meeting. A short, low ramp covers the shallow step into the cabin. Inside the door rustic wood period chairs and tables are grouped around the fireplace. Other rooms may be accessed to the rear and to the right.

data.listingDescription: West of Dornans, Holiday Menor homesteaded along the east bank of the Snake River in 1908. He moved here to join his brother Bill who homesteaded across the river and operated a ferry and general store. Under the shed next to the river is one of the pontoons from the ferry-the last remaining part of the original boat. Holiday operated a limekiln burning limestone at high temperatures to produce pure lime. Settlers used lime to chink cabins and to whitewash their buildings.

images.altText: Looking across the Snake River toward the cabins of Bill Menors homestead with the Teton Range beyond.
images.caption: Snake River and Bill Menors Homestead

data.bodyText:
West of Dornans, Holiday Menor homesteaded along the east bank of the Snake River in 1908. He moved here to join his brother Bill who homesteaded across the river and operated a ferry and general store. Under the shed next to the river is one of the pontoons from the ferry-the last remaining part of the original boat.

Holiday operated a limekiln burning limestone at high temperatures to produce pure lime. Settlers used lime to chink cabins and to whitewash their buildings. Bill's cabin is one of the few whitewashed buildings in the area.
data.audioDescription: From the parking lot at Dornans Service District a paved trail leads down to the east side of the river and the ferry crossing. There are three wayside signs along the trail. From the first sign at the edge of the parking lot, a brushy meadow stretches out in front of you to a thin line of trees at the waters edge. The right side of the sign shows a map of the area with the Teton Range to the west, the valley of Jackson Hole to the east and Menor's Ferry along the Snake River in the middle. An inset photograph shows a historic image of the ferry crossing the river carrying a wagon and team of horses.Text on the left reads, "Menor's Ferry Historic District. This area was settled by two brothers, Bill and Holiday Menor, originally from Ohio. Bill settled on the west side of the river in 1894 and established an important river crossing with his ferry. Holiday followed in 1905 and eventually homesteaded on the east side, just across the river from his brother."Jackson Hole was one of the last areas of the West to be settled, probably because its geographic isolation, harsh climate, and high elevation were not conducive to agriculture. The first settlers came in 1884, and by 1888 Jackson Hole had a population of 20 men, two women, and one child. During the 1890s Mormon settlers came from Idaho and Utah. Many of them crossed the Snake River at Menors' Ferry and settled just east of here in an area the called Grovont, now known as Mormon Row. The census of June 1, 1900 revealed that 638 people lived in the valley of Jackson Hole; the major occupation was farming."At the bottom left are small portraits of two men. Bill Menor is on the left and Holiday Menor on the right.About halfway down the gently sloped paved trail is another wayside just to the right of the walkway. It looks out over a scrubby meadow with a high bank on the right and the trees lining the river on the left. The background image on the panel shows a historic photograph of the same view. A dirt tack runs along the base of the bank towards three small log buildings with a larger, framed barn in the background. Text reads, "Holiday Menor's Homestead. Holiday Menor first came to Jackson Hole in 1905 after working as a gold prospector in Montana. He lived with his brother Bill until 1908, when he established a 160-acre homestead on this land. He grew wheat, barley, and alfalfa, which he sold to ranchers to feed to their cattle during the long harsh winters.He also built a limekiln that was used for several days each year to burn the limestone he quarried from Blacktail Butte. Lime was important to settlers; they mixed it with sand and water to make mortar for chinking log cabins and for laying bricks and stonework. Lime was also used as a whitewash (see Bill's cabin across the river) and to reduce odors in outhouses. About 250 bushels of lime, which sold for 50 cents a bushel, were produced each year."At the top right of the panel is a small historic photo of a man wearing a hat ad a black vest, leaning against a log wall. The caption reads, "Holiday sold his homestead to the Snake River Land Company in 1928 and joined Bill, who had already retired and was living in San Diego, California."At the bottom left of the panel is an illustration of a lime kiln. A tall shaft, surrounded by dirt, is full of white stones. At the bottom a stack of wood burns. The caption reads, "From Limestone to Pure Lime. Cooking lime involved an enormous amount of work. Holiday Menor dug his frontier-style kiln into the edge of a dirt bank. Lined with bricks and rocks, the rounded chamber rose 30 feet. Limestone was loaded in from the top. Inside a second chamber housed the fire. A limestone "burn" required round-the-clock vigilance. Stacks of firewood were fed through a draw door to maintain white hot temperatures. Once the ashes were cooled, this pure lime could be packed in barrels."Close to the water's edge, near the bottom of the trail, just past a row of benches to the left of the walkway, is an open roofed structure covering an old boat-shaped, wooden pontoon. It is supported by a wooden frame and surrounded by a fence. The pontoon is about 30 feet long and is mostly intact, its sides covered with weathered green paint. A small sign at the front of the structure shows an historic photograph of an old automobile full of people being carried across the river on the ferry. Text reads, "Water Powered. Bill Menor began operating a ferry here in 1894. Menor's ferry provided one of the most important points of access to the land west of the Snake River until 1927. This wooden pontoon (ca. 1910) is the last remaining part of the ferry that operated during this period."A few yards past this structure, the walkway takes a switchback to the left, then back to the right to end at the water's edge. The paved landing is edged with a wooden curb and benches line the side nearest the bank. Across the wide river you can see the white-washed Menor's Ferry General Store and other buildin
