images.altText: Front of Menors cabin and general store that are whitewashed. The Teton Range dominates the skyline above the cabin.
images.caption: Menors General Store

data.bodyText:
Menors General Store is one wing of Bill Menor's original homestead cabin. The cabin was constructed in three distinct phases. Menor built the west wing in 1894 (the Tetons are to the west). Around 1895, he added the central section. The larger east wing was built around 1905. The west wing served as a bedroom and sitting room while the central section housed the kitchen and pantry. Menor opened a store in the east wing where settlers and travelers could purchase tobacco, coffee, tea, sugar, flour, canned foods and some items of clothing. The store, ferry and blacksmith shop generated cash to supplement Menor's subsistence farming.

Except for a few items such as glass and nails, pioneers used local materials to construct shelters. Abundant stands of nearby lodgepole pine provided a convenient source of lumber. The rough-sawn boards of the central section indicate the presence of a sawmill in the valley around 1894. Menor painted his cabin with lime-based white-wash that he got from his brother, Holiday Menor who homesteaded across the river. Holiday Menor quarried lime from Blacktail Butte and prepared it in a kiln near the east landing of the ferry.
data.audioDescription:
This building is made of weathered whitewashed logs with chinking, finished in places with rough planking. The building is "T" shaped, with the entrance being at the end of one of the short arms. A porch extends across this part of the building, reached by two shallow steps. The rest of the building extends to the left. If you go through the door, the store's counter is in front of you, extending to the right and back to the rear of the store. Shelving lines the other walls. If you turn left in front of the counter, you can go down two steps and enter the attached cabin.

A small sign along the path leading to the store shows an historic photograph of Holiday Menor wearing white hat, dark vest and a close-cropped beard. The text reads, "Mean and Menor. Store owner Bill Menor, prone to swearing and a surly attitude, ran this general store in the early 1900s. Menor and his brother, Holiday, painted this building with whitewash from Holiday's limekiln. Referring to Bill, Holiday was known to say: "My partner's Mean, but I'm Menor.""

data.bodyText: The BarBC regularly hosted celebrity visitors, including the Rockefeller family, William Faulkner, and Ernest Hemingway, who supposedly stayed in this cabin. Struthers Burt's friendship with Horace Albright, the superintendent of Yellowstone National Park, gradually brought Burt around to the idea of creating a national park in Jackson Hole. Burt became a strong conservationist in his own right and a key advocate for the future Grand Teton National Park, using his position of prominence to generate support for it. In 1930, he sold his share in the Bar BC to demonstrate the importance of preserving the valley as a park, and he and his family relocated to a ranch farther north. Burt also encouraged his friend, John D. Rockefeller, Jr., to contribute funds to buy up property in the valley to donate to the park, which was a critical step in the formation of Grand Teton National Park as we know today.

data.title: Moose Entrance Station
data.listingDescription: The Moose Entrance Station is one of four entrances to Grand Teton National Park. It is one of the first places where you will be prompted to pay an entrance fee since there is no fee to travel on US Highway 89/191/26.

images.altText: Two entrance booths with a car going through and the Teton range in the background.
images.title: Moose Entrance Station
images.caption: Welcome to Grand Teton National Park!

data.bodyText:
The Moose Entrance station is one of four entrances to Grand Teton National Park. After driving twenty miles north from the town of Jackson on US 26/89/191, turn west at Moose Junction to get on Teton Park Road. In a mile, you will see the entrance booths. The actual border of Grand Teton lies on the highway south towards the town of Jackson. But because there are no fees to access the highway through the park, this is one of the first locations where you will be prompted to pay for entry.

Coming from Moose Junction, you will pass the Craig Thomas Discovery and Visitor Center before reaching the entrance station. Although the station will offer you a map and newspaper, the visitor center is staffed with knowledgeable rangers, exhibits, and a park film. Eight miles past the entrance station is Jenny Lake.
 
No reservations are required to enter Grand Teton National Park but there are entrance fees. The park is open 24 hours a day, so if no one is at the entrance station when you arrive, you can drive through and pay your park fee online.

Name Origin

The small community of Moose was once known as Menors Ferry until the USPS requested the name change.

Moose frequent the nearby Snake River in summer and the sagebrush flats of the terraces above in late fall and early winter.

data.title: Moose Landing
data.listingDescription: Today, this spot serves as the primary pick-up location for commercial float trips in the park. Always check with your tour operator for specific instructions. Recreational users of the river can also put in and take out from this location. Informational signs and educational exhibits provide further insight and context to the wild nature of the Snake River. Restrooms are available for public use.

images.altText: Multiple visitors walking on the sidewalk near restrooms. Trees and mountians in the background.
images.title: Moose Landing
images.caption: Meet here for your float trip adventure!

data.bodyText:
What if you could get a bird’s eye view of the Snake River, like the osprey that hunts from above? What would you see? While you wait to be picked up for your float trip, experience that perspective by exploring the in-ground Snake River sculpture beneath your feet. Beloved access points like Jackson Lake Dam, Pacific Creek Landing, Deadman’s Bar, and Moose Landing are marked along the way. Review the route of your float trip before you embark on your journey.

This area, known as Moose, became a significant crossing point of the Snake River. Because of the braided and winding nature of the river, there are no safe places to ford twenty miles north or south of this location. An early homesteader, Bill Menor, set up his homestead and ferry just north of this location. That ferry would open up the western side of the valley, drawing people in and eventually leading to conversations about the creation of the park.

Today, this spot serves as the primary pick-up location for commercial float trips in the park. Always check with your tour operator for specific instructions. Recreational users of the river can also put in and take out from this location. Informational signs and educational exhibits provide further insight and context to the wild nature of the Snake River. Restrooms are available for public use.
data.audioDescription: Between the bull boat and river raft exhibits, welcoming you to the main plaza area, is a two-foot-wide by three-and-a-half-foot-tall bronze panel, vertically positioned a few feet off the ground against a five-foot-tall granite boulder speckled with shades of white, black, and grey. The bronze panel displays a map of Grand Teton National Park’s waterways, text, and other symbols, all engraved into bronze that you can touch and feel. The engraving depicts the location of the Snake River and the various lakes within the park. The map is oriented running north to south. Small diamond-shaped engravings near the waterways indicate the locations of other boat launches, such as Pacific Creek, Deadmans Bar, and Moose Landing. Next to the Moose Landing diamond marker is a star and text that reads, “You Are Here”. At the top of the panel, a small arrow points north above text that reads, “To Yellowstone National Park (39 miles, 44km)”. At the bottom of the panel, located next to the Snake River engraving, a small arrow points in the southwest direction below text that reads, “To Pacific Ocean (1201 miles, 1933 km)”. The words, “Moose Landing” run vertically along the left side of the panel in extra-large text. The panel bends 90 degrees around the left side of the rock and is approximately one-third the width of the front side. At the top, engraved into the bronze, text reads: This river landing revitalization was made possible by a public-private partnership between Grand Teton National Park and Grand Teton National Park Foundation. Below is a smaller panel with information about indigenous words related to the river with silhouettes of Engelmann spruce branches in the background. The text reads: Bia Ogwaide (Shoshone) “Pavahuude (Bannock)” “big flow” Jackson Lake Moose Landing has long been an important crossing point across the Snake River for Native Americans on seasonal rounds and more recently for homesteaders and travelers. The long-legged animals who are the namesake for this place—moose—can often be seen nearby. They and other wildlife use the river’s edge for safe passage through the park. In the park today, Moose Landing continues to be a central meeting place for people to access the river. Below the text is a small circle logo for the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes of the Fort Hall Reservation. The logo has a braided border and a graphic of an indigenous man in the center. Along the border are the words, “Shoshone-Bannock Tribes of the Fort Hall Reservation Idaho”. Next to the logo, text reads: The park and its partners are grateful for the collaboration with the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes of the Fort Hall Reservation on the Snake River Gateways project exhibits. In the bottom right corner, a nine-inch-tall branch of an engelmann spruce tree with a partial line border is engraved into the bronze. Behind the bronze panel is a small inner island of river rocks and native plants. It is about 20 feet long and 8 feet wide. On the eastern edge of the island is a large wooden bench. It is about 8 feet long and three feet deep with a backrest and armrests with dark metal features. To the west of the bronze panel and north of the float trip parking area are the restrooms. It is a brown metal building with a slightly slanted roof. Four doors face east. They are individual restrooms for either gender, and the two middle doors are accessible for people with disabilities. They are flush toilets with a sink. Around the northern face of the building is a water fountain. North of the restrooms, bench, and boat exhibits is the main meeting location for float trips. This sidewalk is smooth, dark concrete with small pebbles. It is roughly 70 feet wide, east to west, and 125 feet north to south, before the sidewalk narrows. A three-foot-high and three-foot-deep stacked rock wall lines the western edge of the plaza, giving visitors a place to sit while they wait for their float trip. Two 20 to 30-foot-high wooden awnings provide shade. Angled metal beams support the slightly slanted wooden awnings. On the eastern edge of the plaza, the parking lot is marked as “unloading only”. There are two four-foot-high, four-sided wooden posts on the sidewalk at the plaza’s eastern edge. They are about 30 feet apart from each other. The words, “Float Trips Meet Here” are laser cut into the sides of the posts in large text. One side, near the top of the post in small text reads “Visitor Center” with an arrow pointing south and “Boat Ramp” with an arrow pointing north. Moving north, the sidewalk narrows and the smooth dark concrete funnels into the beginning of an in-ground concrete river sculpture. The surrounding sidewalk here turns a light brown color and is smooth with no pebbles. The in-ground river sculpture was poured and shaped to the same route of the Snake River. It shows the Snake River as it flows from Jackson Lake Dam to Oxbow Bend to Pacific Creek Landing to Deadmans Bar to Moose Landing, your current location. These points are each marked by one-foot-in-diameter raised bronze medallions in the sidewalk. The Moose Landing medallion has a star symbol and the text, “You Are Here” with Engelmann spruce branches bordering the edge. The Deadmans Bar medallion also notes, “10 miles (16 km) upstream” with aspen leaves bordering the edge. The Pacific Creek medallion notes, “22 miles (35 km) upstream” with narrow-leaf cottonwood branches bordering the edge. The Oxbow Bend medallion notes “24 miles (39 km) upstream” with mare’s tail (an underwater plant) bordering the edge. The Jackson Lake Dam medallion notes, “26 miles (42 km) upstream” with cotton leaf branches bordering the edge. Feeling the difference in concrete, explore the route of the Snake River through Grand Teton National Park as you move north to the second plaza area.

data.title: Moose Landing Boat Launch
data.listingDescription: Informational panels on river safety are located at the launch area for you and your group to review. You will find resources like a map, things to do before going on the water, things to bring, and things to know.

images.altText: A van pulling a large raft out of the river with informational signs.
images.title: Moose Landing Boat Launch
images.caption: Experience the beauty of Grand Teton on a Snake River float trip.

data.bodyText:
The Snake River winds through the valley floor carrying snowmelt from the mountains westward toward the Pacific Ocean. This river is an artery of the park, offering stunning views of the Tetons. Many species of wildlife use the river, from the browsing moose to the industrious beaver. Whether you are fishing, viewing wildlife, or enjoying the scenery, floating on this river is an unforgettable experience. Moose Landing is the primary take-out location for boating and float trips in the park. Many authorized float trip operations pick up their guests here and then drive to the put-in location. If you are continuing your trip past Moose Landing or starting your trip here, you should have advanced boating and navigation skills. The next take-out is fourteen miles south in Wilson, WY.

The course this river follows is not straightforward. It travels in and out of numerous channels that change every year. This is a powerful river that requires river reading and navigation skills. Before you float, know what skills you need to float the river, where you are going, and what things you need.

Informational panels on river safety are located at the launch area for you and your group to review. You will find resources like a map, things to do before going on the water, things to bring, and things to know.

For a complete overview of boating rules, regulations, and permit requirements, please review our webpage on boating and floating before getting out on the water.

Additional information about floating the Snake River, including an interactive map, is available too. 

Permits and Regulations


To meet the permit requirements for Grand Teton National Park you must:

  • Have a Grand Teton Boat Permit
  • Have a valid Wyoming AIS Decal
  • Complete an AIS inspection

Grand Teton Boat Permit


All boats are required to have a Grand Teton Boat Permit before launching on any of the park’s waters. Permits are required for all motorized and non-motorized boats, including stand-up paddleboards (SUPs) and windsurfing boards. Privately owned vessels must register each year with Grand Teton National Park. Permits may be purchased on Recreation.gov or at the visitor centers in Moose or Colter Bay during summer operations. Boaters can also have their permit mailed directly to them within two weeks.

Wyoming AIS Decal


PREVENT THE SPREAD OF PATHOGENS - CLEAN. DRAIN. DRY.
All watercraft using Wyoming waters are required to display a Wyoming Aquatic Invasive Species decal. The decal can be purchased online at the Wyoming Game and Fish Department website or from a variety of local vendors. Additionally, all boats entering the park must stop for an Aquatic Invasive Species (AIS) inspection. By law, boats coming from out of state must be inspected or have valid proof of inspection before they launch on waters in Wyoming, including waters in the park. This includes motorized boats, rafts, drift boats, canoes, kayaks, stand-up paddleboards, and all watercraft 10 feet and longer. Aquatic Invasive Species, such as whirling disease and zebra or quagga mussels, are a serious ecological and economic threat to the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. Boats, waders, and anything else that comes in contact with a body of water has the potential to spread non-native plants, pathogens, and other invasive species among water bodies. Clean, drain, and dry all boating and fishing equipment after use. Learn more about preventing the spread of AIS.

Note: Non-motorized inflatable watercraft 10 feet or less in length, all solid and inflatable paddleboards regardless of length, and all devices defined as water sport toys are exempt from the Wyoming State AIS Decal requirement.

Stretches of River

Beginner
Jackson Lake Dam to Pacific Creek 5 miles
This stretch features scenic views, calmer water and few obstructions. At Pacific Creek landing the water is swift, boaters should scout this landing prior to launching.

Intermediate
Pacific Creek to Deadmans Bar 10 miles
This section drops significantly creating swift water and braided channels requiring careful route-finding.

Flagg Ranch to Lizard Creek Campground 10 miles
The braided channels make route-finding a challenge. The river winds for 6 miles before reaching Jackson Lake. Depending on the lake level, the trip is another 4 miles to Lizard Creek Campground. Strenuous rowing or paddling may be required. Afternoon thunderstorms and winds produce waves that may swamp canoes. Motors may be used on Jackson Lake.

Advanced
Deadman’s Bar to Moose Landing 10 miles
This is the most challenging stretch of river in the park—many accidents occur here. The river drops more steeply and the current increases. Complex braiding may obscure the main channel and strong currents can sweep boaters into side channels blocked by logjams.

Moose to Wilson 14 miles
This section of the river is as difficult as the preceding section. Advanced boating skills are required due to fast current, braided channels, and logjams. The park extends 5 miles downstream from Moose on the west bank and 2 miles downstream on the east bank. There is no take-out or access to the river at the park boundary. The next take-out is at the Snake River Bridge east of Wilson, WY, 14 miles downstream from Moose.

Use our advanced Snake River Map on our website for more route details.
data.audioDescription: The sidewalk from the plazas curves east to the northeast corner of the parking lot where the boat ramp is. At the end of the sidewalk, is a roughly 30 foot wide concrete ramp to the river. There is lots of open space in this area of the parking lot so vehicles with boat trailers can safely rig their boats, wait in line, and then either put in or take out boats. Just to the north of the boat ramp, along the sidewalk are two seven-foot-tall stained wooden posts that stand upright and hold three vertical 32-inch by 48-inch informational panels, each encased in a brown metal frame with a few inches between each panel. The upper one third of the left panel is solid blue with white title text that reads: Moose Landing Boat Launch Moose to Wilson Below the title text is a small white rectangle with a blue square and text that reads: Advanced skill level Next to the skill level marker are two paragraphs of text that read: Boating on the Snake River downstream from here takes you out of the park and into a challenging section of the river with faster water and a straighter course. Advanced boating skills are required for the rapid water, braieded channels, and logjams. The next take-out is at the Snake River Bridge, 14 miles (22km) from here. Know your skills, the capabilities of your watercraft, the weather forecast, and river conditions. The bottom two-thirds of the vertical panel is a map of the different sections of the Snake River and their difficulty level within Grand Teton National Park . The map is oriented north to south. You can see some of the glacial lakes, some topography of the landscape, and the Snake River. In the top left corner, a smaller, zoomed-out map of the Snake River, shows the area the large map is depicting. It is titled: Map Location. The main map shows the Snake River from Moose to Wilson. The sections of river have symbols and are highlighted specific colors to indicate their difficulty level. Information in the top right corner explains the ratings. Beginner is indicated by a green circle and the river is colored light green. Intermediate is indicated by a light blue square and the river is colored light blue. Advanced is indicated by a grey diamond and the river is colored light grey. Moose to Wilson is rated as advanced. Beneath the ratings is a reminder that: “In case of emergency CALL 911” and a QR code for a “River Channel and Hazard Map”. You can either “Scan the code or visit go.nps.gov/tetonfloating”. The middle panel focuses on River Safety. The top two-thirds of the panel discusses river safety, shows an image of a river hazard, and goes over things to do before going on the river. Small black and white graphics advise of steps to take before going on the river. Text reads: River Safety The Snake River—always changing and challenging. This river can be dangerous. River channels shift week to week, currents are fast, the water is cold, and blocking hazards appear overnight. Respect the river, be prepared, and take responsibility for your own safety. Things to do before going on the river Check the weather forecast. Tell someone where you are going and when you expect to be back. Always wear a personal flotation device (PFD). Know your skill level. The bottom third of the panel discusses things to bring. A large circle is filled with purple graphics of items recommended to bring on the river. Items listed are a throw bag, first aid, whistle, drinking water and snacks, knife, layers, proper footwear, and a PFD. It sits on top of a photograph of a raft on the river with the Tetons in the background. The right-side panel is split into two panels stacked on top of one another. The top panel discusses things to know before going on the river. Small graphics indicate regulations and prohibited actions. A large photograph shows a river raft full of guests with a guide standing and pointing while floating down the river with trees in the background. Text reads: Things to know Park boating permit is required for all watercraft floating the Snake River. Boat permits and Aquatic Invasive Species decals are required for watercraft including kayaks, canoes, rafts, and stand-up paddle (SUP) boards, inflatable or hard-sided. Permits may be purchased at the Craig Thomas Discovery or Visitor Center in Moose or Colter Bay Visitor Center. AIS decals may be obtained through Wyoming Game and Fish licensed sellers or on the web, check wgfd.wyo.gov/ais. Fish requires a Wyoming fishing license. Park regulations can be obtained from visitor centers. Help preserve high quality angling for native wild fish. This is only a partial list of regulations. For more information consult Title 36 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) and the Superintendent’s Compendium available at go.nps.gov/tetonlaws. Pets are not allowed on the river or on park trails. Where permitted, pets must be leashed. Drones are prohibited in the park. Launching, landing, or operating unmanned aircraft, such as drones, is prohibited within Grand Teton National Park. Motorboats and inner tubes are prohibited. Camping and fires are prohibited along the river. Prevent the transport of nuisance species. Clean all equipment and remove any visible mud, plants, fish, or animals before transporting equipment. The bottom third of this panel is dedicated for park-related bulletins and has no text, graphics, or images. To the left of the panel are two brown metal bear boxes. They are about four feet high, six feet wide, and four feet deep. They have two doors each with a bear proof handle that you have to reach your hand under a covering to undo the latch. The bear boxes sit on an extended portion of the sidewalk. Just left of the bear boxes are bear proof recycling bins and trash can. The recycling bins are about four and half feet high with three doors at the top for plastic, glass, and aluminum. The trash can has one door at the top to dispose of waste. To the left of the trash cans is a three and a half foot tall post with a 6 inch in diameter pvc pipe attached. The opening of the pvc pipe at the top has rubber flaps that allow anglers to safely dispose of fishing line. South of the boat ramp, veering east, a paved sidewalk runs south towards the Snake River Bridge. If you veer west south of the boat ramp paved sidewalk runs along most of the eastern side of the parking lot.

Folks hand launching their vessels should use this location if launching from Moose Landing. Be aware of and respect both commercial and private boaters.

images.altText: A five and half foot tall vertical panel near a paved pathway.

images.caption: Explore Moose!

data.bodyText: Explore Moose! Not the animal, but the area. There is the Craig Thomas Discovery and Visitor Center, Moose Landing—where folks meet for their float trip, and the Moose Post Office. This panel and others at Moose Landing have maps to help you navigate and explore.
data.audioDescription: As you turn off of or walk across Teton Park Road to the Craig Thomas Discovery and Visitor Center, there is an informational panel along the paved pathway before the first turn into the parking lot. Next to the title small photograph of a bull moose standing in water and text about the distinction between the town and the animal. The text reads: Moose—the town or the animal? Once known as Menors Ferry, this area was renamed to Moose at the request of the U.S. Postal Service in 1929. Living up to its name, moose frequent the area. The shores of the Snake River, and the river itself, create suitable habitat for these water loving animals. Below are three photographs and text. Going left to right, the first photograph is of the inside of a visitor center with visitors walking around and looking at exhibits. At the bottom of the photograph, text reads: Craig Thomas Discovery and Visitor Center Enjoy the variety of exhibits, attend a ranger program, or watch a movie about the park. Various park permits are available. The next photograph is looking into a park store. Visitors are walking around looking at the different products. At the bottom of the photograph, text reads: Grand Teton Association Park Store Support the park by purchasing a souvenir from the Grand Teton Association Park Store, an official park partner. The final photograph is of people walking around the Moose Landing Plaza with trees and mountains in the background. At the bottom of the photograph, text reads: Moose Landing Meet here for your float trip and experience the park from the water. Exhibits display the different types of boats and wildlife found along the Snake River. The bottom two thirds of the panel is large map showing the Moose area. A yellow highlighted pathway shows the route to get to and from the Craig Thomas Discovery and Visitor Center to Moose Landing. Small black and white square graphics and labels mark the locations of restrooms, the post office, picnic tables, parking, boat ramp, hand launch, accessible parking spaces, and a trailhead. A text box marks your current location as “You Are Here”. The Snake River and Snake River bridge are on the right side map. Near the bottom right of the page is a photograph of an older couple in flannels standing outside. This is Mardy and Olaus Murie. Text below the photograph reads: Murie Ranch Start at the Murie Ranch Trailhead outside of the visitor center and walk the half mile to visit the home of influential conservationists, Mardy and Olaus Murie. The Murie Ranch is also accessible by car. The other side of the panel is nearly identical.

data.title: Moose Pathway Hub
data.listingDescription: Access and enjoy our multi-use pathway at the Moose Pathway Hub. This hub is situated along Teton Park Road in front of the Moose Post Office.

images.altText: Three informational panels in a wooden frame next to a paved pathway heading away from the viewer.
images.title: Moose Pathway Hub
images.caption: Walking, running, biking—plenty of ways to enjoy the multi-use pathway.

data.bodyText:
Access and enjoy our multi-use pathway at the Moose Pathway Hub. This hub is situated along Teton Park Road in front of the Moose Post Office. You can park at the post office or the nearby Craig Thomas Discovery and Visitor Center to access the multi-use path. Heading west along the pathway will bring you to the Moose Entrance Station. Please have a park pass ready or be prepared to purchase a pass (specific rates for walkers/bikers). Continue on the path along Teton Park Road to get to popular destinations like the Taggart Lake Trailhead and Jenny Lake. Heading east of the hub will take you to the underpass of US Highway 89/26/191, where the pathway heads 12 miles south to the town of Jackson. No matter the direction you head, you will have sweeping views of the Teton Range. 

For a complete overview of biking in the park and an interactive map, please check out our biking page on our website.

data.title: Moose Ponds
data.listingDescription: This two-mile round-trip hike takes you out to and around Moose Ponds. It has earned its namesake numerous times, with moose frequently seen in the water. The shallow water, full of vegetation, is the perfect riparian habit for the large ungulate.

images.altText: A moose stands in Moose Ponds with Teewinot mountain up high behind it.
images.title: Moose Ponds
images.caption: As it's name suggests, moose like to hang out at Moose Ponds.

data.bodyText:
From Jenny Lake, you can veer off the loop trail to Moose Ponds. This is a two-mile round-trip hike that takes you out to and around the ponds.

It has earned its namesake numerous times, with moose frequently seen in the water. The shallow water, full of vegetation, is the perfect riparian habit for the large ungulate.

While it is an amazing experience to witness moose in the wild, respect their space and stay 25 yards away.
data.audioDescription: Along the horse trail leading back to the main Jenny Lake visitor plaza from Hidden Falls is a small clearing that overlooks a basin below Teewinot Mountain with two ponds, known as Moose Ponds. Note a single, log rail fence at the edge of a rocky, sandy clearing at the edge of the hillside. Use caution here to remain behind the fence. This entire basin area is prime moose habitat. This wetland area supports a dense thicket of willows, with several aspen groves just above the wetlands, making this a great place to possibly spot a moose. You may notice a lot of beaver activity in the area as well, including downed trees and a beaver lodge on one of the ponds. Further on, the horse trail meets the head of the Moose Ponds loop trail, a moderate 3.4 mile (5.4 km) hike with an average 5% grade, numerous rocks, exposed tree roots, and approximately 20 stair steps total. The horse trail continues east back to the Jenny Lake boat launch and East Shore shuttle boat launch.

data.title: Moose Post Office
data.listingDescription: The Moose Post Office across the Teton Park Road from the Craig Thomas Discovery & Visitor Center, offers all USPS services but has limited hours.

images.altText: A brown wooden building with the wording Moose Post Office with trees and a flag surrounding it.
images.title: Moose Post Office
images.caption: Stop by to mail your postcards!

data.bodyText:
Located in Moose, Wyoming, the Moose Post Office is fully operational USPS location but it does have limited hours. Just bought a post card from the Craig Thomas Discovery and Visitor Center across the street? You can purchase stamps and mail it out from here. 

For hours and addtional information check the Moose Post Office web page.

Name Origin

The area known as Moose, Wyoming wasn't always called Moose, it actually started out as Menor's Ferry, referencing the nearby homestead and ferry operation of Bill Menor. But as the Jackson Hole Valley grew, the post office was built and was called the Moose Post Office. It was at that time in 1929 that small town of Menor's Ferry became known Moose. 

The area's namesake is also representive of its frequent visitor, the moose. The nearby Snake River and Sawmill Ponds makes the region perfect habitat for the large water-loving ungulate.

data.title: Moran Entrance Station
data.listingDescription: The Moran Entrance Station is one of four entrances to Grand Teton National Park. It is one of the first places where you will be prompted to pay an entrance fee since there is no fee to travel on US Highway 89/191/26.

images.altText: Multiple vehicles and a motorcycle line up outside of two entrance station booths.
images.title: Moran Entrance Station
images.caption: Welcome to Grand Teton National Park!

data.bodyText:
The Moran Entrance Station is one of four entrances to Grand Teton National Park. Coming from the town of Jackson, drive 30 miles north on US Highway 89/191/26 before turning west to continue on US Highway 89/191/287 to the northern area of the park and the south entrance of Yellowstone National Park. Continuing straight will take you on US Highway 26 towards the eastern border of the park and onto Dubois, WY. If coming from the town of Jackson or Dubois, you have already entered into the park's borders. Because there are no fees to travel on the highway, this is one of the first locations where you will be prompted to pay an entrance fee. 

No reservations are required to enter Grand Teton National Park but there are entrance fees. The park is open 24 hours a day, so if no one is at the entrance station when you arrive, you can drive through and pay your park fee online. 

Beyond the entrance station, the road will take you past Oxbow Bend, to Jackson Lake Junction (where you can make a loop by heading south on Teton Park Road, towards Jackson Lake Lodge and Colter Bay, or to the south entrance of Yellowstone. 

Name Origin

Landscape artist Thomas Moran accompanied the 1872 Hayden expedition into Yellowstone. Moran produced many sketches and watercolors introducing the Greater Yellowstone area to Easterners. He visited the west side of the Teton Range, but never saw the mountain named for him.

data.bodyText:
The buildings on Mormon Row tell the story of a once vibrant community. The Homestead Act of 1862 promised 160 acres to any person willing to build a house and cultivate the land for 5 years. This act enabled the settlement to come together. The promise of land eventually drew settlers to Mormon Row, originally known as Grovont in the 1890s. Healthy sagebrush indicated richer soil and drew the first Mormon families with hopes of beginning a new life. Forming a true community, they constructed ranches, homes, a church and a school,.

By the mid-1900s, many Mormon Row settlers sold their land and moved into Jackson other surrounding communities, and beyond.This land was later incorporated into Grand Teton National Park. You now see a landscape of sagebrush, cottonwood trees and quaking aspen. As you watch bison and pronghorn roaming the sagebrush flats, imagine the grazing cattle and hayfields filling the horizon.

Name Origin

Members from the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints spread north from Utah and homesteaded on the east side of Blacktail Butte in the 1890s. Known as Mormons, they settled the community known as Grovont and used their collective efforts to survive in the valley's harsh environment.

images.altText: Wayside sign for Mount Moran Turnout with sagebrush in foreground and Mount Moran in background.
images.caption: Mount Moran

data.bodyText:
Mount Moran, named for the famous landscape painter Thomas Moran, is the dominant peak of the northern Teton Range. The mountain also reflects all the geologic forces that formed the Teton Range. Ancient igneous and metamorphic rocks comprise the mountain core, sedimentary rocks drape the summit and Little Ice Age glaciers flank the slopes. The most noticeable feature is a vein (or dike) of black diabase that slices vertically across the east face of Mount Moran. The feature appears man-made, but molten magma squeezed into cracks in the existing bedrock almost a billion years ago. Later, erosion stripped away the surrounding rock allowing the dike to protrude.

Name Origin

Landscape artist Thomas Moran accompanied the 1872 Hayden expedition into Yellowstone. Moran produced many sketches and watercolors introducing the Greater Yellowstone area to Easterners. He visited the west side of the Teton Range, but never saw the mountain named for him.
data.audioDescription: This wayside sits at the edge of a cement semicircle next to the paved parking area. The curb has wheelchair access in the middle. The sign looks out over a flat sagebrush covered meadow with Mount Moran beyond. The background of the sign has a photograph of Mount Moran, the rocks tinged red by the sun with snowy patches. Text on the right side of the panel reads, "Mount Moran. Mt. Moran reflects all the geologic forces shaping the Teton Range. Formed of a massive block of metamorphic gneiss, cut by dikes of igneous granite and diabase, capped by sedimentary sandstone, and flanked by glaciers, this formidable peak dominates the park's northern skyline. "The gneiss and granite are among the oldest rocks in North America, 2.7 and 2.5 billion years old respectively. These resistant rocks form the core of the Teton Range. The vertical "Black Dike" of 775 million year old diabase is about 150 feet wide and juts from the mountain's face because the surrounding gneiss has eroded away." An inset photo in the lower left hand corner shows a close view of the tan-colored rocky summit of the mountain with a brown vertical strip down the middle. The caption reads, "Tan sandstone caps the summit of this massive peak the remnant of a 510 million year-old beach that stretched for hundreds of miles north and south of here. Sandstone overlies the Black Dike and other ancient igneous and metamorphic rocks." To the right of that another photo shows an icy patch below the summit, labeled "Falling Ice Glacier." The caption reads, "Five glaciers - Falling Ice, Skillet and Triple - flank Mount Moran. These glaciers formed during a cool period called the Little Ice Age that ended around 1850 AD. Over the past 40 years, the park's glaciers have shrunk by more than 20 percent due to our changing climate."

data.title: Mountain View Turnout
data.listingDescription: The Teton Range appears unchanging, but the opposite is true. The rocks found in the mountains formed hundreds of millions to billions of years ago. Movement on the Teton fault generated earthquakes that began to lift the mountains less than 10 million years ago. Ice age glaciers carved canyons and lakes. All the while, erosion due to water, wind and ice continue to sculpt the range, and any day another earthquake could violently change the landscape.

images.altText: Mountain View Turnout wayside surrounded by sagebrush. View of Mt. St. John to the left and Mt. Moran to the right.
images.caption: Young, Restless and Still Rising

data.bodyText: The Teton Range appears unchanging, but the opposite is true. The rocks found in the mountains formed hundreds of millions to billions of years ago. Movement on the Teton fault generated earthquakes that began to lift the mountains less than 10 million years ago. Ice age glaciers carved canyons and lakes. All the while, erosion due to water, wind and ice continue to sculpt the range, and any day another earthquake could violently change the landscape.
data.audioDescription: This wayside sits at the edge of a paved semicircle with an accessible ramp from the parking area. The sign looks out over a meadow dotted with patches of dark conifers and the flat summit and rocky sides of Mount Moran in the background. The background of the sign has a photograph of Mount Moran, the rocks tinged red by the sun with patches of snow and glaciers on its slopes. Text on the left side of the panel reads, "Young, Restless and Still Rising. Imagine the Teton Range and the valley in front of you like two parts of a giant hinge. The Earth's crust stretches and breaks into two blocks along the 40-mile long Teton fault. Fractures generate large earthquakes along the fault. The western block hinges up and becomes the Teton Range." "The eastern block tilts down and forms the valley. As the mountains rise, wind, water, and ice wear down the jagged skyline and erode away sandstone and limestone layers from the east side of the range. The landscape continues to change. Geoscientists predict future earthquakes up to a 7.5 magnitude." In the bottom left is an illustration showing the Teton Range with an orange line along its eastern base indicating the line of the Teton Fault. A vertical cutaway shows the land underneath the range rising and the land to the east subsiding. In the bottom right hand corner is a drawing showing a close-up view of Mount St. John and Mount Moran with the Teton Fault line at their base marked in yellow. A caption reads, "Young Range, Old Rocks. The Teton Range is one of the youngest mountain ranges in North America, but the rocks are some of the oldest. The stretching-cracking-tilting that formed the Tetons began about nine million years ago. In contrast, geologic forces squeezed the Earth's crust and thrust up the Rockies ending around 55 million years ago."

data.bodyText:
In 1945, the Muries bought the STS Ranch, with Adolph and Louise living in the original building now known as the Homestead. In 1926, the Murie brothers began their master's degree programs at the University of Michigan in the young science of ecology. While Olaus' studies were a one-year break in his Biological Survey work, Adolph completed his Ph.D. with a firm commitment to the value of all wildlife.

Through his career as a wildlife biologist, Adolph's research challenged long-standing values in wildlife management. His groundbreaking studies on carnivores opened the door to our modern understanding of predator-prey relationships. His 1937 study of coyotes in Yellowstone National Park was the first serious predator study in the park service's history. His findings ignited a controversy by stating the value of all species and condemning the ongoing practice of killing coyotes in the park.

Adolph served as Grand Teton National Park's only biologist throughout the 1950s. Even as they held long assignments in Alaska and other places during Adolph's thirty-year Park Service career, the Homestead cabin at the Ranch remained Adolph and Louise's home base.
data.audioDescription: This building is a long, low log cabin with a grey metal roof, set on a stone foundation. A wide stone chimney rises towards the back of the roof, right of center. The walls are built of smooth logs with small wooden poles used as chinking. The ends of the logs are painted green. The covered entrance is in the center of the building. The windows are small and located just under the roofline - two on the right side and one on the left side of the door. At the far left end of the building is a section where the top half of the wall is screened in. On the wall to the right of the door are two plaques. The top one is of metal and reads, "Original Buster Estes Homestead Cabin, 1920-1945. Home of Adolph and Louise Murie, 1945-1974. Restoration by The Murie Center. Exterior funded by The National Park Foundation through a generous gift from Aurora Foods, Inc. Log Cabin Brand." The sign below reads, "The Murie Ranch Historic District was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on August 24, 1998, due to its importance to the American Conservation Movement. Preservation of the Murie Ranch Historic District is being supported in part by a federal Save America's Treasures award administered by the National Park Service, Department of the Interior. Thanks go to the patrons of The Murie Center for supporting this rehabilitation effort to recreate the magic of the early years on the Murie Ranch and continue to influence the conservation movement."

data.title: Murie Ranch
data.listingDescription: Brothers Olaus and Adolph Murie married sisters Margaret and Louise and acquired the STS Ranch in 1945. The Ranch, later known as the Murie Ranch, became the setting for their research, writings, and gatherings. Through science, art and writing, the Muries captured and personified the spirit of wilderness, inspiring generations to visit the Murie Ranch and become advocates of wild places. Olaus and Adolph Murie were pioneering wildlife biologists.

images.caption: Murie Ranch Office

data.bodyText:
Brothers Olaus and Adolph Murie married sisters Margaret and Louise and acquired the STS Ranch in 1945. The Ranch, later known as the Murie Ranch, became the setting for their research, writings, and gatherings. Through science, art and writing, the Muries captured and personified the spirit of wilderness, inspiring generations to visit the Murie Ranch and become advocates of wild places. Olaus and Adolph Murie were pioneering wildlife biologists. Their innovative studies helped move wildlife management toward holistic management of ecosystems rather than the promotion of individual species.

Today the Murie Ranch is part of the Teton Science Schools offering extended learning opportunities for adults. For more information please visit the Murie Ranch website.

images.altText: A historic log cabin in a forest
images.title: Murie Ranch
images.caption: The Muries' historic log home is one of several cabins and buildings preserved at Murie Ranch.

data.bodyText:
From the Craig Thomas Discovery and Visitor Center, enjoy an easy one‑mile round‑trip stroll to the historic Murie Ranch. Parking is available at the visitor center. The trail begins just behind the Moose statue outside the visitor center.

The Murie Ranch was once the home of Olaus and Mardy Murie, two of the most influential leaders in the American conservation movement. Their research, writing, and advocacy helped shape modern ideas about protecting wild places and expanding America’s public lands.

For decades, this rustic homestead served as a gathering place for scientists, writers, and environmental leaders. Here, they shared ideas and worked together on major conservation efforts. Discussions at the ranch helped inspire landmark laws such as the Wilderness Act of 1964 and the Alaska Lands Act of 1980. Together, these acts permanently protected millions of acres of federal land and strengthened the foundation of American wilderness conservation.

Today, the Murie Ranch is recognized as a National Historic Landmark, honoring the Muries’ lasting legacy in protecting some of the nation’s most treasured landscapes.

During the summer, you can join a daily docent‑led tour of the ranch. Check the park calendar for current times and details.
data.audioDescription: Murie Ranch is a small historic homestead set in a level forest of lodgepole pine near Moose, Wyoming. The site consists of about fifteen one‑story log buildings, spaced irregularly across a gently open woodland. Most buildings are simple rectangular cabins made of weathered, horizontal logs with shingled roofs. Several have small front porches with wooden steps and railings.

data.bodyText: In 1945 the Murie families jumped at the opportunity to purchase this ranch from Buster and Frances Estes. Buster was a local cowboy while Frances came from a wealthy Philadelphia family. She first came to Jackson Hole as a guest at the Bar B C Dude Ranch where Buster worked.. Olaus and Mardy moved to the ranch one year later and lived in the Alatna cabin before purchasing the adjacent Woodbury home in 1947. The STS Ranch provided accommodations for many gatherings of the Wilderness Society during Olaus' leadership and provided a home base for writers and activists. With numerous cabins from the dude ranch days, every summer saw many guests, relatives and friends. As Mardy observed: "every conservationist or fiend of a conservationist came to stay."

data.bodyText:
In 1927, Olaus and Mardy Murie moved to Jackson Hole where the federal government assigned him to study the valley's famous elk herd. He published his extensive field research in the book, The Elk of North America. Based on his scientific understanding of elk movements, Olaus lobbied for an expansion of Grand Teton national Pak to account for elk migration through Jackson Hole. Eventually, park boundaries were expanded to include, not just the rugged mountains, but also the valley floor.
During this time, Olaus also conducted studies of coyotes and mice and continued drawing and painting wildlife. He wrote numerous scientific papers and books, one being, "Field Guide to Animal Tracks" (1954) which is still in print today and a valued tracking classic.

data.title: Outlet Overlook
data.listingDescription: Outlet Overlook offers visitors another opportunity to view the beauty of Jenny Lake while learning about the area's indigenous history.

images.altText: View Jenny Lake while learning about the indigenous history of the area.
images.title: Outlet Overlook
images.caption: Indigenous history in this area dates back to more than 11,000 years ago.

data.bodyText:
Outlet Overlook offers visitors another opportunity to view the beauty of Jenny Lake while learning about the area's indigenous history.

Tribes like Shoshone, Crow, Bannock, Blackfoot, Flathead, Nez Perce, and Gros Ventre continue to use their ancestral lands to hunt, fish, and gather plants used in traditional foods, medicines, and ceremonies.

Learn about traditional foods and clothing, the Tribal Youth Corps, and ancient campsites as you read the interpretive signs overlooking the shore. Discover the origin of how "Jenny" Lake got its name. 

From this location you can continue north along the paved path for more lakeshore views and acces or head south to reach the shuttle boat area.
data.audioDescription: Outlet Overlook is located about 200 yards (180 m) west from the main Jenny Lake visitor plaza along the south branch of the Discovery Trail. A 30-foot wide by 15-foot deep semi-circular area paved with flat granite stones overlooks the roughly oval Jenny Lake in front of you. Over two miles (3.5 km) long by 1.2 miles (1.9 km) wide, the lake is situated at the base of the Teton Range at the mouth of Cascade Canyon. The pristine waters of the lake act as a mirror, reflecting the surrounding peaks and evergreen forests that reach all the way down to the rocky shoreline. The crystal-clear water also makes it easy to see fish and the rocky lakebed. At the back center of the overlook, an eight-foot wide by three-foot deep, bronze, tactile map of the Teton Range sits atop a gap in a low, three-foot tall granite block wall. Touch the map to feel the peaks, identified by raised letters along the front of the map spelling out their names. Jenny Lake is located in the front of the map in the center, marked with a raised star and the words, “You Are Here.” Reach further back on the map to touch the other lakes and canyons of the park, also identified with raised letters. Across the six-inch tall, front vertical face of the map, additional raised letters list the latitude (43.752) and longitude (-110.724) of Jenny Lake at the left, and its elevation at the right: 6,786 feet (2,068 m). A note at the front of the map states that some major peaks, including Grand Teton, are not visible from here. At the far right of the overlook, a second, smaller inclined, rectangular metal information panel sits atop the low, granite wall. A photograph at the left side of the panel shows three American Indian men in the valley below the Tetons dressed in long, brightly colored leather robes and moccasins. They are each adorned with elaborate, feather headdresses, beaded belts, and carry large, feather fans. Text reads: Legacy on the Land American Indians have been well-established on this land for thousands of years. Shoshone, Crow, Bannock, Blackfoot, Flathead, Nez Perce, and Gros Ventre tribes continue to use their ancestral lands to hunt, fish, and gather plants used in traditional foods, medicines, and ceremonies. Many tribal groups have strong spiritual connections to this place, including using several locations in the Teton Range as Vision Quest sites. A second color photograph in the center shows a field of tall, green stalks covered with long, lavender-petaled flowers. A caption reads: The roots of Camas flowers are a traditional food still used by modern tribes. In a third color photograph at the far right, a half-dozen native youth dressed in jeans, matching green T-shirts, work boots, and hard hats stand in an open field. Text below reads: Building Connections The Tribal Youth Corps fosters connections between native communities and the lands their ancestors called home. Students work on infrastructure and preservation projects in exchange for housing and educational credits. At the far left of this overlook, a third, inclined, rectangular metal information panel spans a gap in the low, granite wall. In the center, text on a blue field reads: A Lake Named Jenny Jenny Leigh, a Shoshone Indian, assisted the 1872 Hayden Survey. The expedition named this lake in her honor. Jenny and her husband Richard were expert guides who knew Jackson Hole well from summers spent hunting, trapping, and gathering native plants here. A black-and-white photograph at the far left shows Jenny Leigh sitting on the ground at a tipi door with three of her six children. At the top of the photograph, an 1873 quote by Frank H. Bradley in the Hayden Survey Report reads: About a mile south of Leigh’s Lake, another, of about the same size, which we have called Jennie’s Lake, after Mrs. Leigh, lies in the Mouth of the Great Canon of the Teton Range. Moving to the center of the panel, a color photograph shows the sun glinting over a mountaintop through a small stand of pine trees by a rocky shoreline. Text reads: Ancient Campsites Jenny Leigh’s Shoshone ancestors first passed through this area mote than 10,000 years ago. Tribal groups made seasonal camps on the peninsula in front of you, spending summers hunting, fishing, picking berries, and gathering roots. Shoshone people and other American Indian groups still have strong connections to this place today. At the far right of the panel is a pair of bronzed, Shoshone women’s moccasins, which you may touch. Feel the design on the top of the instep. A caption reads: The “Shoshone Rose” design is characteristic of many Shoshone moccasins, in contrast to the geometric designs used by Plains Indians. From this location, you may continue south along the flat, asphalt path toward the shuttle boat launch, or north to the Teewinot Overlook, Rock Beach, and Aspen Knoll, or move back east along the Discovery Trail to the main Jenny Lake plaza. Along the path leading south toward the boat launch, note another wide area paved with flat granite stones overlooking the lake with a line of large, granite boulders at the back. A gap in the center of the boulders opens to a small, granite stairway leading down to the water’s edge with no handrails. There is a low, wooden bench on the flat, stone-paved area at the top of the stairway, just south of the opening.

data.title: Oxbow Bend Turnout
data.listingDescription: A channel of the Snake River "bends" towards the turnout with the water often reflecting the towering Mount Moran in the background. Year round, Oxbow Bend has some of the most iconic views of the Teton Range.

images.altText: A sign saying Oxbow Bend with cars parked in the foreground and Mount Moran in the background.
images.title: Oxbow Bend
images.caption: Sweeping views and bountiful wildlife make this turnout an iconic stop in the park.

data.bodyText:
While there are countless breathtaking views of the Teton Range throughout the park, Oxbow Bend is one of the most iconic. A channel of the Snake River "bends" towards the turnout with the water often reflecting the towering Mount Moran in the background. Year-round, this location provides stunning views of scenery AND wildlife. Trumpeter swans, otters, beavers, and bears are some of the animals occasionally seen from this turnout. What did you love most about the view?

Name Origin

Geologically speaking, an oxbow forms when a meander channel is cut off from the main stream forming a pond.
data.audioDescription: This turnout sits on top of a high bank overlooking the Snake River below. The river sweeps away from you in both directions, forming a sharp bend called an oxbow. The other side of the river is thickly wooded. The side you are on has more open flat land with shrubs and a few trees on the bank in front of you. There is a large meadow to the left, to the right is a stand of Aspen trees. In the distance to the right Mt Moran towers over the landscape. There are two wayside signs along this turnout. The one on the left has a large picture of two moose in the river, one with antlers. The text reads, "Spot Any Wetlands Wildlife? This oxbow bend in the Snake River provides food, water, shelter, and nesting sites for wildlife. Plants thrive in the sediments and shallow waters. Moose browse on willows and tender plants. Mergansers, teals, and white pelicans feed on aquatic life. Playful otters swim and dive. Ospreys and bald eagles soar above the river searching for food. Beavers gnaw on saplings to build lodges or dams. In the quiet backwater, cutthroat trout rise to the surface, and great blue herons fish in the shallows." In the upper right corner is an inset photo of an American White pelican. In the lower left are 4 inset photos, left to right of two beavers, Trumpeter swans and Canada geese, a river otter, and a cutthroat trout. Towards the right end of the paved area, another wayside is titled "11,000 Summers in the Tetons." The background shows a black-and-white picture of Indians on Jackson Lake, a 1930s oil painting by Herbert A. Collins. The painting shows about fifteen American Indian figures, men, women, and children at a camp on the edge of a lake with the mountains in the background. Some of the people are around a large campfire; others dress an antelope carcass. Two teepees stand on the edge of the lake. The text reads, "This slow-moving channel of the Snake River at Oxbow Bend sustains many different animals. Every year thousands of visitors come here to see them. Like you, Indian tribes such as Shoshone, Bannock, Blackfoot, Crow, Nez Perce and Gros Ventre have been drawn to places like this for more than 11,000 years. American Indians ventured into this valley as glaciers receded. They came to Jackson Hole in the spring to hunt game, and harvest roots and berries. They collected soapstone for bowls, obsidian for projectile points, and quartzite for tools and roasting hearths. As winter approached, they left their summer home in the Teton Range for warmer places."

data.title: Pacific Creek Boat Launch
data.listingDescription: Informational panels on river safety are located at the launch area for you and your group to review. You will find resources like a map, things to do before going on the water, things to bring, and things to know.

images.altText: A paved road leads to a boat ramp where a truck unloads. There are trees and river in the back.
images.title: Pacific Creek Boat Ramp
images.caption: Start your Snake River adventure here!

data.bodyText:
The Snake River winds through the valley floor carrying snowmelt from the mountains westward toward the Pacific Ocean. This river is an artery of the park that offers stunning views of the Tetons. Many species of wildlife use the river, from the browsing moose to the industrious beaver. Whether you are fishing, viewing wildlife, or enjoying the scenery, floating on this river is an unforgettable experience. Pacific Creek Landing is a popular take-out location for people doing a short trip from the dam. Past Pacific Creek Landing, the river becomes faster and more braided requiring more advanced navigation skills.

The course this river follows is not straightforward. It travels in and out of numerous channels that change every year. This is a powerful river that requires river reading and navigation skills. Before you float, know what skills you need to float the river, where you are going, and what things you need. 

Informational panels on river safety are located at the launch area for you and your group to review. You will find resources like a map, things to do before going on the water, things to bring, and things to know.

For a complete overview of boating rules, regulations, and permit requirements, please review our webpage on boating and floating before getting out on the water.

Additional information about floating the Snake River, including an interactive map, is available too.

Permits and Regulations

To meet the permit requirements for Grand Teton National Park you must:

  • Have a Grand Teton Boat Permit

  • Have a valid Wyoming AIS Decal

  • Complete an AIS inspection

Grand Teton Boat Permit

All boats are required to have a Grand Teton Boat Permit prior to launching on any of the park’s waters. Permits are required for all motorized and non-motorized boats, including stand-up paddleboards (SUPs) and windsurfing boards. Privately owned vessels must register each year with Grand Teton National Park. Permits may be purchased on Recreation.gov or at the visitor centers in Moose or Colter Bay during summer operations. Boaters can also have their permit mailed directly to them within two weeks.

Wyoming AIS Decal


PREVENT THE SPREAD OF PATHOGENS - CLEAN. DRAIN. DRY.
All watercraft using Wyoming waters are required to display a Wyoming Aquatic Invasive Species decal. The decal can be purchased online at the Wyoming Game and Fish Department website or from a variety of local vendors. Additionally, all boats entering the park must stop for an Aquatic Invasive Species (AIS) inspection. By law, boats coming from out of state must be inspected or have valid proof of inspection before they launch on waters in Wyoming, including waters in the park. This includes motorized boats, rafts, drift boats, canoes, kayaks, stand-up paddle boards, and all watercraft 10 feet and longer. Aquatic Invasive Species, such as whirling disease and zebra or quagga mussels, are a serious ecological and economic threat to the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. Boats, waders, and anything else that comes in contact with a body of water has the potential to spread non-native plants, pathogens, and other invasive species among water bodies. Make sure to clean, drain, dry, all boating and fishing equipment after use.Learn more about preventing the spread of AIS.

Note: Non-motorized inflatable watercraft 10 feet or less in length, all solid and inflatable paddleboards regardless of length, and all devices defined as water sport toys are exempt from the Wyoming State AIS Decal requirement.
 

Stretches of River

Beginner
Jackson Lake Dam to Pacific Creek 5 miles
This stretch features scenic views, calmer water and few obstructions. At Pacific Creek landing the water is swift, boaters should scout this landing prior to launching.

Intermediate
Pacific Creek to Deadmans Bar 10 miles
This section drops significantly creating swift water and braided channels requiring careful route-finding.

Flagg Ranch to Lizard Creek Campground 10 miles
The braided channels make route-finding a challenge. The river winds for 6 miles before reaching Jackson Lake. Depending on the lake level, the trip is another 4 miles to Lizard Creek Campground. Strenuous rowing or paddling may be required. Afternoon thunderstorms and winds produce waves that may swamp canoes. Motors may be used on Jackson Lake.

Advanced
Deadman’s Bar to Moose Landing 10 miles
This is the most challenging stretch of river in the park, many accidents occur here. The river drops more steeply and the current increases. Complex braiding may obscure the main channel and strong currents can sweep boaters into side channels blocked by logjams.

Moose to Wilson 14 miles
This section of the river is as difficult as the preceding section. Advanced boating skills are required due to fast current, braided channels and logjams. The park extends 5 miles downstream from Moose on the west bank and 2 miles downstream on the east bank. There is no take-out or access to the river at the park boundary. The next take-out is at the Snake River Bridge east of Wilson, WY, 14 miles downstream from Moose.

Use our advanced Snake River Map on our website for more route details.

images.altText: A plaza overlooking the river with a large rock with a bronze sign in the front with trees.
images.title: Pacific Creek Landing
images.caption: Enjoy a perfect afternoon float from Jackson Lake Dam to Pacific Creek Landing.

data.bodyText: Pacific Creek Landing is a popular put-in and take-out location for boaters recreating on the Snake River. Maybe you start at Jackson Lake Dam for an afternoon float and take out here. Or maybe you begin your river adventure at this scenic river access point with plans to float to Deadmans Bar or Moose Landing. Beyond river adventures, a rich ecosystem of plants and animals thrives in and around the river. Designated parking is available for boat trailers. Pit toilets are open in the summer.
data.audioDescription: Turning off Highway 89/191 into the Pacific Creek Landing area takes you into a large parking lot roughly 300 feet east to west and 150 feet north to south. The southern edge of the parking lot is lined with approximately 40 single-vehicle spaces and a four-foot-wide sidewalk, with simple single-log wooden fencing running along the outer edge. The sidewalk and fencing run west towards the restrooms, plaza overlook, and boat ramp. The center of the parking lot has roughly 25 spaces for vehicles with trailers. At the western edge of the parking lot, the paved lot turns into a road that loops down to the boat ramp and back to the parking lot with an island of native trees, shrubs, and grasses in the middle. This loop is about two-thirds the length of the main parking lot. In the middle of the parking lot and boat ramp loop is a circular pavement slab with a large industrial dumpster. South of the dumpster and the western end of the parking lot sidewalk are the restrooms. The restrooms are housed in a light brown wooden building with dark brown wooden features and an A-frame roof. An alcove extends about five feet out of the building. There are two doors with a single restroom in each. The left door has a toilet with no seat, just a hole in the floor that you squat over. The right restroom is a traditional pit toilet. Signs on the outside of the doors indicate that either sex can use either restroom. To the west of the restrooms are the bike racks designed as five curved steel tubular features about three feet high. 20 feet west of the restrooms and parking lot is a two-foot-wide by three-and-a-half-foot-tall bronze panel, vertically positioned a few feet off the ground against a five-foot-tall granite boulder speckled with shades of white, black, and grey. The bronze panel displays a map of Grand Teton National Park’s waterways, text, and other symbols, all engraved into bronze that you can touch and feel. The engraving depicts the location of the Snake River and the various lakes within the park. The map is oriented running north to south. Small diamond-shaped engravings near the waterways indicate the locations of other boat launches, such as Pacific Creek, Deadmans Bar, and Moose Landing. Next to the Pacific Creek diamond marker is a star and text that reads, “You Are Here”. At the top of the panel, a small arrow points north above text that reads, “To Yellowstone National Park (39 miles, 44km)”. At the bottom of the panel, located next to the Snake River engraving, a small arrow points in the southwest direction below text that reads, “To Pacific Ocean (1201 miles, 1933 km)”. The words, “Pacific Creek” run vertically along the left side of the panel in extra-large text. The panel bends 90 degrees around the left side of the rock and is approximately one-third the width of the front side. A small panel on the bronze has silhouettes of willow branches in the background with text that reads: Bia Ogwaide (Shoshone) “Pavahuude (Bannock)” “big flow” Snake River This land and river, with all the plants and animals, hold special cultural significance to today’s Shoshone, Bannock, Blackfoot, Crow, Flathead, Gros Ventre, Nez Perce, and other tribes. This is part of the tribes’ ancestral homelands. These waters flow to the Pacific Ocean and this is one of the most free-flowing sections of the entire river. Congress passed laws—the Wild & Scenic Rivers Act and Grand Teton National Park’s enabling legislation—that help protect and preserve the Snake River. Engraved in the bottom right corner is a five-inch-tall branch of a willow plant and text that reads: Pacific Creek Landing revitalization was made possible by public-private partnership between Grand Teton National Park and Grand Teton National Park Foundation. Private philanthropy leveraged national park foundation funds authorized by the National Park Service Centennial Act of 2016. To the right, the sidewalk runs 150 feet towards the boat ramp.

data.title: Path of the Pronghorn Turnout
data.listingDescription: Pronghorn and bison frequent the sagebrush meadows before you during the summer. Pronghorn are the fastest land animal in North America sprinting to speeds of 60 mph (96 kph). As winter sets in, pronghorn (also known as pronghorn antelope) migrate southeast on the second-longest terrestrial migration in North America. They encounter many obstacles along their route including fences and roads. Studying their migration has led to efforts to protect this pathway.

images.altText: Path of the pronghorn wayside with view looking across sagebrush meadows of Anetlope Flats toward Blacktail Butte and the Teton Range
images.caption: Path of the Pronghorn with Teton Range

data.bodyText:
Pronghorn and bison frequent the sagebrush meadows before you during the summer. Pronghorn are the fastest land animal in North America sprinting to speeds of 60 mph (96 kph). As winter sets in, pronghorn (also known as pronghorn antelope) migrate southeast on the second-longest terrestrial migration in North America. They encounter many obstacles along their route including fences and roads. Studying their migration has led to efforts to protect this pathway.

Name Origin

Pronghorn ( Antilocapra americana ) also known as antelope are the fastest terrestrial animal in North America, and have the second longest migration! They can sprint 60 mph and sustain over 40 mph for one mile! After spending summers in the sagebrush flats along the base of the Teton Range, they migrate up to 150 miles south and east up the Gros Ventre drainage and down past Pinedale, WY. Fences are a significant barrier to migration. Pronghorn are reluctant to jump fences and will generally crawl under them.
data.audioDescription:
This wayside overlooks a sweeping sagebrush flat flanked by hills and mountains in the distance. The left side of the sign shows a map of the pronghorn migration route. At the bottom right of the sign is a photo of a pronghorn's head, clearly showing the horns with a sharp curve at the ends. The caption reads, "Pronghorn are named for their forked, hollow horns, being the only animal to annually shed a branched horn. Pronghorn are the fastest land mammal in North America."

The main text in the upper right of the sign reads, "The pronghorn that summer in Jackson Hole make the longest terrestrial mammal migration remaining in the contiguous United States. Pronghorn use migration as an adaptation for surviving the long Wyoming winters by moving to where they can find food and avoid deep snow.

"The southward fall migration usually occurs during November, with animals returning to northern summer ranges in late April and May. Round-trip migration distances for this her range from 200 - 300 miles annually.

"A Threatened Migration? History has shown that migrations are fragile. Three quarters of pronghorn migrations in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem have already been lost to land development. Further development could threaten the future of this remaining corridor."

The map on the left shows a red area covering the eastern side of Grand Teton National Park marking the pronghorn's summer range. This wayside is located on the eastern edge of that range, about two-thirds of the way down. From this point the migration path is shown as a red line moving east and then south, into the Green River Basin past the intersection of US Highways 189 and 191. There the winter range is shown as another red area. The caption reads, "Jackson Hole pronghorn migrate along an ancient corridor to Green River basin wintering areas near Pinedale, Wyoming. Archaeological evidence of pronghorn at Trapper's Point dates back 6,000 years."

Smaller photos show a small herd in a meadow during summer and a larger group moving through belly-deep snow in winter.

data.title: Potholes Turnout
data.listingDescription: This odd stand of conifer trees took root in a depression within the sagebrush flats. Locals called these depressions "potholes" while other regions of the country call these features "kettles." As ice-age glaciers retreated, blocks of ice dropped from the glacier's face onto the valley floor. Sediment carried by meltwater buried the ice. Later, the ice melted leaving behind a depression. Water may pond in pothole, and spring runoff and wind may carry sediment into the hole. With time, a pothole develops a micro-ecosystem supporting trees and accompanying wildlife-providing a shady respite from the exposure of the sagebrush flats.

images.altText: Looking past the Pothole Wayside sign toward a stand of conifer trees surrounded by sagebrush
images.caption: Potholes Turnout

data.bodyText:
This odd stand of conifer trees took root in a depression within the sagebrush flats. Locals called these depressions "potholes" while other regions of the country call these features "kettles." As ice-age glaciers retreated, blocks of ice dropped from the glacier's face onto the valley floor. Sediment carried by meltwater buried the ice. Later, the ice melted leaving behind a depression. Water may pond in pothole, and spring runoff and wind may carry sediment into the hole. With time, a pothole develops a micro-ecosystem supporting trees and accompanying wildlife-providing a shady respite from the exposure of the sagebrush flats.

Name Origin

Potholes, also known as kettles, are depressions in the glacial outwash plain. A pothole forms when an ice chunk breaks off a retreating glacier and lands on the plain. Run-off sediments deposit around the ice and may bury the ice. After the ice melts, a depression is left behind. This depression forms a micro-environment trapping moisture and dust allowing trees to take root.
data.audioDescription:
This wayside sits at the edge of the paved parking area and looks roughly southward over a flat plain. Here and there are small patches of dark conifer woods. A paved trail leads to your left towards one such patch.

The right side of the panels is filled with an aerial view of the area showing a pockmarked landscape, some of the indentations with trees or ponds in their bottom. Text reads, "Potholes. Curious depressions known as "Potholes,' dimple the glacial outwash plain here. Some 15,000 years ago, sediment carried by glacial meltwater buried huge blocks of ice that calved off retreating glaciers. As the ice melted, the ground sank leaving depressions behind known locally as â€˜potholes,' but known more commonly as â€˜kettles.'

"Kettles are bowl-shaped and range in size from 15 feet to Â¼ mile in diameter. These depressions begin as steep-sided features but wind and water smooth the edges and deposit sediment in the bottom.

"Trees take root in some kettles creating forest islands, while water pools in other kettles forming tiny wetland communities. On the semi-arid outwash plain, these islands provide food and shelter for a variety of wildlife.

"Kettles are fragile, isolated ecosystems under constant stress from human impacts. Essentially fossil icebergs, the Potholes here relate to kettles found in other glaciated regions of North America providing insight into our changing environment.

"A short Â¼-mile trail leads around the forested Pothole nearby."

data.title: Preserving a Legacy
data.listingDescription:
The Burt family lived in this cabin for many summers on the ranch. Their son, Nathaniel, was even born on the kitchen table one winter. Several other people and families cared for the Bar BC over the decades, including Horace Carncross, Struthers Burt's original partner; Irving Corse and his family, who took the ranch over from the Burts; Peggy Conderman of the neighboring 4 Lazy F Ranch; and Margaretta Sharpless, Irving Corse's widow. The Western Center for Historic Preservation and Grand Teton National Park, in partnership with the Grand Teton National Park Foundation, are working on a multi-year project to stabilize and preserve this cabin and other buildings here, so that visitors can continue to enjoy them and learn about the Bar BC.

Though the families who lived here and the guests who came to stay are gone, their legacy remains in these buildings, the beginnings of tourism in Jackson Hole, and the formation of Grand Teton National Park. Visitors to the valley today experience the same wonder and joy at the high peaks, the cool swimming holes, and the novelty of Western life. Though the dudes and wranglers have left, and these cabins are now empty, you can still explore the Bar BC and imagine the experiences they had here.

Excerpt from "Diary of a Dude Wrangler": "I have a thousand and one golden memories as well as a thousand and one tales. Memories of faces and voices and laughter, of rides and camps and loveliness seen in company. Of crisp mornings when snow-clad peaks soared against blue skies with the still whiteness of gigantic pelicans, of nights when the moon, coming up behind the sleeping ranges to the east, picked out for a moment a ragged pine, and made isolation suddenly another companion, and flooded the sage-brush with light so that you saw ambergris floating in a sea of silver.
